UrbanSip should combine these findings with a larger, more representative survey of commuters and updated rail-journey data. This would allow it to test whether enough commuters value insulation and are willing to pay £28 before selecting social media, railway stations, or both. Using several sources reduces uncertainty, although it cannot guarantee that the launch will succeed.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: A UK coffee-shop chain wants feedback from its loyalty-app customers before changing its rewards scheme.
question.stem: Which method is an example of random sampling?

options.label: A
options.text: The chain selects every customer who visits its busiest city-centre branch on Saturday morning.

options.label: B
options.text: The chain uses a computer to select customers at random from its complete loyalty-app customer list, with each customer having a known chance of selection.

options.label: C
options.text: The chain chooses enough respondents from each age group until set targets for the groups are filled.

options.label: D
options.text: The chain emails a survey only to customers who made a purchase in the previous week.

option_rationale: A is a convenience-based selection of accessible customers at one place and time, rather than a random selection from the target group.
B is correct because customers are selected from the full list using a method that gives each customer a known chance of being chosen.
C describes quota sampling because predetermined category targets are filled.
D excludes customers who have not recently purchased, so it is not a random selection of all loyalty-app customers.
mark_scheme.model_answer: : B

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Northshore Leisurewear is planning to survey customers before introducing a new range of walking jackets. Its customer database shows that 60% of customers are aged under 40 and 40% are aged 40 or over. The marketing manager wants responses from both age groups.
question.stem: Explain one difference between stratified sampling and quota sampling that Northshore Leisurewear could use when selecting customers for its survey.

points.descriptor: Identifies or explains stratified sampling as dividing the customer population into relevant subgroups, such as the two age groups.
accept: A sample is selected from each age group.
Customers are grouped by age before the sample is chosen.

points.descriptor: Applies stratified sampling to Northshore Leisurewear by selecting customers from each age group in proportion to the database, for example 60% under 40 and 40% aged 40 or over.
accept: A sample of 100 could include 60 customers under 40 and 40 customers aged 40 or over.
The age composition of the sample reflects Northshore's customer database.

points.descriptor: Identifies or explains quota sampling as setting a required number of responses for categories, without necessarily selecting customers randomly within each category.
accept: The business sets targets for each age group.
Researchers fill age-group response targets using available respondents.
Selection within each category does not have to be random.

points.descriptor: Applies quota sampling to Northshore Leisurewear, for example by collecting responses until it has reached its target number from under-40s and from customers aged 40 or over.
accept: Staff could approach customers until the quota for each age group is full.
Northshore could stop surveying an age group once its set number of responses has been obtained.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Stratified sampling would divide Northshore's customers into age groups and select respondents from each group in the same proportions as its database. For example, in a sample of 100 customers, 60 could be under 40 and 40 could be aged 40 or over. Quota sampling would set a required number of responses from each age group, but staff could fill these quotas using available customers rather than selecting customers randomly within each group.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice. GreenThread Clothing is considering launching a repair subscription for its customers. It surveys 600 customers chosen from its full customer database. The survey estimates that 48% would be likely to subscribe, with a confidence interval of 44% to 52%.
question.stem: Explain what the confidence interval means for GreenThread Clothing’s estimate of customer interest in the repair subscription.

points.descriptor: Identifies that a confidence interval is a range used to show uncertainty around a result from a sample.
accept: A range around a sample estimate.
It shows that the 48% figure is not an exact value for all customers.
A range expressing sampling uncertainty.

points.descriptor: Applies the interval correctly to GreenThread’s survey result.
accept: The estimate of likely subscribers is between 44% and 52%.
The true proportion of GreenThread customers likely to subscribe may be within the range 44% to 52%, subject to the survey assumptions.
48% is the central estimate, but the result could reasonably vary from 44% to 52%.

points.descriptor: Explains that the interval indicates the precision of the sample estimate.
accept: The 8-percentage-point-wide range shows there is uncertainty caused by surveying a sample rather than every customer.
A narrower interval, using a comparable method, would give GreenThread a more precise estimate.
GreenThread should not treat 48% as certain when planning the launch.

points.descriptor: Explains a relevant limitation in the context of the survey design.
accept: The interval does not prove the survey is unbiased.
If the customer database excludes relevant potential customers, the interval will not correct this selection bias.
Poorly worded questions or customers not responding could still distort the result.
The interval addresses sampling uncertainty, not every possible error in GreenThread's research.

mark_scheme.model_answer: A confidence interval is a range that shows the uncertainty around a result obtained from a sample. GreenThread’s estimate is that 48% of its customers are likely to subscribe, but the interval suggests that the proportion for its wider customer population could be from 44% to 52%, assuming the survey method is appropriate. This means GreenThread should not assume that exactly 48% will subscribe; the survey has sampling uncertainty. However, the confidence interval would not correct bias, such as customers being excluded from the database or misleading survey questions.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: A UK meal-kit business is planning a new promotion.
question.stem: Which customer group is segmented by behaviour?

options.label: A
options.text: Customers who live in rural areas

options.label: B
options.text: Customers aged 25–34

options.label: C
options.text: Customers who regularly reorder vegetarian meal kits

options.label: D
options.text: Customers with household incomes above £70,000

option_rationale: A is geographic segmentation because it groups customers by where they live.
B is demographic segmentation because it groups customers by age.
C is correct because it groups customers according to their purchasing behaviour and product preference.
D is income segmentation because it groups customers by household income.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Harbour Hearth is a small UK retailer selling compact, energy-efficient wood-burning stoves. Rather than advertising to all homeowners, it focuses on customers renovating narrowboats and small rural cottages. These customers need stoves that fit restricted spaces and comply with relevant installation requirements. Harbour Hearth offers detailed fitting advice and a limited range of compact models.
question.stem: Explain how Harbour Hearth uses targeting and niche marketing.

points.descriptor: Identifies targeting as choosing the customer segment or segments that a business will prioritise.
accept: Targeting means selecting a group of customers to focus on.
Targeting is choosing which market segment to serve.

points.descriptor: Applies targeting to Harbour Hearth selecting people renovating narrowboats and small rural cottages, rather than all homeowners.
accept: It prioritises narrowboat and small-cottage renovators.
It does not aim its offer at every homeowner.

points.descriptor: Identifies niche marketing as focusing on a narrow, specialised target market with particular needs.
accept: A niche market is a specialised part of a wider market.
Niche marketing serves a small or narrowly defined customer group.

points.descriptor: Applies niche marketing to Harbour Hearth's compact stoves and fitting advice meeting customers' restricted-space and installation needs.
accept: Compact models suit the limited space on narrowboats and in small cottages.
Its fitting advice supports the specialist requirements of this customer group.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Targeting is selecting the customer segment a business will prioritise. Harbour Hearth targets people renovating narrowboats and small rural cottages instead of all homeowners. This is niche marketing because it focuses on a narrow, specialised group with particular needs. Its compact stoves and detailed fitting advice are designed for customers who have restricted space and installation requirements.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: FizzUp Ltd sells cans of sparkling fruit water through supermarkets, petrol stations and university cafés across the UK. It uses the same core range and national advertising campaign to appeal to a very broad group of customers. FizzUp wants customers to see its drinks as an affordable, refreshing alternative to fizzy soft drinks.
question.stem: Explain why clear positioning may be important to FizzUp when it uses mass marketing.

points.descriptor: Identifies that mass marketing aims to sell a broadly similar offer to a large, wide market rather than focusing on a narrow specialist group.
accept: A definition of mass marketing as targeting a broad market or many customers with one main offer.
Reference to using the same product range or campaign for a large customer group.

points.descriptor: Applies mass marketing to FizzUp by explaining that its national campaign and sale through supermarkets, petrol stations and university cafés are intended to reach many different customers.
accept: FizzUp reaches a broad UK customer base.
FizzUp uses widely available outlets and national advertising.
FizzUp is not concentrating only on a small niche of buyers.

points.descriptor: Identifies positioning as the intended perception of a product in customers' minds compared with alternative offers.
accept: Positioning means how customers should view FizzUp relative to competing drinks.
Positioning is the place the brand aims to hold in customers' minds.
Positioning differentiates an offer from alternatives.

points.descriptor: Applies positioning by explaining that presenting FizzUp as an affordable, refreshing alternative may help customers distinguish it from fizzy soft drinks and choose it when faced with many mass-market alternatives.
accept: Customers may be more likely to choose FizzUp if they understand its value proposition.
The affordable and refreshing message can differentiate FizzUp from rival soft drinks.
A clear position can reduce uncertainty for customers choosing between many drinks.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Mass marketing means aiming a similar offer at a large, broad market. FizzUp does this through national advertising and by selling in widely used outlets such as supermarkets and petrol stations. Positioning is the intended perception of the product compared with alternatives. If customers see FizzUp as an affordable, refreshing alternative to fizzy soft drinks, they may find it easier to distinguish from rival drinks and choose it.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice question. PulsePod operates 24-hour gyms in UK city centres. It is considering which customer segment to target when opening a new site in Leeds. The business can only afford to design its service primarily for one segment in its first year.
question.stem: Analyse why PulsePod may choose to target time-poor office workers rather than university students at its new Leeds gym.

table.title: Research and operational data for PulsePod's proposed Leeds gym

cells: Estimated number within a 15-minute walk of the site
Early mornings, lunch breaks and after work
Average monthly amount customers say they would pay
Low price, social classes and flexible cancellation
24-hour access, short guided sessions and showers
One studio; no space for large classes
24-hour entry system, six showers and 30-minute guided sessions
Number of established gyms mainly aimed at this group within 1 mile

levels.descriptor: Clear, developed analysis of why office workers may be selected, using the data and linking segment attractiveness and PulsePod's capability to likely business outcomes. A balanced consideration of the larger student segment or stronger competition may be included.
Some analysis with relevant application to PulsePod. Explains at least one reason connected to customer needs, revenue potential, competition or operational fit, though development may be incomplete.
Basic relevant knowledge or simple application. Identifies a difference between the segments or a feature of targeting, with limited or no developed chain of reasoning.

indicative_content: Targeting means choosing the customer segment that PulsePod will prioritise, rather than attempting to serve all customers in the same way.
Office workers report a willingness to pay £42 per month, compared with £19 for students. This could support greater revenue per member and help fund facilities such as showers and 24-hour entry.

PulsePod's planned 24-hour entry, showers and 30-minute guided sessions closely match office workers' needs for convenient exercise around work. A close fit could create a credible position and encourage repeat membership.

Students are a larger potential local market, with 18,000 within walking distance compared with 11,000 office workers. However, their preference for social classes may be difficult to meet because PulsePod has only one studio and no space for large classes.

There are five established gyms aimed at office workers within one mile, so PulsePod would need its short sessions and 24-hour access to differentiate successfully. Competition could make the office-worker segment less attractive despite the operational fit.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
PulsePod may target time-poor office workers because the segment appears to fit its capability. Office workers want 24-hour access, showers and 30-minute guided sessions. These are already included in PulsePod's planned service, so the business can provide a consistent offer rather than promising features it cannot deliver. This could make the gym convenient for customers before work, at lunchtime or after work, increasing the chance that members renew.

Office workers also say they would pay £42 per month, over twice the £19 stated by students. Although there are fewer office workers within walking distance, higher income from each member could help PulsePod cover the cost of operating a city-centre gym and its shower facilities.

However, office workers may not automatically be the best target. Five existing gyms already focus on them, compared with two aimed at students. PulsePod would therefore need its short guided sessions and 24-hour access to be sufficiently different. Students are a larger nearby segment, but their demand for social classes is less well matched to a gym with only one studio and no space for large classes. Overall, the operational fit and higher willingness to pay give PulsePod reasons to prioritise office workers, provided it can differentiate from rival gyms.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice. LoopCycle is a small UK business that sells refurbished bicycles online and through a workshop in Leeds. It is considering launching a commuter bicycle aimed at city customers. Managers have produced a market map using customer interviews. They used price and ease of obtaining repairs as the two dimensions because interviewees said these affected their choice of a refurbished bicycle.
question.stem: Using the market map data, evaluate whether LoopCycle should position its new commuter bicycle as high-priced with very easy access to repairs.

table.title: Perceived positions in the Leeds refurbished commuter bicycle market
columns: Ease of obtaining repairs (customer rating out of 10)

levels.descriptor: Shows limited knowledge of market mapping and/or makes simple statements about the proposed position. Application to LoopCycle may be asserted rather than developed. Judgement is absent or unsupported.

Explains how the proposed position could affect LoopCycle, using relevant data from the market map. Considers at least one benefit and/or drawback, with some analysis of customer response, competition or delivery. A judgement may be present but is not fully supported.

Develops a balanced, context-specific evaluation of the positioning decision. Analyses the implications of the apparent gap and the risks of using the map, including whether LoopCycle can deliver the intended position. Reaches a clear, justified judgement that is conditional where appropriate.

indicative_content: A market map displays customers' perceived positions of competing offers against selected dimensions; here these are price and ease of repairs.
The proposed £430 and 10/10 repair-access position is differentiated from PedalBack at £390 and 8/10, which could reduce customer uncertainty for commuters who value reliable, convenient repairs.

A higher price may be credible if LoopCycle can actually provide very easy repairs, for example through sufficient workshop capacity, convenient booking and quick service. The service delivery must reinforce the premium position, not merely promotion.
The apparent gap at the high-price, high-repair-access end may be a niche opportunity, but it may also indicate limited demand from customers willing to pay £430 for a refurbished bicycle.
The map is based on selected dimensions and customer interviews. It may omit other factors customers value, such as bicycle quality or style, and perceptions may change.

LoopCycle should proceed only if it has evidence of a sufficiently profitable target segment and operational capability to deliver repair access consistently; otherwise a position closer to PedalBack, or further research, may be less risky.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
LoopCycle could use the proposed position because the market map suggests that it would be clearly differentiated. Its proposed price of £430 is above PedalBack's £390, but its repair-access rating of 10/10 is also higher than PedalBack's 8/10. For city commuters, easy repairs could reduce the risk of being unable to travel to work. This may make a higher price more acceptable and could create a clear premium niche rather than competing directly with WheelWise at £240 and a repair rating of 3/10.

However, the map does not prove that the gap is attractive. There may be no large group of customers prepared to pay £430 for a refurbished bicycle. The chosen axes also simplify customer choice: customers may care more about bicycle quality, appearance or range than repair access. In addition, the position will fail if LoopCycle cannot deliver it. For example, if its Leeds workshop has long waits or too few repair appointments, customers will not experience the promised 10/10 access and its premium position will be undermined.

Overall, LoopCycle should position the bicycle as high-priced with very easy repairs only if further evidence shows that a profitable commuter segment values this service and LoopCycle can provide it consistently. The map identifies a possible differentiated niche, but relying on it alone would be risky because it reflects only two subjective dimensions.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice question. Willow & Bean is designing a new reusable coffee cup for commuters.
question.stem: Identify which action is part of product and service design.

options.label: A
options.text: Choosing the cup’s insulated lid, colour options and replacement-lid service.

options.label: B
options.text: Setting a monthly sales target for the new cup.

options.label: C
options.text: Selecting the interest rate for a business loan.

options.label: D
options.text: Calculating the corporation tax due on annual profit.

option_rationale: A is correct because product and service design includes decisions about product features, appearance and supporting services.
B is wrong because sales targets are part of sales planning, not the design of the offer.
C is wrong because loan interest is a finance decision.
D is wrong because corporation tax is a financial/legal calculation rather than product or service design.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Northshore Drinks sells a range of canned soft drinks. Its original lemon drink, Zest, has experienced falling sales for the past two years, while its newer low-sugar berry drink is growing quickly. Northshore plans to introduce a sparkling version of Zest and sell it through gyms as well as supermarkets.
question.stem: Explain how Northshore Drinks could use product portfolio analysis when deciding whether to use this extension strategy for Zest.

points.descriptor: Identifies that product portfolio analysis considers the collection of products managed by a business, such as comparing their sales position or role.
accept: A product portfolio is the range/collection of products or brands sold by a business.
Portfolio analysis compares products to support product decisions.

points.descriptor: Applies portfolio analysis to Northshore by recognising that Zest has declining sales whereas the low-sugar berry drink has rapidly increasing sales.
accept: Zest and the berry drink have different sales trends.
The berry drink is growing while Zest is declining.

points.descriptor: Explains that an extension strategy is an action intended to renew or prolong customer demand or relevance for an existing product.
accept: An extension strategy tries to revive or maintain demand for a product.
It changes the offer or market to keep a product relevant for longer.

points.descriptor: Applies the explanation by showing that sparkling Zest and gym distribution could attract different customers or create new occasions to buy, potentially improving Zest sales; the business should consider whether this could take sales from its berry drink.
accept: A sparkling version could make Zest more appealing and potentially increase its sales.
Gyms could provide access to health-focused customers or a new sales channel.
The extension may cannibalise sales of the growing low-sugar berry drink.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Product portfolio analysis examines the different products a business sells and the role each has in the range. Northshore could compare Zest, whose sales are falling, with its fast-growing low-sugar berry drink before allocating resources. An extension strategy aims to make an existing product relevant to customers for longer. A sparkling Zest sold through gyms may reach new customers or create another buying occasion, increasing demand. However, Northshore should check that the extension does not mainly divert customers from the growing berry drink.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Mersey Meal Kits sells recipe boxes to busy households. It is developing a new vegetarian recipe box after identifying a potential customer need. The business must decide the selling price before launch. Developing recipes, producing prototypes and testing the box with customers will be costly. Rival meal-kit businesses already offer vegetarian options.
question.stem: Explain one way in which new product development could influence the price Mersey Meal Kits sets for its new vegetarian recipe box.

points.descriptor: Identifies that new product development (NPD) takes a new product from an idea through stages such as testing, development and launch.
accept: Defines NPD as the process of taking a new product from idea to market.
Recognises development, prototyping or testing as part of NPD.

points.descriptor: Explains that NPD can be costly, for example because prototypes and customer testing require resources.
accept: Explains that developing and testing a new product creates costs.
Explains that NPD requires investment before the product is launched.

points.descriptor: Applies the cost influence to Mersey Meal Kits by referring to its recipe development, prototypes or customer testing for the vegetarian box.
accept: Uses the costs of developing new vegetarian recipes.
Uses the costs of producing or testing prototypes of the vegetarian box.

points.descriptor: Explains that the business may set a higher price to help cover these development costs, although rival vegetarian meal-kit options may limit how high the price can be.
accept: Explains that a higher price could support the recovery of NPD costs.
Explains that competition from rival vegetarian options could constrain the price.
Explains that the final price must balance development costs with the need to attract customers.

mark_scheme.model_answer: New product development is the process of taking a product from an idea to market, including development and testing. Mersey Meal Kits will incur costs when developing vegetarian recipes, making prototypes and testing the new box with customers. It may set a higher selling price to help cover these costs. However, because rival meal-kit businesses already sell vegetarian options, the business may be unable to charge too much without reducing customer demand.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice question. Tideway Outdoor sells reusable water bottles under the Tideway name. Its products are known for their simple design and include after-sales support for replacement lids. Tideway plans to sell insulated lunchboxes using the same Tideway branding.
question.stem: Explain one way that using the Tideway branding on its new lunchboxes could influence customer value.

points.descriptor: Identifies that branding can be part of the customer value provided by a product, rather than the physical product alone.
accept: Branding can contribute to the value or experience that customers receive.
A product offering includes meanings or brand as well as its physical features.

points.descriptor: Explains that a shared brand can connect products in a business's portfolio.
accept: Products in a portfolio can share a brand.
Using the same brand links the lunchboxes with Tideway's existing bottles.

points.descriptor: Applies the point to Tideway by explaining that customers may associate the lunchboxes with the simple design of its existing bottles.
accept: Customers may expect the lunchboxes to have Tideway's simple design.
The Tideway name can create a connection between the lunchboxes and the existing bottles.

points.descriptor: Explains the resulting effect on customer value, such as the lunchbox offering seeming more relevant or preferable to customers who value Tideway's existing product experience and support.
accept: Customers who value Tideway's bottles or replacement-lid support may see more value in the lunchboxes.
The connection may encourage customer response because the lunchboxes appear to fit what customers value about Tideway's offer.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Branding can contribute to customer value because a product is more than its physical features. By using the Tideway name, the new lunchboxes are connected to Tideway's existing bottle portfolio. Customers who value the simple design and replacement-lid support associated with Tideway may therefore see the lunchboxes as a more relevant and preferable offering.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice. BrewBright sells ready-to-drink cold-brew coffee in recyclable cans through supermarkets, gyms and independent cafés across the UK. Its original 250 ml Black Cold Brew was launched four years ago. BrewBright's managers believe that the product may be entering maturity, so they are considering an extension strategy: launching a 250 ml vanilla-oat version under the same brand. The proposed product would use the existing canning line, but requires a new oat supplier and a marketing campaign aimed at younger customers.
question.stem: Evaluate whether BrewBright should launch the vanilla-oat cold brew as an extension strategy for its original Black Cold Brew product. Use the product life cycle and the data provided in your answer.

table.title: BrewBright data

cells: Annual sales volume of Black Cold Brew
2023: 4.8 million cans; 2024: 5.0 million cans; forecast for 2025: 5.0 million cans
Average selling price of Black Cold Brew
Number of rival canned cold-brew flavours in major supermarkets
42% said they would be likely to buy a vanilla-oat version; 18% said they would switch from Black Cold Brew to vanilla-oat rather than buy both
£180,000 marketing campaign and £70,000 supplier testing and packaging changes
900,000 cans if listed by two national supermarket chains
The existing canning line has spare capacity for 1.2 million cans per year. The new oat supplier can initially provide ingredients for up to 1 million cans per year.

levels.descriptor: Shows limited understanding of the product life cycle and/or extension strategies. Makes simple assertions about launching or not launching, with little use of BrewBright's data. Judgement is absent or unsupported.

Shows sound understanding that a product with slowing sales and greater competition may be in maturity, and explains how an extension strategy could affect demand or relevance. Applies relevant data to analyse advantages and/or disadvantages. Reaches a judgement, although it may be conditional or not fully developed.

Shows thorough, well-focused understanding and analysis of product-life-cycle thinking as a conditional model rather than a fixed timetable. Develops balanced arguments using the data, including commercial and operational constraints such as cannibalisation, costs, capacity or competition. Reaches a clear, justified judgement that weighs the most important evidence and recognises uncertainty.

indicative_content: Black Cold Brew's sales rose only from 4.8 million to 5.0 million cans and are forecast to remain at 5.0 million. Together with the rise in rival flavours from 6 to 14, this may indicate maturity, where competition is stronger and sales growth is slowing.

A vanilla-oat variant could be an extension strategy because it may refresh customer interest and make the range more relevant to customers seeking a different flavour or oat-based option. The 42% survey result and expected sales of 900,000 cans suggest potential demand.

The launch can use 1.2 million cans of spare production capacity, so expected sales of 900,000 cans could be produced without buying another canning line. However, the oat supplier's maximum of 1 million cans leaves little room if demand exceeds expectations.

The £250,000 total launch cost may be justified only if the product generates sufficient additional demand. The data gives expected volume but not the new product's selling price, contribution or repeat-purchase rate, so profitability cannot be confirmed.
Cannibalisation is a significant risk: 18% of existing customers say they would switch from Black Cold Brew. Some vanilla-oat sales may replace, rather than add to, sales of the original product.

The PLC is not a certain prediction. Stable sales could reflect a loyal niche rather than unavoidable decline, and different customer segments may be at different stages. BrewBright should test demand, monitor whether sales are incremental and review the launch rather than assume the variant will restart the original product's life cycle.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
BrewBright has some evidence that Black Cold Brew is approaching maturity. Sales increased only slightly from 4.8 million to 5.0 million cans and are forecast to stay flat, while the number of rival flavours has more than doubled from 6 to 14. In a mature market, an extension strategy can be useful because a new vanilla-oat option could make the brand more relevant and encourage customers to choose BrewBright rather than a competitor.

Launching is operationally feasible because expected first-year sales of 900,000 cans are below the 1.2 million cans of spare capacity. Also, 42% of surveyed existing customers say they are likely to buy the flavour. This could create additional sales and help BrewBright defend its supermarket listings as competition grows.

However, the launch may not genuinely extend total demand. Since 18% of existing customers would switch from Black Cold Brew, part of the new product's sales could cannibalise the original product. BrewBright would then incur £250,000 of launch costs without increasing total sales by as much as expected. The oat supplier can provide for only 1 million cans, so demand above forecast could also constrain availability.

Overall, BrewBright should launch vanilla-oat, but initially as a controlled extension rather than assuming the original product is inevitably in decline. The sales trend and competitive data make a maturity interpretation plausible, and spare capacity reduces operational risk. However, the PLC is only a guide: BrewBright should monitor whether the variant brings new customers and additional sales after launch. If most sales simply replace Black Cold Brew, it should reconsider the strategy.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Northbridge Coffee sells roasted coffee beans online. Many customers repeatedly buy Northbridge Coffee rather than trying competing brands.
question.stem: Which statement best identifies brand loyalty?

options.label: A
options.text: Customers continue choosing Northbridge Coffee because they prefer it or find switching to another brand inconvenient.

options.label: B
options.text: Customers recognise Northbridge Coffee's logo when they see it online.

options.label: C
options.text: Northbridge Coffee uses a distinctive name and packaging design.

options.label: D
options.text: Northbridge Coffee charges a higher price than competing coffee brands.

option_rationale: A is correct because brand loyalty is the tendency for customers to continue choosing a brand, including through preference, habit or switching inconvenience.
B is wrong because recognising a logo is brand awareness, which does not necessarily lead to repeat choice.
C is wrong because a name and packaging are brand identifiers rather than evidence that customers repeatedly choose the brand.
D is wrong because charging a higher price may reflect a pricing strategy; it does not itself show that customers are loyal.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Northmoor Coffee is considering changing the price of its reusable travel mugs.
question.stem: Identify the statement that correctly defines price elasticity of demand (PED).

options.label: A
options.text: The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a percentage change in price.

options.label: B
options.text: The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a percentage change in consumer income.

options.label: C
options.text: The amount by which a business increases its price above unit cost.

options.label: D
options.text: The percentage of total market sales made by a business.

option_rationale: A is correct because PED measures how quantity demanded responds to a percentage change in price.
B is incorrect because this defines income elasticity of demand.
C is incorrect because this describes a pricing margin or mark-up, not demand responsiveness.
D is incorrect because this defines market share.
mark_scheme.model_answer: A

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: FreshDrop is launching concentrated household cleaning sprays in the UK. Its market research found that when household disposable income rose by 5%, demand for similar eco-friendly cleaning products rose by 10%. However, household incomes are currently under pressure. FreshDrop is considering a low launch price of £2.50, compared with £3.50 charged by established brands.
question.stem: Explain one reason why penetration pricing could be suitable for FreshDrop.

points.descriptor: Identifies penetration pricing as setting a low price when a product is launched.
accept: A low initial price to attract customers quickly.
A low launch price intended to gain market share.

points.descriptor: Explains that the low price may encourage customers to try FreshDrop and help it gain sales or market share from established brands.
accept: Customers may switch from the £3.50 brands because FreshDrop is cheaper.
The low price could build sales volume quickly.

points.descriptor: Recognises that demand for similar products has positive income elasticity of demand, meaning demand rises when consumer income rises and is likely to fall when income falls.
accept: The products are normal goods because income elasticity is positive.
The 10% rise in demand following a 5% income increase suggests demand is income sensitive.

points.descriptor: Applies this income sensitivity to conclude that FreshDrop's low launch price may maintain demand while household incomes are under pressure.
accept: A £2.50 price may make FreshDrop more affordable during an income squeeze.
Customers whose incomes are falling may be more willing to trial the lower-priced FreshDrop product.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Penetration pricing means FreshDrop would set a low price when launching its sprays. At £2.50, rather than £3.50 for established brands, the price could encourage customers to try FreshDrop and help it win market share. Demand for similar eco-friendly cleaning products has positive income elasticity of demand, as a 5% income rise led to a 10% increase in demand. Therefore, with household incomes under pressure, the low launch price could make FreshDrop more affordable and reduce the risk of a large fall in demand.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice: NovaSound Ltd has developed new wireless earbuds that translate spoken words between languages. The earbuds have features not offered by most competing products. NovaSound plans to launch them at £240 and reduce the price after several months as more customers become aware of the product.
question.stem: Explain why price skimming may be suitable for NovaSound Ltd when it launches its wireless earbuds.

points.descriptor: Identifies that price skimming involves charging a high price when a new or innovative product is launched.
accept: A high initial launch price for a new product.
Charging early customers a premium price.

points.descriptor: Explains that the price is then reduced over time to attract more price-sensitive customers.
accept: The business lowers the price later.
A lower later price can widen the potential market.

points.descriptor: Applies the method to NovaSound by explaining that customers who value its unusual translation feature may be willing to pay £240 at launch.
accept: The earbuds have features that most competitors do not offer, so some customers may pay a premium.
Customers wanting instant translation may be less price-sensitive initially.

points.descriptor: Applies a benefit by explaining that the high early price could generate high margins and help NovaSound recover the costs of developing the earbuds before the price is reduced.
accept: High initial revenue per unit could help cover development costs.
A premium launch price may provide a high margin from early sales.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Price skimming means setting a high price when a new product is launched and then lowering it over time. NovaSound could charge £240 because customers who want the distinctive translation feature may be willing to pay a premium. This could give NovaSound a high margin on early sales and help recover development costs before it reduces the price to attract more customers.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Harbour Escapes Ltd operates short coastal boat tours from Whitby. Its standard adult tour is aimed mainly at UK households taking day trips. The business is considering increasing the ticket price because fuel costs have risen. At the same time, a local tourism body forecasts that average disposable income among the firm’s target customers will fall.
question.stem: Analyse the likely effects of the planned ticket-price increase and the forecast fall in customer income on Harbour Escapes Ltd’s revenue.

table.title: Data for Harbour Escapes Ltd’s standard adult boat tour

cells: Result of a previous 5% price increase, with other conditions similar
Forecast change in target customers’ disposable income
Previous relationship between income and demand
A 4% fall in customer income was associated with an 8% fall in customer numbers

levels.descriptor: Shows limited understanding of how either a price change or an income change may affect customer numbers or revenue. Application to Harbour Escapes may be asserted or incomplete.

Analyses at least one relevant chain of reasoning using the data. Explains how the price increase and/or lower incomes could change customer numbers and revenue, with some relevant calculations or comparison.

Provides developed, well-applied analysis of both changes and their combined effect on revenue. Uses the data accurately to compare revenue effects and recognises that the estimates depend on comparable conditions or may change as customers find alternatives.

indicative_content: The previous price rise suggests price elasticity of demand of -0.6 (-3% divided by +5%). Demand is relatively price inelastic in this observed situation, so a 5% rise to £42 may reduce customers by 3% to 9,700. Revenue from the price change alone would rise from £400,000 (10,000 × £40) to £407,400 (9,700 × £42).

The income evidence suggests income elasticity of demand of +2.0 (-8% divided by -4%). Boat tours appear to be a normal good whose demand is highly responsive to income. The forecast income fall could therefore reduce customer numbers by 8%, damaging revenue.

If the two estimated effects occur together, customer numbers could fall to about 8,924 (10,000 × 0.97 × 0.92). At £42 each, revenue would be about £374,808, below the current £400,000. The fall in income could therefore more than offset the revenue benefit of the higher price.
The evidence is based on past relationships. Customers may become more price-sensitive if they have more time to find substitute leisure activities, so the actual revenue outcome may differ.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Harbour Escapes’ previous price evidence indicates relatively price-inelastic demand. A 5% price increase caused customer numbers to fall by only 3%, giving PED of -0.6. Therefore, increasing the price from £40 to £42 could reduce monthly customers from 10,000 to 9,700, but revenue would increase from £400,000 to £407,400. The higher price per ticket would more than compensate for the lower number of customers.

However, the forecast fall in disposable income is likely to have a larger negative effect. A 4% fall in income previously led to an 8% fall in customer numbers, indicating YED of +2.0. This suggests the boat tour is a normal leisure purchase for which demand is income-elastic. If incomes fall, some households may avoid or postpone the tour, reducing revenue.

If both effects apply, customers could fall to around 8,924 per month. Revenue would then be approximately £374,808 (8,924 × £42), which is lower than current revenue of £400,000. Thus, although the price rise alone may increase revenue, the income fall could outweigh this gain. This forecast is uncertain because the earlier elasticity evidence may not remain valid if competitors, substitute activities or customer behaviour change.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Harbour & Hearth, a small homeware retailer, wants to promote its new range of reusable kitchen products to university students.
question.stem: Which activity is an example of social media promotion?

options.label: A
options.text: Paying a TikTok creator to demonstrate the products and share a discount code with followers

options.label: B
options.text: Using a wholesaler to deliver the products to independent shops

options.label: C
options.text: Reducing the price of all reusable kitchen products for one week

options.label: D
options.text: Changing the products’ cardboard packaging to include recycling information

option_rationale: A is correct because social media promotion can include working with influencers and sharing paid content with a selected audience on platforms such as TikTok.
B is wrong because this is a distribution decision about how products reach retailers.
C is wrong because this is a price promotion rather than promotion through a social media platform.
D is wrong because packaging is part of the product and physical presentation, not social media promotion.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Cotswold Crunch makes premium oat-and-fruit snack bars in Gloucestershire. It sells through its own website and 35 independent farm shops. The business plans to post a short video inviting customers to share their favourite walking spot while holding a Cotswold Crunch bar. Customers can buy bars online at any time or from the farm shops.
question.stem: Explain one benefit to Cotswold Crunch of using viral marketing alongside multi-channel distribution.

points.descriptor: Identifies that viral marketing involves customers choosing to share a marketing message or content with others, allowing it to spread through their networks.
accept: A correct definition of viral marketing.
Customers pass the video or message on to other people.

points.descriptor: Explains that shared customer content could give Cotswold Crunch wider awareness or reach at relatively little promotional cost.
accept: The video could reach many potential customers without the business paying for every share.
Customer sharing may create inexpensive publicity.

points.descriptor: Identifies that multi-channel distribution means using more than one route for customers to obtain a product.
accept: A correct definition of multi-channel distribution.
Cotswold Crunch uses both its website and farm shops to sell the bars.

points.descriptor: Applies the benefit by explaining that people who see the shared video can buy in the channel most convenient to them: online at any time or from one of the 35 farm shops, increasing the chance that awareness becomes sales.
accept: Viewers can order through the website or visit a farm shop.
Having two ways to buy makes it easier for people reached by the video to purchase.
The online channel serves customers who do not live near a farm shop.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Viral marketing is when customers choose to pass content on through their own networks. If walkers share Cotswold Crunch's video, the business could gain awareness among many potential customers at little extra cost. Its multi-channel distribution means those people can buy through the website at any time or from one of the 35 farm shops. This convenience makes it more likely that interest created by the video will lead to sales.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Harbour & Hearth is an independent café in Whitby. It charges prices above nearby chain cafés and aims to appeal to tourists seeking a high-quality local experience. The owner has refurbished the café with wooden furniture, local artwork and clear menu boards. Harbour & Hearth also posts short videos of its cakes and sea views on Instagram, using location-targeted paid adverts during school holidays.
question.stem: Explain how Harbour & Hearth’s physical environment and digital marketing could support its high-quality positioning.

points.descriptor: Identifies or explains physical environment as the tangible look, layout or atmosphere customers use to judge an otherwise intangible service.
accept: Physical evidence includes tangible cues such as décor, furniture, signs or menu boards.
The café environment can influence customers’ perceptions of service quality.

points.descriptor: Applies physical environment to Harbour & Hearth: its wooden furniture, local artwork and clear menu boards can make the café appear distinctive and high quality, supporting its above-chain prices.
accept: The refurbishment can create a premium local experience for tourists.
The physical setting makes the high-quality position more believable.
Any valid link between the named café features and a premium customer experience.

points.descriptor: Identifies or explains digital marketing as using digital channels, data or technology to reach and interact with customers, including social media advertising.
accept: Instagram posts and paid adverts are forms of digital marketing.
Digital marketing can target communication at particular audiences.
Digital channels can raise awareness of a business.

points.descriptor: Applies digital marketing to Harbour & Hearth: location-targeted Instagram adverts and videos can reach tourists during school holidays and show the cakes and sea views, encouraging visits.
accept: Targeting people near Whitby can make promotion more relevant to likely tourists.
Videos can communicate the café’s attractive experience before customers visit.
School-holiday advertising may increase awareness among visitors when demand is likely to be high.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Physical environment is the tangible atmosphere and appearance that customers use to judge the quality of a service. Harbour & Hearth’s wooden furniture, local artwork and clear menu boards could create a distinctive, high-quality experience, making its higher prices seem more justified. Digital marketing uses online channels to communicate with chosen audiences. Its location-targeted Instagram adverts can reach tourists in Whitby during school holidays, while videos of cakes and sea views may encourage them to visit the café.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Harbour Glow is a small premium skincare retailer in Cornwall. It sells moisturisers and facial oils in a boutique shop. The business plans to launch its own e-commerce website so customers across the UK can order products online. Harbour Glow wants its premium image to be consistent whether customers shop online or in the boutique.
question.stem: Explain one way that e-commerce could help Harbour Glow create an integrated marketing mix.

points.descriptor: Shows knowledge of e-commerce as buying and selling goods or services online, such as through a business website.
accept: A correct definition of e-commerce.
Recognition that customers can purchase Harbour Glow products through its website.

points.descriptor: Shows knowledge that an integrated marketing mix involves marketing decisions being coordinated and consistent with the business's target market or positioning.
accept: A correct explanation that product, price, promotion and place should support each other.
Recognition that a premium position requires consistent marketing decisions.

points.descriptor: Applies e-commerce to Harbour Glow by explaining that its website gives customers outside Cornwall a way to buy its skincare products.
accept: The website extends Harbour Glow's reach beyond its local boutique.
UK customers can order online rather than needing to visit the Cornwall shop.

points.descriptor: Explains how consistency between the website and other marketing decisions could reinforce Harbour Glow's premium image.
accept: Using premium-looking website design, product information and packaging to match the boutique experience.
Keeping online prices, promotion and customer service consistent with the premium boutique position.
Explaining that a consistent online experience may encourage customer trust and sales.

mark_scheme.model_answer: E-commerce means selling products online through Harbour Glow's own website. This gives customers across the UK access to its skincare, rather than limiting sales to people who can visit the Cornwall boutique. To create an integrated marketing mix, the website should support its premium position through high-quality images, detailed product advice, premium packaging and prices that are consistent with the boutique. This gives customers a similar premium experience whichever channel they use.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice. Hearth & Herb is a small UK business selling premium loose-leaf tea and gift boxes. It currently sells through 18 independent delicatessens. The owners want to grow sales among customers aged 25–40, who often buy gifts online. They are considering launching a direct-to-consumer website supported by paid social media adverts.
question.stem: Analyse how Hearth & Herb's decision to add a direct-to-consumer website could influence its marketing mix decisions.

table.title: Channel information for Hearth & Herb
columns: Selling through Hearth & Herb's proposed website

cells: Typical retail price of a gift box
Amount received by Hearth & Herb per gift box before its own costs
Additional costs paid by Hearth & Herb per gift box
£7 for packaging, delivery and payment processing
Customer data received by Hearth & Herb
Email address and purchase history, where customers give permission
Delicatessen staff answer most customer queries
Hearth & Herb must answer delivery and returns queries
In-store displays chosen by each delicatessen
Paid social media adverts can link directly to the website

levels.descriptor: Shows limited knowledge of a marketing-mix element and/or makes a simple application to Hearth & Herb. Analysis is absent or only asserted.

Explains one or more relevant effects of the website on marketing-mix decisions, using some contextual data. A logical chain to customer response, costs or sales is present, although development may be uneven.

Provides developed analysis of how the direct website influences coordinated marketing-mix decisions. Uses the data selectively and links channel, promotion and/or service delivery to customer experience and commercial outcomes.

indicative_content: Adding the website changes place because customers can buy at any time and from beyond the areas served by the 18 delicatessens. This may suit the target customers buying gifts online, increasing convenience and potentially sales.

The direct channel gives Hearth & Herb £24 revenue per gift box rather than £14 through a delicatessen, but it incurs £7 of additional packaging, delivery and payment-processing costs. This may influence pricing or promotional decisions: the business could retain the £24 premium price, but must ensure the offer still covers its wider website, fulfilment and customer-service costs.

Paid social media adverts can link directly to the website, allowing promotion to target likely gift buyers and create a clearer route from advert to purchase. However, clicks or advert engagement alone would not demonstrate that the adverts have produced profitable sales.

The website gives access to permissioned email addresses and purchase histories. Hearth & Herb could use this data for more relevant repeat-purchase messages, but must use it appropriately and cannot assume that collecting data automatically creates loyalty.

The direct channel requires the business to manage delivery and returns queries. People, process and physical evidence such as reliable delivery, attractive packaging and a professional website need to support the premium £24 positioning; poor fulfilment could undermine repeat purchases even if promotion generates initial orders.

The online and delicatessen channels should be coordinated. For example, the same premium product image and pricing should be maintained so that the new website does not confuse customers or weaken relationships with delicatessen stockists.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
The website would alter Hearth & Herb's place decision because customers could order gift boxes directly rather than needing to visit one of the 18 delicatessens. This is likely to be convenient for the 25–40 target market buying gifts online, so it could widen the business's reach and increase sales.

It would also affect promotion. Paid social media adverts could take customers straight to the website, creating a short route from awareness to purchase. Hearth & Herb could then use permissioned email and purchase-history data to send relevant repeat-purchase messages. However, the business should judge the adverts by profitable orders and repeat buying, not simply by clicks.

The channel decision must fit the rest of the mix. Hearth & Herb receives £24 online, compared with £14 through a delicatessen, but it has £7 of extra delivery, packaging and payment costs for each online sale. It must also handle returns and delivery queries itself. Therefore, reliable delivery, premium packaging and responsive customer service are needed to justify the £24 price and protect the premium brand. If fulfilment is poor, the website could damage customer experience despite generating more online traffic.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Harbour Homeware Ltd sells kitchen products to independent UK retailers. Its directors use a Boston Matrix when reviewing four product ranges. For this review, a relative market share of 1.0 or above is treated as high, and market growth of 5% or above is treated as high. Relative market share has been calculated by dividing Harbour Homeware's market share by that of the largest competing brand in the defined market. The directors are considering withdrawing the Oak Utensils range and moving its factory capacity to the Aero Air Fryers range.
question.stem: Using the data, evaluate whether Harbour Homeware should withdraw the Oak Utensils range based mainly on its position in the Boston Matrix. [9 marks]

table.title: Performance of Harbour Homeware product ranges

cells: Sales are rising quickly, but an extra £0.8m of advertising and retailer incentives would be needed next year to challenge the market leader.
The range has long-term supply contracts and produces regular cash inflows.
The range uses spare capacity. Its oak handles are also used in the profitable Heritage Knife range, reducing the knife range's material costs by £0.12m per year.
Demand is increasing, although a competitor has recently announced a lower-priced model.

levels.descriptor: Shows limited understanding of the Boston Matrix and makes a simple assertion about withdrawal. Use of the case data is limited or inaccurate, with little developed reasoning.

Explains how the Boston Matrix can inform the decision and applies relevant data to Harbour Homeware. Gives some analysis of benefits and/or drawbacks of withdrawal, although the judgement may be weak or not fully supported.

Provides a well-developed, balanced evaluation of using the Boston Matrix for this decision. Analyses relevant case evidence, challenges the assumptions behind a matrix-only decision and reaches a clear, justified judgement that is conditional where appropriate.

indicative_content: Oak Utensils is a dog/pet under the stated thresholds because it has low market growth of 1% and low relative market share of 0.5. The matrix may suggest that management should limit investment or consider withdrawal.

Withdrawing Oak Utensils could release factory capacity for Aero Air Fryers, a question mark with high market growth of 18% but relative market share of only 0.7. Investment could potentially help Aero gain share in a growing market.
A withdrawal should not be automatic: Oak Utensils generates £0.45m annual contribution, so it is currently making a positive contribution towards fixed costs rather than necessarily draining cash.
Oak Utensils creates a portfolio synergy because its oak handles reduce Heritage Knife material costs by £0.12m each year. This benefit could be lost if the range is withdrawn.

The matrix has only two dimensions. It does not directly measure contribution, the £0.8m investment required by Aero, capacity constraints, future competitor actions or the cost of replacing the oak-handle supply.

The recommendation depends on whether spare capacity has a valuable alternative use and whether Aero's additional contribution after the £0.8m investment is likely to exceed the lost contribution and synergy from Oak Utensils.

The directors should review market definitions and thresholds, since a relative market share of 0.5 and growth of 1% do not by themselves prove that Oak Utensils lacks a profitable niche or future strategic role.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Oak Utensils would be classified as a dog/pet because its market growth is only 1%, below the 5% high-growth threshold, and its relative market share is 0.5, below 1.0. Using the Boston Matrix alone, withdrawal could appear sensible. It would allow Harbour Homeware to concentrate resources on Aero Air Fryers, which is a question mark in an 18% growth market. If the additional £0.8m of promotion helped Aero increase its relative share, it could become a stronger product and offer future growth.

However, the matrix classification should not determine the decision. Oak Utensils produces £0.45m annual contribution, so it is not necessarily consuming cash simply because it is a dog/pet. It also lowers Heritage Knife material costs by £0.12m each year through shared oak-handle purchasing. Closing Oak could therefore reduce total portfolio profit by more than the directors expect. In addition, Aero needs a substantial £0.8m investment and a lower-priced competitor may make it difficult to gain market share.

Overall, Harbour Homeware should not withdraw Oak Utensils mainly because of its Boston Matrix position. The directors should first forecast the extra contribution Aero would generate from the capacity and investment, then compare this with the £0.45m contribution and £0.12m synergy that may be lost from Oak. Withdrawal would be justified only if Aero has a credible route to profitable growth and the oak-handle benefit can be retained or replaced at low cost.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice question. BrightNest is a UK home-care business selling environmentally focused cleaning products. Its established refillable surface-cleaner range is sold through supermarkets and BrightNest's website. The business has recently launched laundry detergent sheets, which are lighter to post than liquid detergent and are aimed at younger, environmentally conscious households. BrightNest has a limited marketing budget and its warehouse team is already busy fulfilling online orders.
question.stem:
Evaluate the view that BrightNest should use cash generated by its refillable surface-cleaner range to heavily promote its laundry detergent sheets.

In your answer, consider BrightNest's product portfolio, the likely stage of each product's product life cycle, and the influences on its marketing-mix decisions.

table.title: BrightNest product portfolio and market information
columns: Current marketing mix and relevant evidence

cells: The UK refill-cleaner market has grown by 2% in the last year. BrightNest has a 31% market share; the largest competing brand has a 24% share.
Sold in major supermarkets and online. The range has repeat purchasers and generates £1.8m annual contribution. Supermarkets want reliable availability and are unwilling to give more shelf space.
The UK detergent-sheet market has grown by 28% in the last year. BrightNest has a 6% market share; the market leader has a 35% share.

Sold mainly through BrightNest's website at a price 12% above the leading brand. A social-media campaign has produced many video views, but only 3% of website visitors buy. Customers who buy give positive feedback about the compact packaging. BrightNest's warehouse can process only 20% more online orders without temporary staff or investment.
The smart-dispenser market has grown by 24% in the last year. BrightNest has a 29% market share; the market leader has a 27% share.
The product is sold through BrightNest's website and selected department stores. Product development and customer-support costs are high.

levels.descriptor: A well-focused and balanced evaluation of the proposed funding and promotion decision. The response accurately uses the Boston Matrix and product-life-cycle thinking as conditional frameworks, with sustained application to BrightNest's evidence. It develops chains of reasoning about integrated marketing-mix choices, commercial consequences and implementation constraints, before reaching a justified judgement that is qualified by relevant conditions.

A clear analysis of the proposed decision with good application to BrightNest. The response uses both portfolio and life-cycle ideas appropriately and explains relevant marketing-mix influences. There is a supported judgement, although evaluation may be less consistently developed, less balanced or less conditional than at the highest level.

Some relevant analysis, with application to the business. The response shows sound knowledge of at least some of the Boston Matrix, product life cycle and marketing mix, but explanation may be uneven or may treat a model too mechanically. A conclusion is present but is likely to be asserted or only partly supported.

Limited analysis with some relevant business knowledge. The response may describe the cash cow, question mark, growth or promotion, but application and developed consequences are limited. Evaluation is weak, unbalanced or largely generic.

Basic and fragmented knowledge of marketing or product portfolios. Assertions may be generic, inaccurate or unsupported, with little use of BrightNest's circumstances. There is little or no meaningful evaluation.

indicative_content: BrightNest's refill range could be viewed as a cash cow because it has high market share in a low-growth market. Its £1.8m annual contribution and repeat purchasers may make it a realistic source of funds for other products.

The detergent sheets are a question mark: the market is growing quickly but BrightNest's 6% share is far below the market leader's 35%. Investment could increase awareness, trial and share, potentially moving the product towards a stronger portfolio position.

The Boston Matrix should prompt questions rather than dictate transferring funds. High share does not guarantee that the refill range has spare cash after supermarket service, stock and promotional requirements. A low-share product may fail despite investment, and the star also needs funds because its market is growing and product-development and support costs are high.

The detergent sheets may be in an introduction stage, as BrightNest has only recently launched them and has low market share. Promotion could build awareness and encourage trial. Alternatively, high market growth does not prove the product itself is at a particular life-cycle stage, and different customer segments may respond differently.

A promotion-only response may be poorly integrated. The 12% price premium needs to be justified by a clear value proposition, such as compact packaging, environmental benefits or convenience. If customers do not perceive enough extra value, more promotion may create website traffic but not purchases.

The 3% website conversion rate and high video views suggest that attention has not yet become sales. BrightNest should investigate whether the message, price, product information, website experience or checkout process prevents conversion before committing heavily to further social-media promotion.

Place and operational capacity matter. A heavy digital campaign could increase online orders beyond the warehouse's 20% spare capacity, leading to delays and poor service. Temporary staff or investment would raise costs, so direct online selling is not automatically more profitable.

BrightNest could test a targeted campaign, improve product pages or offer carefully controlled trials before a large spend. It could also consider appropriate retail or other distribution partners for reach, but intermediaries could reduce margin and control.

The mature refill range may require an extension strategy, such as new scents, bundles or a revised offer, to protect repeat purchases and supermarket support. Diverting too much funding could weaken the cash cow and reduce the funds available for the wider portfolio.

A supported final judgement could favour selective, measured investment in detergent sheets rather than heavy promotion immediately. This would depend on evidence that the product's value proposition, conversion rate, fulfilment capacity and likely margins can support growth, while sufficient funding is retained for the refill range and smart dispenser.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
BrightNest has a strong reason to invest some of the refill range's cash in detergent sheets. The refill range appears to be a cash cow: it has a relatively high 31% market share in a market growing by only 2%, and it generates £1.8m annual contribution. In contrast, detergent sheets are a question mark because the market is growing by 28% but BrightNest has only 6% share, compared with 35% for the leader. Promotion could raise awareness and trial, helping BrightNest gain share in a growing market. If this succeeds, the sheets could become a more valuable part of the portfolio rather than leaving BrightNest dependent on a mature range.

Product-life-cycle thinking also supports some investment. As the sheets have recently launched, they may be in introduction. At this stage, customers may need information about why the product is useful, particularly because detergent sheets are less familiar than liquid detergent. BrightNest could communicate the compact packaging and convenience benefits to younger environmentally conscious households. However, the life cycle is not a timetable. Rapid market growth does not prove that every detergent-sheet brand will grow, and the product's low share may reflect weaknesses in BrightNest's particular offer rather than low awareness alone.

Heavy promotion is especially risky because the current evidence suggests a conversion problem. Social-media videos have attracted views, but only 3% of website visitors buy. More spending on the same promotion may increase traffic without producing enough sales to cover the campaign cost. The 12% price premium may be discouraging purchase unless the promotion and product information make the extra value clear. BrightNest should consider an integrated mix: targeted communication could be combined with clearer online explanations, a trial-sized offer or a bundle, rather than relying on views as evidence of success.

Place and capacity further weaken the case for heavy promotion immediately. Direct online sales give BrightNest customer data and control, but the warehouse can handle only 20% more orders without extra staff or investment. A successful campaign could create delivery delays and damage the customer experience. Using retailers might increase reach, but would reduce margin and control. BrightNest must therefore compare the likely extra contribution from sales with the cost of fulfilment, customer service and any channel expansion.

The Boston Matrix should not be treated as an automatic instruction to take money from the cash cow. The refill range may need investment to keep supermarket availability and retain repeat customers. It could also need an extension strategy, such as new bundles, to remain relevant in a low-growth market. In addition, the smart dispenser is a star in a fast-growing market and has high development and support costs, so it may compete for funds.

Overall, BrightNest should invest selectively in detergent sheets, but should not heavily promote them straight away. A small, targeted test campaign and improvements to conversion and fulfilment capacity would provide better evidence of profitable demand. Larger investment would be justified only if BrightNest can show that its premium price is accepted, extra orders can be served well, and funding the sheets does not undermine the refill range or the smart dispenser.

B is incorrect because increasing flavours is a flexibility or product-range objective, not an environmental objective.

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice. Willow & Thread is a small UK business selling handmade tote bags. Each bag is sold for £28. The bought-in fabric, handles and labels for each bag cost £11. Willow & Thread uses original printed designs and offers customers a free gift-wrapping service.
question.stem: Explain one way Willow & Thread adds value to its tote bags.

points.descriptor: Identifies that added value is the difference between a product’s selling price and the cost of bought-in materials and services.
accept: A correct definition of added value.
Recognition that it is value created above the cost of bought-in inputs.

points.descriptor: Applies the idea to Willow & Thread by identifying an appropriate source of added value.
accept: Original printed designs differentiate the tote bags.
Free gift-wrapping improves the service offered to customers.
Branding or design makes the bags more appealing to customers.

accept: Customers may prefer a distinctive design.
Gift-wrapping makes the bag more convenient as a present.
The feature can increase perceived quality or desirability.
