accept: A higher selling price relative to bought-in costs increases added value.
Higher added value can support higher margins.
Customers may be more willing to pay £28 for the differentiated bag.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Added value is the difference between a product’s selling price and the cost of bought-in materials and services. Willow & Thread adds value through its original printed designs. These make the tote bags more distinctive and attractive to customers than a plain tote bag. Customers may therefore be willing to pay its £28 price, creating more value above the £11 cost of fabric, handles and labels and helping the business achieve a higher margin.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice. SwiftBite Kitchen prepares chilled evening meal boxes for customers in Leeds. Its customer promise is delivery within a two-hour slot selected by the customer. The business has received complaints when deliveries arrive late, particularly on Fridays. The operations manager is considering keeping an additional packing team available on Friday evenings. This would provide spare capacity, but would increase weekly staffing costs.
question.stem: Using the data provided, analyse whether SwiftBite Kitchen should prioritise speed and dependability by employing the additional Friday evening packing team.

table.title: SwiftBite Kitchen: Friday operations data
columns: If an additional packing team is employed

cells: Average time from order cut-off to dispatch
Deliveries arriving within the customer’s selected two-hour slot
Number of Friday meal boxes that can be packed
Customer comments received about late Friday deliveries each week

levels.descriptor: Clear, developed and contextual analysis of whether speed and dependability should be prioritised. The response uses the operational data to explain linked consequences for customers and the business, considers the higher cost of spare capacity, and reaches a justified conclusion for or against employing the additional team.

Some analysis applied to SwiftBite Kitchen. The response explains at least one relevant effect of improving speed or dependability and makes some use of the data, although chains of reasoning or consideration of the cost trade-off are not fully developed.
Basic knowledge or application. The response identifies speed, dependability, capacity or cost, with limited explanation and little or no effective use of the data.

indicative_content: Employing the team would reduce dispatch time from 95 minutes to 60 minutes, helping SwiftBite meet its two-hour delivery promise and improving speed.
On-time deliveries would increase from 82% to 96%. More dependable delivery may reduce the 38 weekly late-delivery comments and protect repeat purchases or the business’s reputation.

Current capacity of 900 boxes is below average Friday demand of 1,000 boxes. This shortfall can contribute to delays; capacity of 1,150 boxes provides 150 boxes of spare capacity, making the operation more resilient to busy Fridays.
The extra team raises Friday staffing costs by £850 per week, from £4,800 to £5,650. Spare capacity can therefore increase unit cost if demand remains at 1,000 boxes.

Because the customer proposition is a chosen two-hour slot, speed and dependability are likely to matter more than minimising staffing cost alone. However, the decision depends on whether fewer complaints and stronger customer retention are worth the additional weekly cost.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
SwiftBite should probably employ the additional packing team because its delivery promise depends on speed and dependability. At present, it can pack only 900 boxes despite average Friday demand of 1,000 boxes. This means the business is likely to face a capacity shortfall on a busy day, contributing to dispatch taking 95 minutes and only 82% of deliveries arriving within the selected slot.

The extra team would increase capacity to 1,150 boxes, giving spare capacity of 150 boxes above average demand. Dispatch time would fall to 60 minutes and on-time delivery would rise to 96%. This should make the service more dependable and may reduce late-delivery comments from 38 to 10 each week. As customers choose SwiftBite partly for a convenient delivery slot, improved reliability could protect repeat demand and reputation.

However, this improvement costs an extra £850 each Friday, as staffing costs rise from £4,800 to £5,650. If Friday demand falls or customers are not willing to value reliable slots, this spare capacity could raise costs unnecessarily. Overall, SwiftBite should prioritise speed and dependability because current capacity is below demand and late delivery directly undermines its customer promise, provided the business can afford the higher staffing cost.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Oak & Thread Ltd makes personalised curtains for local customers. Most cutting, sewing and fitting is carried out by experienced employees using basic tools.
question.stem: Identify the statement that best describes Oak & Thread Ltd’s production method.

options.label: A
options.text: It is labour-intensive because it relies mainly on employees to complete production tasks.

options.label: B
options.text: It is capital-intensive because basic tools are used by employees.

options.label: C
options.text: It is labour-intensive because its largest costs are likely to be fixed costs.

options.label: D
options.text: It is capital-intensive because personalised products always need expensive machinery.

option_rationale: A is correct because labour-intensive production depends mainly on people, with labour typically being the largest cost.
B is wrong because using some tools does not make production capital-intensive; the main reliance is on employees.
C is wrong because labour-intensive production generally has labour as a major cost rather than mainly fixed machinery costs.
D is wrong because personalised work often suits labour-intensive methods and does not always require expensive machinery.
mark_scheme.model_answer: A

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Harbour Bakehouse supplies traybakes to independent cafés across Devon. It currently produces four flavours in weekly batches. The production manager is considering rearranging the kitchen into a product layout, placing mixing, baking, cooling and packing equipment in the order used. The proposal would also use standardised trays and automated portioning equipment. This would require staff training and an initial investment in equipment.
question.stem: Analyse how the proposed changes could improve Harbour Bakehouse’s capacity use and labour productivity.

table.title: Harbour Bakehouse: current performance and proposed changes

cells: Average distance a worker moves ingredients and trays

levels.descriptor: Shows limited knowledge of capacity use, efficiency or labour productivity, with a simple point linked to Harbour Bakehouse’s data.

Explains one or more developed chains of reasoning about how the proposed layout, standardisation or automation could affect capacity use and/or labour productivity, using relevant application to Harbour Bakehouse.

Provides clear, developed analysis of both capacity use and labour productivity. Chains of reasoning are well applied to the bakery’s data and show how operational changes affect output, waiting, movement or worker time.

indicative_content: A product layout places activities in production sequence, so workers move ingredients and trays a shorter distance. This can reduce movement and waiting between tasks, allowing more productive working time and helping labour productivity rise from 5.4 to 6.3 trays per worker hour.

Using standardised trays and automated portioning could make repeated tasks more consistent and reduce the time needed to prepare or portion each batch. More trays may therefore be produced by the same workforce, increasing efficiency and output.

Fewer, shorter changeovers reduce time when equipment is not producing traybakes. This could allow output to rise from 6,500 to 8,200 trays without increasing maximum weekly capacity of 10,000 trays, improving capacity use.

The expected output of 8,200 trays is close to forecast demand of 8,000 trays. Better capacity use could therefore help the business meet demand, although output above demand could create waste if cafés do not buy the extra trays.

Staff training is needed for the new equipment. If staff cannot use it effectively, expected productivity gains may be delayed; however, effective training could help the automated process deliver its intended efficiency gains.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Rearranging the kitchen into a product layout could improve labour productivity because mixing, baking, cooling and packing would be in the sequence needed to make traybakes. Workers would move ingredients and trays only 45 metres per batch rather than 120 metres. Less movement and less waiting between activities gives employees more time to produce trays, helping productivity increase from 5.4 to 6.3 trays per worker hour.

The changes could also improve capacity use. Reducing changeovers from 12 at 45 minutes each to 8 at 30 minutes each means less production time is lost when switching between flavours. Standardised trays and automated portioning may also make repeated tasks quicker and more consistent. Harbour Bakehouse could therefore raise weekly output from 6,500 to 8,200 trays while its maximum capacity remains 10,000 trays. This means more of its available capacity is being used and it should be able to meet forecast demand of 8,000 trays. However, the productivity improvement depends on staff being trained to use the new equipment effectively.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice. Northmoor Bakery supplies packaged biscuit batches to supermarkets. Its packing line currently relies on staff to weigh, seal and label packs. The business is considering an automated packing machine that would carry out these tasks with reduced direct human intervention. Managers expect supermarket orders for the existing biscuit range to remain stable for the next two years.
question.stem: Analyse how installing the automated packing machine could affect the efficiency of Northmoor Bakery's packing operation.

table.title: Northmoor Bakery packing-line data

cells: Packs rejected because of incorrect weight or label per 10,000 packs
Annual maintenance and technician training cost

levels.descriptor: Shows limited knowledge of automation or efficiency, with a simple point linked to the bakery data. Analysis is absent or unclear.

Shows sound understanding of how automation can change operational efficiency and applies this to Northmoor Bakery. Includes at least one developed chain of reasoning, although analysis may be one-sided or not fully developed.

Shows detailed and well-applied analysis of how the automated machine could affect efficiency. Develops clear chains of reasoning using relevant data, including both productivity or quality benefits and operational implications such as maintenance, training or flexibility.

indicative_content: Automation reduces direct human intervention in weighing, sealing and labelling, which can make repeated tasks more consistent.

Output could rise from 600 to 900 packs per hour. If demand is stable, the bakery may meet orders in fewer operating hours or have spare capacity for additional orders, improving use of the packing operation.
The number of packing employees required could fall from 10 to 4 per shift. This may reduce labour input per pack and allow some employees to be redeployed, improving productivity.
Rejected packs could decline from 180 to 60 per 10,000 packs. Fewer incorrect weights or labels may reduce waste, reworking and delays, improving quality and efficiency.
The annual £24,000 maintenance and technician training cost could reduce the net efficiency gain if the machine requires frequent attention or staff lack the skills to operate it.

The benefits are more likely where the bakery continues producing a stable, standardised biscuit range. Automation may be less efficient if frequent product changes require substantial adjustment or programming.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Automation could improve Northmoor Bakery's efficiency because it reduces the need for direct human intervention in routine packing tasks. The machine is forecast to increase output from 600 to 900 packs per hour. This means the bakery could process the same supermarket orders in fewer hours, reducing waiting in the packing stage and potentially creating capacity for more orders.

It could also improve labour productivity. Only four employees rather than ten would be needed on each packing shift. If the six employees no longer needed on packing can be redeployed to other useful work, fewer labour inputs would be used for each pack produced. In addition, rejected packs are forecast to fall from 180 to 60 per 10,000 packs. More accurate weighing and labelling should reduce wasted biscuits, packaging and time spent correcting errors.

However, the machine is not automatically more efficient in all circumstances. It brings £24,000 each year of maintenance and technician-training costs. Breakdowns or insufficiently skilled staff could stop a high-volume packing stage and reduce the expected output benefit. As orders for the existing standard biscuit range are expected to remain stable, Northmoor is more likely to gain from the machine's consistent, high-volume operation than if it regularly had to alter the process for highly customised products.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice. Northfield Bakes produces packaged oat bars. In one week, it made 7,200 boxes. Its maximum possible output for the same week was 9,000 boxes.
question.stem: Calculate Northfield Bakes' capacity utilisation for the week.

option_rationale: A is incorrect because 20% is the spare capacity percentage (1,800 ÷ 9,000 × 100), not capacity utilisation.
B is correct because capacity utilisation = 7,200 ÷ 9,000 × 100 = 80%.
C is incorrect because it results from dividing maximum possible output by actual output and multiplying by 100.
D is incorrect because it uses the 1,800-box spare capacity as though it were a percentage without first dividing by maximum possible output.
mark_scheme.model_answer: Capacity utilisation = actual output ÷ maximum possible output × 100 = 7,200 ÷ 9,000 × 100 = 80%.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice question.
question.stem:
Northfield Bakery produced 18,900 loaves during April. It employed 42 production employees throughout the month.

Calculate Northfield Bakery’s labour productivity for April. Show your working.

accept: output per period / number of employees

450 units per employee in April

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Northshore Kitchens makes fitted kitchen units. It is reviewing how work moves from cutting materials to final assembly.

options.label: B

options.label: D

B is correct because lean production seeks to reduce avoidable waste through ongoing process improvement.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Harbour Homeware assembles kitchen appliances in the UK. It holds three weeks of component stock because deliveries from one supplier are sometimes late. The operations manager wants to introduce just-in-time production, with components delivered only shortly before they are needed. She also wants assembly workers to suggest and test small changes to reduce delays and defects.
question.stem: Explain how just-in-time production and Kaizen could help Harbour Homeware improve its operations.

points.descriptor: Shows knowledge of just-in-time production as reducing inventory buffers by receiving or producing items close to when they are required.
accept: A valid definition of just-in-time.
Explains that stock is held for less time or deliveries match production needs more closely.

points.descriptor: Applies just-in-time to Harbour Homeware by explaining that holding fewer weeks of components could release cash or reduce storage costs.
accept: Less money tied up in component stock.
Lower warehouse or storage costs.
Less risk of excess component inventory.

points.descriptor: Shows knowledge of Kaizen as ongoing small improvements based on identifying problems, testing changes and learning from results.
accept: A valid definition of continuous incremental improvement.
Repeated small changes to working methods.
Using employee knowledge to identify waste or causes of problems.

points.descriptor: Applies Kaizen to Harbour Homeware by explaining that assembly workers could suggest and test changes that reduce delays or defects, then use successful methods more widely.
accept: Workers' knowledge could identify causes of assembly delays.
Testing a small process change could lower defects.
Successful changes could be standardised across the assembly process.

mark_scheme.model_answer:
Just-in-time means receiving components close to the time they are needed for assembly, rather than holding large inventory buffers. For Harbour Homeware, reducing its three weeks of component stock could reduce storage costs and release cash currently tied up in inventory.

Kaizen is continuous improvement through repeated small changes to work processes. Harbour Homeware's assembly workers could identify a cause of delays or defects, test a small change to the assembly method and standardise it if it improves performance.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice question.
question.stem: Northfield Cycles uses an inventory control chart for brake cables. The chart shows a maximum inventory level of 1,250 brake cables and buffer inventory of 300 brake cables. Calculate the re-order quantity.

options.label: A
options.text: 550 brake cables

options.label: B
options.text: 950 brake cables

options.label: C
options.text: 1,250 brake cables

options.label: D
options.text: 1,550 brake cables

option_rationale: A is wrong because it subtracts the re-order quantity from the buffer inventory incorrectly.
B is correct: re-order quantity = maximum inventory level − buffer inventory = 1,250 − 300 = 950 brake cables.
C is wrong because it gives the maximum inventory level without subtracting buffer inventory.
D is wrong because it adds buffer inventory to the maximum inventory level instead of subtracting it.
mark_scheme.model_answer: Re-order quantity = maximum inventory level − buffer inventory = 1,250 − 300 = 950 brake cables.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Oak & Ember Gifts sells seasonal gift hampers. Its managers are concerned that deliveries of chocolates may occasionally arrive late before the Christmas peak.
question.stem: Identify the just-in-case (JIC) inventory approach Oak & Ember Gifts could use.

options.label: A
options.text: Hold extra chocolates as buffer stock in case supplier deliveries are delayed or demand is unexpectedly high.

options.label: B
options.text: Order chocolates only after each customer has bought a hamper, so no stock is held.

options.label: C
options.text: Sell all chocolates immediately to convert inventory into cash before the Christmas peak.

options.label: D
options.text: Reduce the number of chocolate suppliers to make stock deliveries unnecessary.

option_rationale: A is correct because JIC involves holding buffer stock to deal with unexpected demand or supply delays.
B is wrong because ordering only after a customer order is closer to producing to order and minimising stock, rather than holding buffers.
C is wrong because selling stock may release cash but does not provide inventory protection against late deliveries or unexpected demand.
D is wrong because reducing suppliers does not itself mean holding buffer inventory and could increase supply risk.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Harbour Scoops is an ice-cream kiosk at a UK seaside resort. Customer numbers rise sharply at weekends and during school holidays but are much lower on weekday mornings. The owner uses sales forecasts to order enough ingredients and employs temporary, part-time staff for holiday periods.
question.stem: Explain how employing temporary, part-time staff could help Harbour Scoops match its supply to customer demand.

accept: Workers employed only for holiday periods.
Workers scheduled for fewer hours than full-time employees.

points.descriptor: Explains that these staff provide flexible labour capacity which can be increased when demand is high and reduced when demand is low.
accept: The kiosk can roster more workers at busy times and fewer at quiet times.
Labour supply can be adjusted to demand.

accept: Extra staff can be employed at weekends.
Extra staff can be used during school holidays.
The owner can reduce staffing on quiet weekday mornings.

accept: More staff at peaks can reduce customer waiting times.

The business avoids paying full-time workers when there are few customers.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Temporary and part-time staff work for limited periods or fewer hours. Harbour Scoops can employ extra workers during school holidays and at weekends, when many more customers want ice cream. On quiet weekday mornings, fewer staff can be scheduled, so the kiosk does not pay for employees who would have little work to do.

Time between placing an order and receiving it
Time taken for an order to be completed and delivered

points.descriptor: Explains that Oak & Hearth’s customers may face a longer lead time because making begins only after their order and timber may take 12 days to arrive before production can be completed and the table delivered.
accept: Customers may have to wait at least for the 12-day timber delivery plus making and delivery time
The business cannot immediately supply a finished table because it holds no completed stock
A longer wait may reduce customer satisfaction if customers need a table quickly

mark_scheme.model_answer: Producing to order means Oak & Hearth starts making a table only after a customer has ordered it. This allows the customer to choose a particular size and finish. However, lead time is the time from placing an order to receiving it, so customers may wait longer. Oak & Hearth may first need to wait 12 days for timber, then make and deliver the bespoke table because it has no completed tables ready for immediate sale.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Oak & Hearth is a UK retailer of handmade scented candles. Its supplier normally takes five days to deliver wax. Demand can rise unexpectedly before Christmas, so Oak & Hearth keeps 300 kg of wax as buffer inventory. The operations manager has set a re-order level for wax, which tells staff when to place a new order.
question.stem: Explain why Oak & Hearth uses a re-order level and buffer inventory for its wax.

points.descriptor: Identifies that a re-order level is the level of inventory at which a business places a new order.
accept: A correct definition of re-order level.
Orders are triggered when stock reaches a specified level.

points.descriptor: Applies the re-order level to Oak & Hearth by explaining that staff can order wax before supplies run out during the supplier's five-day delivery period.
accept: Ordering at the set level allows for the five-day lead time.
It gives the supplier time to deliver wax before Oak & Hearth has no wax left.

points.descriptor: Identifies that buffer inventory is minimum stock held to protect the business against unexpected demand or late deliveries.
accept: A correct definition of buffer inventory.
Safety stock held for uncertainty.
Stock held to reduce the risk of a stock-out.

points.descriptor: Applies buffer inventory to Oak & Hearth by explaining that its 300 kg of wax can help it continue making candles if Christmas demand rises unexpectedly or a delivery is late.
accept: The 300 kg can prevent lost sales when Christmas demand is higher than expected.
The buffer can keep candle production going if the wax delivery is delayed.
It helps Oak & Hearth avoid disappointing customers because it has run out of wax.

mark_scheme.model_answer: A re-order level is the amount of inventory at which Oak & Hearth places a new order. This means it can order wax early enough for its supplier's five-day delivery time, reducing the chance that production stops. Buffer inventory is stock held to deal with uncertainty. Oak & Hearth's 300 kg buffer of wax could allow it to keep making candles if Christmas demand increases unexpectedly or if a delivery arrives late.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Hearth & Home is a UK retailer of kitchen equipment. It imports blenders from a supplier with a three-week lead time. Recently, deliveries have sometimes arrived late and demand rises sharply before Christmas. The business is considering holding buffer inventory of its best-selling blender.
question.stem: Explain why holding buffer inventory of the best-selling blender could help Hearth & Home manage its supply chain.

points.descriptor: Identifies that buffer inventory is stock held to protect a business against uncertainty, such as unexpected demand or late deliveries.
accept: A correct definition of buffer/safety stock.
Stock held as protection against supply delays or changes in demand.

points.descriptor: Explains that late supplier deliveries or the three-week lead time could otherwise cause Hearth & Home to run out of blenders before replacement stock arrives.
accept: Reference to avoiding a stock-out while waiting for the supplier.
Explanation that the delivery delay means replacement stock may not arrive in time.

points.descriptor: Explains that buffer inventory allows Hearth & Home to continue meeting customer demand during the Christmas peak.
accept: Maintains availability when demand increases before Christmas.
Allows the retailer to keep selling blenders despite higher-than-expected demand.

points.descriptor: Explains that avoiding stock-outs protects customer service, for example by reducing lost sales or preventing customers from buying from another retailer.
accept: Fewer lost sales.
Customers are less likely to be disappointed or switch to competitors.
Improved customer service because blenders remain available.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Buffer inventory is stock held to absorb uncertainty, such as a late delivery or unexpected demand. Hearth & Home has a three-week lead time and its supplier has sometimes delivered late, so the buffer could prevent the retailer from running out before a new delivery arrives. This is particularly useful before Christmas, when demand for blenders rises. Keeping blenders available should reduce lost sales and help maintain customer service.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context:
Revision-authored AQA-style practice question.

Hearth & Home Ltd makes scented candles for independent gift shops. Demand increases sharply in the eight weeks before Christmas. The business currently buys wax from a local supplier, but is considering a cheaper overseas supplier. The production manager is concerned that a late wax delivery could stop candle production and cause gift shops to buy from competitors. However, the finance manager wants to reduce cash tied up in inventory.
question.stem: Using the data, analyse how Hearth & Home Ltd’s choice of wax supplier could influence the level of wax inventory it should hold.

table.title: Wax supplier data
columns: Forecast weekly wax usage before Christmas

levels.descriptor: Shows some relevant knowledge of supplier choice or inventory, with limited application to Hearth & Home. Analysis is likely to be descriptive or include an undeveloped consequence.

Explains how one or more differences between the suppliers affect an appropriate inventory decision for Hearth & Home. There is clear use of the data and at least one developed operational, customer-service or cash-flow consequence.

Provides a coherent, developed analysis of the trade-off created by supplier choice. The response uses relevant data to link lead time and/or reliability to buffer inventory, then traces consequences for production continuity, customer service and/or cash and storage. A well-supported conclusion about the likely inventory approach is made.

indicative_content: Global Wax Trading has a much longer lead time of 18 days, compared with 3 days for Local Wax Co. Hearth & Home would need to order earlier and is likely to require more buffer wax to keep production running while it waits for a delivery.

Global Wax Trading is less reliable, with only 82% of deliveries on time. This raises the risk that wax runs out during the Christmas peak, stopping production and potentially causing gift shops to switch to competitors. Higher buffer inventory would reduce this risk.

At forecast usage of 600 kg per week, a long supplier lead time means inventory is used for longer before a new delivery arrives. A larger inventory holding would tie up more working capital and could approach the 2,400 kg storage limit.

The local supplier is more expensive at £4.80 per kg, but its 98% on-time delivery rate and 3-day lead time may allow Hearth & Home to hold less buffer inventory. This can release cash and reduce storage needs while maintaining availability.
The cheaper £4.10 per kg overseas supplier could lower material costs, but this saving may be outweighed if extra inventory, storage constraints or lost Christmas sales result from late deliveries.

Because demand is especially important before Christmas and stock-outs could halt production, Hearth & Home may favour the local supplier or retain substantial buffer stock if it chooses the overseas supplier.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Global Wax Trading would probably cause Hearth & Home to hold a higher level of wax inventory. Its lead time is 18 days rather than 3 days, so the business must place orders much earlier and use existing wax for longer before replacement stock arrives. As the business expects to use 600 kg each week before Christmas, it will need a larger buffer to avoid production stopping during this period of high demand.

The overseas supplier is also less reliable: 82% of deliveries arrive on time compared with 98% for Local Wax Co. Therefore, a delivery delay is more likely, increasing the need for safety stock. Without this buffer, the firm may be unable to make candles, and gift shops could purchase from competitors. However, more wax inventory ties up cash and the maximum storage capacity is only 2,400 kg.

Although Global Wax Trading is cheaper at £4.10 per kg, the local supplier is likely to let Hearth & Home hold lower inventory because it is both faster and more reliable. Given the importance of avoiding stock-outs before Christmas, the local supplier may be the better choice unless the saving from the overseas supplier is large enough to justify the extra buffer inventory and associated cash commitment.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice. PeakBrew is a UK online retailer selling coffee machines and coffee pods. Its best-selling reusable metal coffee filter is supplied by one manufacturer. The operations manager uses an inventory control chart to monitor the filter stock level. The chart identifies the maximum inventory level, re-order level, buffer inventory, lead time and re-order quantity. PeakBrew has experienced cash pressure because money is tied up in stock, so the finance manager proposes reducing buffer inventory from 300 filters to 100 filters. The operations manager is concerned that the supplier has recently made some deliveries late and that demand rises sharply during promotional weekends.
question.stem: Evaluate whether PeakBrew should reduce its buffer inventory of reusable metal coffee filters from 300 filters to 100 filters.

table.title: Information from PeakBrew's inventory control chart and operations records

cells: Usually 4 days; on two occasions in the last three months it was 6 days
PeakBrew estimates that a stock-out could cause customers to buy filters from a competitor

levels.descriptor: Shows limited understanding of buffer inventory or an inventory control chart. Makes simple assertions about reducing stock, with little or no use of PeakBrew's data and no supported judgement.

Explains some relevant advantages and/or disadvantages of reducing the buffer inventory, with application to PeakBrew. Analysis shows some links to cash, holding costs, lead time or customer service. A judgement may be present but is weak or not well supported.

Develops a balanced, well-applied evaluation of the proposed reduction. Analyses how the inventory control chart, variable lead time and promotional demand affect the risk of stock-outs and the benefits of lower holdings. Reaches a clear, justified judgement that is conditional on relevant evidence or actions.

indicative_content: An inventory control chart shows inventory levels over time, including the maximum level, re-order level, buffer inventory, lead time and re-order quantity. Buffer inventory protects PeakBrew when demand is unexpectedly high or deliveries are late.

Reducing the buffer by 200 filters could release working capital and reduce monthly holding costs. At £0.40 per filter per month, holding 200 fewer filters would reduce holding costs by £80 per month.

The lower buffer could make a stock-out more likely. Normal daily sales are 100 filters, but promotional demand can reach 160 filters per day and the supplier has sometimes taken 6 rather than 4 days to deliver.

At a re-order level of 700 filters, PeakBrew normally expects to sell 400 filters during a 4-day lead time, leaving its 300-filter buffer. A 6-day lead time at normal sales would use 600 filters, leaving only 100 filters; high promotional demand would increase the risk further.
A stock-out could lose sales and damage customer loyalty because customers may purchase from a competitor. The cost of lost customer service may exceed the £80 monthly holding-cost saving.

PeakBrew could reduce the buffer only if it also improves demand forecasting, avoids promotions when deliveries are due, negotiates more reliable supply, or changes the re-order level to reflect longer lead times.
The best decision depends on the reliability of the supplier, the frequency of promotional peaks, PeakBrew's cash position and the cost of losing customers.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
PeakBrew could benefit from reducing its buffer inventory because it would hold 200 fewer filters. This would release cash that is currently tied up in inventory and save £80 per month in holding costs (200 × £0.40). This may be valuable because the business is already experiencing cash pressure. A smaller buffer could also reduce the risk of holding unnecessary stock if sales forecasts prove too high.

However, reducing the buffer from 300 to 100 filters could damage customer service. The inventory control chart exists to ensure that an order is placed before stock reaches the buffer level. At the current re-order level of 700 filters, normal sales of 100 per day would use 400 filters during the usual 4-day lead time, leaving 300 filters as protection. If delivery takes 6 days, normal sales would use 600 filters, leaving only 100 filters even before allowing for a promotional weekend. During promotions, sales can rise to 160 filters per day, so the lower buffer could be exhausted quickly. A stock-out could mean lost sales and encourage customers to buy from a competitor.

Overall, PeakBrew should not simply reduce the buffer to 100 filters while supplier deliveries and promotional demand remain unpredictable. The £80 monthly saving is likely to be small compared with the possible loss of sales and customer loyalty. It could reconsider a lower buffer if it secures more reliable delivery times, improves forecasts or raises the re-order level before promotions. Therefore, retaining the present buffer is the safer short-term decision.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

options.label: C
options.text: Increasing the quantity of products held in Riverside Bakery's warehouse

options.label: D
options.text: Reducing the price paid for flour from an existing supplier

B is wrong because the bakery would carry out deliveries using its own resources.
C is wrong because this is a decision about inventory levels, not obtaining an external service.
D is wrong because this is a supplier price negotiation rather than using an external business to provide logistics services.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Oak & Thread makes school uniforms. Before shirts are packed for delivery, selected finished shirts are inspected for loose buttons, incorrect stitching and stains.
question.stem: Identify the activity that is quality control at Oak & Thread.

options.label: A
options.text: Inspecting finished shirts to find defects before they are sent to customers

options.label: B
options.text: Training machinists to follow a standard stitching process to reduce future defects

options.label: C
options.text: Using customer feedback to redesign the shirt range each year

options.label: D
options.text: Charging a higher price because the shirts use premium fabric

option_rationale: A is correct because quality control involves inspecting or testing outputs to detect defects or non-conformance.
B is quality assurance because it aims to prevent defects through controlling the production process.
C uses feedback to support improvement, rather than inspecting outputs to detect defects.
D confuses quality with a high price or premium specification; quality is about meeting relevant requirements and expectations.
mark_scheme.model_answer: A

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Oakline Kitchens makes fitted kitchen units for households. Customers have recently complained that some cupboard doors do not align correctly when installed. Oakline currently checks completed doors before they leave the factory, but this has led to rework and delayed deliveries.
question.stem: Explain how introducing quality assurance could reduce the consequences of poor quality for Oakline Kitchens.

points.descriptor: Identifies quality assurance as preventing defects by designing and controlling production processes, rather than only checking finished products.
accept: Quality assurance uses process systems to stop defects occurring.
Quality assurance focuses on prevention during production.
Training and standard procedures can be part of quality assurance.

points.descriptor: Applies quality assurance to Oakline by explaining that production processes could be standardised or staff trained to measure, cut and fit cupboard-door components accurately.
accept: Checks could be built into the cutting or assembly process.
Workers could follow a consistent process for fitting hinges.
Staff could be trained to use measurements correctly.

points.descriptor: Explains that fewer misaligned doors would reduce rework, scrap or the cost of replacing faulty units.
accept: Oakline would spend less correcting doors.
Less waste would be produced.
Fewer replacement doors would be needed.

points.descriptor: Explains that preventing defects could reduce late deliveries and complaints, helping Oakline retain customer satisfaction or its reputation.
accept: Orders would be delivered on time more often.
Customers would be less likely to complain or return units.
A more reliable service could protect Oakline's reputation.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Quality assurance means controlling the production process to prevent defects, rather than simply inspecting completed cupboard doors. Oakline could train staff and use consistent measurements when doors and hinges are cut and assembled. This should reduce the number of doors that do not align, so the business would have less rework and fewer replacement costs. It could also avoid delivery delays and customer complaints, helping to protect customer satisfaction and Oakline's reputation.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice question. BrewBox is a UK company that delivers meal-kit boxes to customers’ homes. Customers expect ingredients to be fresh, orders to be accurate and deliveries to arrive on the chosen day. BrewBox currently checks completed boxes before dispatch. It is considering a quality assurance system involving staff training, standard packing procedures and checks at key stages of packing to prevent errors.
question.stem: Analyse the likely benefits and difficulties for BrewBox of improving quality through the proposed quality assurance system.

table.title: BrewBox quality and operating data for the last month

cells: Customer complaints about missing or incorrect ingredients
Refunds and replacement deliveries caused by quality problems
Estimated one-off cost of staff training and new packing procedures
Additional time required to train each packer

levels.descriptor: Shows limited knowledge of quality improvement, with a simple benefit or difficulty. Application to BrewBox is weak or absent, and analysis is mainly asserted rather than developed.

Shows clear understanding of how quality assurance aims to prevent errors. Applies one or more points to BrewBox’s data and develops at least one logical consequence, although the analysis may be uneven or consider benefits and difficulties in limited depth.

Shows thorough, balanced analysis of benefits and difficulties of quality improvement. Uses BrewBox’s context and relevant data to develop clear chains of reasoning, including how prevention could affect costs, productivity and customer experience, alongside implementation difficulties.

indicative_content: Quality assurance is process-focused: training, standard procedures and checks during packing are intended to prevent missing or incorrect ingredients, rather than only finding faulty boxes at final inspection.

Fewer packing errors could reduce the 1,200 boxes that need repacking. This may free staff time, reduce disruption and improve productivity because resources are not repeatedly used to correct mistakes.

Improved order accuracy and more reliable deliveries could lower the 800 complaints. Better customer experience may protect BrewBox’s reputation and encourage customers to continue ordering meal kits.
Prevention of defects could reduce some of the £18,000 spent on refunds and replacement deliveries, improving cash flow and potentially lowering operating costs over time.
The £24,000 one-off implementation cost may be significant. Savings from fewer refunds may take time to exceed this cost, especially if not all quality problems are caused by packing processes.

Each packer needs 6 hours of training, which can temporarily reduce available packing capacity or require cover. Staff may also need time to follow new procedures consistently, and excessive procedures could slow packing if poorly designed.

Complaints are useful evidence of customer experience but do not show every defect, since some customers may not complain. BrewBox should use process checks as well as complaint data to judge whether quality has improved.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
The proposed system could improve quality because it is designed to prevent mistakes during packing rather than relying only on checking completed boxes. For example, standard procedures and trained staff may reduce the number of boxes with missing or incorrect ingredients. BrewBox currently has to repack 1,200 boxes, so fewer errors would reduce rework. This could release staff time for packing new orders, increasing productivity.

Improved accuracy could also reduce the 800 customer complaints and some of the £18,000 spent on refunds and replacement deliveries. Customers receiving the correct, fresh ingredients on the chosen delivery day are more likely to have a positive experience. This may protect BrewBox’s reputation and help retain customers, while lower failure costs could improve cash flow.

However, improvement has costs and may disrupt operations initially. BrewBox must pay £24,000 for training and procedures, and each packer requires 6 hours of training. During training, fewer staff may be available to pack boxes, which could slow dispatch unless the business pays for cover. The system will only deliver the benefits if staff follow the procedures consistently and the new checks identify the real causes of errors. Therefore, quality assurance could reduce rework and customer dissatisfaction over time, but BrewBox must manage the initial cost and short-term capacity pressure.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Oakline Furniture previously moved production of its dining tables to a factory in Vietnam. It now plans to move this production back to the UK to reduce delivery distances and improve supply reliability.
question.stem: Identify the term that best describes Oakline Furniture's decision.

options.label: A
options.text: Outsourcing

options.label: B
options.text: Offshoring

options.label: C
options.text: Reshoring

options.label: D
options.text: Diversification

B is incorrect because offshoring is moving activity to another country, whereas Oakline is bringing activity back to the UK.
C is correct because reshoring is returning previously offshored activity closer to, or back to, the home country.
D is incorrect because diversification means expanding into new products or markets, rather than changing production location.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice question.
question.stem:
Harbour Bakehouse Ltd operates six bakery cafés in Devon. During the last financial year, 24 employees left the business. The average number of employees during the year was 160.

Calculate Harbour Bakehouse Ltd’s labour turnover for the year. Show your working.

points.descriptor: Uses the number of employees leaving as the numerator.
accept: 24 employees leaving

points.descriptor: Divides by the average number of employees and multiplies by 100.
Calculates labour turnover as 15%.
accept: 15 percent

mark_scheme.model_answer:
Labour turnover = (number of staff leaving ÷ average number of staff employed) × 100
= (24 ÷ 160) × 100
= 15%

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice question. Northfield Kitchenware Ltd produced 18,000 insulated lunch boxes in June using 60 employees.
question.stem: Calculate Northfield Kitchenware Ltd's labour productivity for June.

options.label: A
options.text: 300 lunch boxes per employee per month

options.label: B
options.text: 18,000 lunch boxes per employee per month

options.label: C
options.text: 60 lunch boxes per employee per month

options.label: D
options.text: 0.003 lunch boxes per employee per month

option_rationale: A is correct: 18,000 lunch boxes ÷ 60 employees = 300 lunch boxes per employee per month.
B is wrong because it gives total output and does not divide by the number of employees.
C is wrong because it uses the number of employees as the result rather than calculating output per employee.
D is wrong because it reverses the calculation: 60 ÷ 18,000 = 0.0033, rather than output ÷ employees.
mark_scheme.model_answer: Labour productivity = output per period ÷ number of employees = 18,000 ÷ 60 = 300 lunch boxes per employee per month.

options.label: C
options.text: £42,000 per unit

options.label: D
options.text: £168,000 per unit

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Hearth & Home Kitchens manufactures fitted kitchen units. Demand has fallen, so managers are reviewing staffing costs and may reduce the number of agency workers. At the same time, the business has started monthly employee meetings, asked production staff for ideas to reduce waste and funded training for machine operators.
question.stem: Explain how Hearth & Home Kitchens is using both hard HRM and soft HRM.

points.descriptor: Identifies or explains hard HRM as focusing on workforce requirements, headcount, costs or performance in order to meet business needs.
accept: Hard HRM treats employees as a resource that must be planned to meet organisational needs.
Hard HRM focuses on controlling staffing numbers and employee costs.
Hard HRM aims to align the workforce with the business's operational requirements.

points.descriptor: Applies hard HRM to Hearth & Home Kitchens by linking the review of staffing costs or possible reduction in agency workers to lower demand.
accept: Reviewing staffing costs is hard HRM.
Reducing agency workers would adjust headcount to match lower demand.
The business is seeking a more cost-efficient workforce because demand has fallen.

points.descriptor: Identifies or explains soft HRM as emphasising employee capability, commitment, involvement, communication or trust.
accept: Soft HRM views employees as a source of capability and commitment.
Soft HRM uses employee involvement and development to improve outcomes.
Soft HRM places importance on communication with employees.

points.descriptor: Applies soft HRM to Hearth & Home Kitchens by linking employee meetings, requests for ideas or training to involvement and development.
accept: Monthly meetings give employees a voice.
Asking production staff for waste-reduction ideas involves employees in improvement.
Training machine operators develops employees' skills and may improve performance.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Hard HRM is shown by the review of staffing costs and the possible reduction in agency workers. This aligns the number and cost of employees with the fall in demand. Soft HRM is shown through monthly meetings, asking staff for ideas and providing operator training. These actions involve and develop employees, which may build commitment and improve production performance.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: HarbourBite is a growing UK producer of chilled sandwiches for supermarkets. It has won a new contract that will increase weekly output by 30% in six months. The business currently has enough packing employees, but does not have enough workers trained to operate its automated filling machines. Some existing employees are approaching retirement.
question.stem: Explain how workforce planning could help HarbourBite recruit employees for its future needs.

points.descriptor: Identifies that workforce planning involves matching future employee numbers and skills to expected business requirements.
accept: Workforce planning forecasts the people and capabilities the business will need.
It considers future workforce needs rather than simply replacing employees who leave.

points.descriptor: Applies workforce planning to HarbourBite by identifying the need for trained automated-filling-machine operators as output rises by 30% and employees retire.
accept: It would identify a skills gap in automated filling-machine operation.
It would forecast vacancies or capability gaps caused by the new contract and forthcoming retirements.

points.descriptor: Explains that the forecast can guide targeted recruitment, such as setting person specifications and advertising for applicants with relevant machine-operating skills.
accept: HarbourBite could recruit people with automated-food-production or machine-operating experience.
The business could use the plan to decide the required skills and number of recruits.

points.descriptor: Explains a likely benefit to HarbourBite of targeted recruitment, such as having capable employees available when the contract starts and reducing disruption to production.
accept: Recruiting early gives new employees time to be appointed and prepared before higher output is required.
Suitable recruits should help HarbourBite meet the supermarket contract reliably.
Targeted recruitment reduces the risk that packing staff cannot operate the machinery.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Workforce planning means forecasting the number and skills of employees needed in the future. HarbourBite could identify that, although it has enough packing employees now, it will need more trained automated filling-machine operators because output is due to rise by 30% and some employees will retire. It can then recruit people with relevant machine-operating skills in advance. This should help ensure it has capable employees ready to produce the additional sandwiches when the supermarket contract begins.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Harbour Homeware Ltd is introducing automated packing machines at its warehouse in Leeds. The machines mean that six packing roles will no longer be needed. However, the business has four vacant customer returns roles and is prepared to train existing packing employees for these jobs.
question.stem: Explain how Harbour Homeware Ltd could use redeployment and redundancy in response to the introduction of automated packing machines.

points.descriptor: Explains redeployment as moving an employee to another role within the same business, potentially with retraining.
accept: Employees whose packing jobs are no longer required could move to a different job at Harbour Homeware.
Redeployment keeps employees within the business by transferring them to another department or role.
Training may be needed before an employee can perform the new role.

points.descriptor: Applies redeployment to Harbour Homeware's vacant customer returns roles.
accept: Up to four packing employees could be trained and moved into the four customer returns vacancies.
Redeployment could allow Harbour Homeware to retain packing employees' experience rather than dismissing all six employees.
Moving suitable packing employees to returns roles may avoid some redundancy costs.

points.descriptor: Explains redundancy as ending employment because a role is no longer required, rather than because of employee conduct.
accept: The packing roles can be removed because automation means fewer packers are needed.
Redundancy is appropriate where the job, rather than the employee, is no longer needed.
The introduction of machines has made six packing roles surplus to requirements.

points.descriptor: Applies redundancy to Harbour Homeware's remaining surplus employees or a relevant consequence.
accept: After filling the four returns vacancies, two packing employees may still be made redundant if no other suitable roles exist.
Harbour Homeware must use a fair process and consult affected employees.
Redundancy may reduce wage costs but can involve redundancy payments, lower morale and loss of skills.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Redeployment would mean moving packing employees into different roles within Harbour Homeware rather than ending their employment. For example, up to four employees could be trained for the vacant customer returns jobs, allowing the business to keep experienced staff and avoid some redundancy costs. Redundancy is the ending of employment because a job is no longer needed, rather than because of poor conduct. Since automation removes the need for six packing roles, the two employees not redeployed may need to be made redundant if there are no other suitable vacancies; Harbour Homeware would need to follow a fair process.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice question. Northbridge Kitchens Ltd makes made-to-measure kitchen units. It currently operates from a factory in Leeds and sells mainly in Yorkshire. The business plans to open a smaller assembly and distribution site in Sheffield in six months to reduce delivery times for customers in the East Midlands. It is also introducing computer-controlled cutting machines at both sites.
question.stem: Analyse how the information in the table may influence Northbridge Kitchens Ltd's HR decisions about the number, skills and location of its employees.

table.title: Northbridge Kitchens Ltd workforce information

cells: 48 production employees, including 8 trained computer-controlled machine operators
Requires 18 production employees, including 4 trained computer-controlled machine operators
Leeds production capacity after new machines are installed
The same output could be produced by 40 production employees if all operators are trained to use the new machines

A Sheffield college has 22 students expected to complete a computer-controlled manufacturing course in four months. In Leeds, only 3 suitable applicants applied for the last 6 machine-operator vacancies.
A staff survey found that 30 Leeds production employees would consider travelling to Sheffield for at least two days each week, but 12 said they would leave if their current role was removed.

levels.descriptor: Shows limited relevant knowledge of workforce planning or HR decisions. Makes a basic point from the data, with little or no developed link to Northbridge Kitchens.
Shows clear understanding of how workforce numbers, skills or location affect HR decisions. Applies relevant data to Northbridge Kitchens and explains at least one consequence for the business.

Shows well-developed analysis of linked HR decisions about workforce numbers, skills and location. Uses the data selectively and explains consequential effects on Northbridge Kitchens' capacity, recruitment, training, retention or operations.

indicative_content: The new machinery may reduce the number of Leeds production employees required from 48 to 40, so Northbridge could avoid replacing leavers, redeploy employees or consider redundancies. However, removing roles could cause some employees to leave, as 12 stated they would leave if their role was removed, creating a risk of lost experience and disruption.

The business needs more employees at Sheffield, including four machine operators. Recruiting locally may be attractive because the Sheffield college has 22 students completing a relevant course, whereas Leeds had only three suitable applicants for six previous operator vacancies.

Northbridge could train existing Leeds employees to operate the computer-controlled machines, helping it retain knowledge and fill the skills requirement. Training has a time and cost implication, and the business must ensure employees are competent before relying on the new machinery.

Some Leeds employees could be redeployed or work across both sites because 30 would consider travelling to Sheffield for at least two days each week. This could transfer experienced workers during the launch, but part-week travel may increase coordination costs and may not provide all 18 Sheffield employees needed.
HR decisions should balance a hard focus on matching headcount to machine-enabled capacity with retention and development decisions that protect skills and reduce the risk of employees leaving.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Northbridge must plan both headcount and capability rather than simply recruit more staff. Once the new machines are installed, Leeds can produce the same output with 40 production employees instead of 48. This creates an apparent surplus of eight employees. HR could use natural wastage or redeployment rather than immediate redundancies, because 12 employees say they would leave if their role disappeared. Losing employees in this way could also remove useful production knowledge and make the change harder to implement.

The Sheffield site requires 18 production employees, including four machine operators. Recruiting locally may be a suitable decision because 22 students at a Sheffield college are about to complete a relevant course. This gives Northbridge a wider potential supply of trained recruits than Leeds, where only three suitable applicants applied for six operator vacancies. Recruiting in Sheffield could therefore help the business fill its skills gap and reduce the need to move all staff from Leeds.

However, Northbridge could also train and redeploy existing Leeds employees. Thirty employees would consider travelling to Sheffield for two days per week, so experienced staff could support the new site while local recruits gain experience. This may improve the reliability of the launch, but it will not necessarily provide full-time cover for all 18 roles and may make communication and scheduling more difficult. Therefore, HR is likely to combine local recruitment in Sheffield with training and selective redeployment of Leeds staff, while managing the risk of employee exits caused by reduced roles in Leeds.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice. Northline Kitchens Ltd makes fitted kitchen units in Leeds. Demand from online retailers has risen, but production staff say that decisions about faults and delivery changes take too long because they must be passed through shift supervisors to the production manager. The business is considering removing one layer of shift supervisors and creating four multi-skilled production teams. Each team would have a trained team leader with authority to allocate daily tasks and resolve routine quality problems. Supervisors whose roles disappear could be redeployed as team leaders after training, where suitable. The production manager believes the HR data should be used alongside staff interviews before making a final decision.
question.stem: Analyse how Northline Kitchens Ltd could use the HR data to decide whether to change to the proposed team-based organisational design.

table.title: Northline Kitchens Ltd HR and operating data

cells: Average time for a routine quality decision
Many production employees reported limited task variety and slow feedback from supervisors

levels.descriptor: Shows limited relevant knowledge of HR data or organisational design. May identify a trend from the data or state a simple benefit of teams, with little or no developed link to Northline Kitchens Ltd.

Shows sound analysis by using relevant HR data to explain why the proposed change may affect workforce performance or decision making at Northline Kitchens Ltd. Applies more than one piece of evidence, although chains of reasoning may be incomplete or one-sided.

Shows well-developed analysis of how several HR indicators and qualitative evidence can inform the decision about organisational design. Clear, contextual chains explain both the potential value of the team-based structure and why the data should be interpreted carefully before implementation.

indicative_content: Labour turnover increased from 8 to 20 employees while the average production workforce remained at 80. This suggests a greater risk of recruitment costs and lost production knowledge; staff interviews may help establish whether limited task variety and slow feedback are important causes before changing job design.

Absence rose from 3% to 7%, while output fell from 48,000 to 44,000 units with the same number of employees. This may indicate lower workforce performance or problems in job design, coordination or working conditions, so Northline should investigate causes rather than assume absence proves poor motivation.

A flatter, team-based design could shorten the route for routine quality decisions because team leaders would have delegated authority. Faster decisions may reduce delays, errors and frustration, potentially improving output, absence and retention.

Multi-skilled teams and greater responsibility could increase task variety and autonomy, addressing concerns raised in interviews. However, Northline needs to assess whether employees have the skills and willingness to take on broader roles and budget for training.

The metrics are indicators, not proof of cause. Turnover and absence could also be affected by local job opportunities, health issues or other workplace conditions. Northline should combine the data with interviews and examine patterns by team, role and period before removing supervisors.

Redeploying suitable supervisors as team leaders could retain experience and reduce the disruption of redundancies, but team leaders need appropriate training and the revised structure must still provide sufficient coordination and support.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Northline should use both the numerical HR data and the staff interviews to identify whether its present structure is contributing to weaker workforce performance. Employee departures rose from 8 to 20 while the production workforce stayed at 80. This could increase recruitment and induction costs and remove experienced workers, which may help explain why output fell from 48,000 to 44,000 kitchens. The interview evidence that employees have limited task variety and receive slow feedback suggests that job design and the extra management layer may be contributing to the turnover.

Changing to multi-skilled teams could therefore add value. Giving trained team leaders authority over routine quality issues may reduce the decision time from four days, allowing faults to be corrected sooner. Team members may also have more varied tasks and responsibility, which could improve engagement and retention. Redeploying suitable supervisors as team leaders would retain their knowledge while supporting the new structure.

However, Northline should not treat the rise in turnover and absence from 3% to 7% as conclusive proof that the structure is the cause. Absence may have health or external causes, and turnover may reflect local employment opportunities. It should use interviews and more detailed data by role or team to check causes and assess training needs before making the organisational change.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

B is incorrect because technology creates value only when supported by suitable processes and capabilities.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Bramble & Bean is a UK producer of chilled oat-based drinks. It has introduced a new high-protein oat drink in recyclable cartons. At the same time, it has installed an automated filling line that reduces the time taken to seal each carton.
question.stem: Explain the difference between product innovation and process innovation at Bramble & Bean.

points.descriptor: Identifies product innovation as the development of a new or significantly improved product.
accept: A valid definition of product innovation.
Developing or significantly improving what is sold to customers.

points.descriptor: Applies product innovation to Bramble & Bean's new high-protein oat drink and/or recyclable carton.
accept: The high-protein oat drink is a new or significantly improved product.
The recyclable carton is an improvement to the product offered to customers.

points.descriptor: Identifies process innovation as an improvement to the way a product is made or delivered.
accept: A valid definition of process innovation.
Improving how the business produces its products.

points.descriptor: Applies process innovation to the automated filling line, which reduces the time needed to seal cartons.
accept: The automated filling line changes production rather than the drink itself.
The filling line makes carton sealing quicker.
The process innovation could increase efficiency by reducing production time.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Product innovation is introducing a new or significantly improved product for customers. Bramble & Bean's high-protein oat drink, sold in recyclable cartons, changes the product it offers. Process innovation improves how a business makes or delivers its products. Its automated filling line changes the production process by reducing the time required to seal each carton.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: BrightBrew Ltd has spent £180,000 on research and development (R&D) to create a self-cleaning valve for commercial coffee machines. The valve reduces cleaning time for cafés. BrightBrew has applied for a patent before launching the new valve.
question.stem: Explain one benefit to BrightBrew Ltd of obtaining a patent for its new self-cleaning valve.

points.descriptor: Shows knowledge of a patent as a legal right that gives an inventor exclusive rights to make and sell a new invention for a limited period.
accept: A patent gives legal protection for a new invention.
A patent can prevent other businesses making and selling the invention without permission.
A patent may last for up to 20 years.

points.descriptor: Applies the patent to BrightBrew's self-cleaning valve.
accept: It protects BrightBrew's self-cleaning valve.
It could stop rival coffee-machine suppliers copying the valve.
It gives BrightBrew exclusive rights to make and sell this valve.

points.descriptor: Explains that reduced copying can allow BrightBrew to retain sales or charge a higher price.
accept: Cafés wanting reduced cleaning time may have to buy from BrightBrew.
BrightBrew may face less direct competition for the valve.
BrightBrew could charge a premium because competitors cannot offer an identical valve.

points.descriptor: Develops the benefit by linking retained revenue or profit to recovering the R&D spending.
accept: Higher sales or prices could help BrightBrew recover its £180,000 R&D cost.
The protection improves the chance that BrightBrew earns a return on its R&D investment.
Less copying helps BrightBrew retain the financial reward from developing the valve.

mark_scheme.model_answer: A patent gives BrightBrew the exclusive legal right to make and sell its self-cleaning valve for a limited period. This could prevent rival coffee-machine suppliers from copying the valve. Cafés seeking to reduce cleaning time may therefore need to purchase from BrightBrew, allowing it to retain sales or charge a higher price. This makes it more likely that BrightBrew can recover the £180,000 it spent on R&D.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Northstar Learning Ltd produces revision workbooks and digital learning resources for sixth-form students.
