The business is introducing automated software to carry out routine tasks, including checking page layouts and sorting customer orders.
question.stem: Explain how copyright and automation could benefit Northstar Learning Ltd.

points.descriptor: Identifies a relevant feature of copyright.
accept: Copyright gives legal protection to original creative work.
Copyright can prevent others copying work without permission.
Copyright protects original writing, images or software.

points.descriptor: Applies the benefit of copyright to Northstar Learning Ltd.
accept: It could stop rivals copying Northstar's original workbook explanations or illustrations.
Protecting its software activities could help Northstar retain the value of its creative resources.
It may help Northstar maintain differentiation because competitors cannot legally copy its original content without permission.

points.descriptor: Identifies a relevant benefit of automation.
accept: Automation uses technology to carry out tasks automatically.
Automation can carry out routine tasks more quickly or consistently.
Automation may reduce the need for employees to complete repetitive tasks manually.

points.descriptor: Applies the benefit of automation to Northstar Learning Ltd.
accept: Automated layout checking could reduce errors or speed up production of Northstar's workbooks.
Automatically sorting customer orders could make order processing faster.
Automation of routine tasks could reduce costs or improve consistency in Northstar's production and order processes.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Copyright automatically protects Northstar's original written explanations, illustrations and software activities. This could prevent competitors from copying its resources without permission, helping Northstar keep its learning materials distinctive. Automation could complete routine work such as checking page layouts and sorting customer orders more quickly and consistently. This could reduce production errors or speed up order processing for customers.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Hearth & Home is a UK retailer of kitchenware with six high-street shops. It plans to launch an e-commerce website where customers can order products for home delivery or click and collect. The website will record searches, products viewed, purchases and delivery postcodes. Managers want to use this data when deciding which products to promote and stock.
question.stem: Explain how using e-commerce as a strategic choice could help Hearth & Home make better use of big data.

points.descriptor: Identifies e-commerce as a strategic move that changes how a business sells or reaches customers, rather than simply being an additional promotional tool.
accept: Selling online as part of the business model
An online channel can extend sales beyond the six shops
E-commerce can alter customer access, delivery or click-and-collect operations

points.descriptor: Applies this to Hearth & Home by explaining that its website can collect a large and varied flow of customer information.
accept: The website records searches, views, purchases and/or postcodes
Online customer activity creates data that the shops alone may not provide
Data may arrive quickly as customers use the website

points.descriptor: Explains that big data requires analysis and interpretation before it can become useful information for decisions.
accept: Managers need suitable systems or skills to analyse the data
Raw website data is not automatically useful insight
The business could identify patterns in customer behaviour

points.descriptor: Applies a likely decision benefit to Hearth & Home, such as using patterns to target promotions or improve stock decisions.
accept: Promote products that particular customer groups search for or buy
Stock more of products with strong demand in particular postcodes
Use online demand patterns to improve forecasting and reduce unsuitable stock

mark_scheme.model_answer: E-commerce is a strategic choice because Hearth & Home would change its sales channel by allowing customers to buy online, including customers who do not visit one of its six shops. The website would generate big data from searches, product views, purchases and delivery postcodes. Managers must analyse this data to find useful patterns rather than treating all collected data as insight. For example, if customers in certain postcodes repeatedly search for a type of pan, Hearth & Home could promote that range to them and hold more stock, which could improve sales and reduce the risk of stocking unwanted products.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: TrailPack UK sells outdoor equipment online. It has records of customers' past purchases, basket values, product returns and website searches. Managers want to use this information before launching its winter clothing range.
question.stem: Explain how TrailPack UK could use data mining to improve its marketing for the winter clothing range.

points.descriptor: Identifies data mining as using analytical techniques to find useful patterns or relationships in data.
accept: Data mining analyses datasets to identify patterns, associations, groups or predictions.
Data mining is more than simply collecting customer data.

points.descriptor: Applies data mining to TrailPack UK's customer records.
accept: It could analyse purchase histories, searches, basket values or returns.
It could use its online customer data relating to outdoor equipment.

points.descriptor: Explains a relevant pattern or customer grouping that could be identified.
accept: It could identify customers who searched for or previously bought cold-weather products.
It could segment customers according to buying behaviour, such as high-value customers or customers likely to buy winter clothing.
It could identify products that are often bought together.

points.descriptor: Explains how the insight could improve marketing for the winter range.
accept: TrailPack UK could send targeted winter-clothing offers or recommendations to the identified customers.
More relevant promotions may increase the chance of sales and reduce spending on advertising to unlikely buyers.
It could bundle related products, such as a winter jacket and thermal base layers, in marketing messages.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Data mining is the use of analytical techniques to find useful patterns in data, rather than just collecting it. TrailPack UK could analyse customers' previous purchases and website searches to identify people who have looked for cold-weather equipment or bought similar products. It could then send these customers targeted offers for its winter clothing range. This makes its marketing more relevant and may increase sales while reducing advertising aimed at customers who are unlikely to buy.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Harbour & Pine is a UK retailer of homewares with 18 shops and an online store. Its current online store provides the same product list to every visitor and customer-service staff answer online enquiries manually. Two national rivals have introduced apps that give customers personalised product suggestions and immediate answers to common delivery questions. Harbour & Pine is considering a digital system that would analyse customers’ previous purchases and browsing activity to personalise online recommendations. It would also use an AI-supported chatbot for routine enquiries, with staff taking over complex cases. The system would require staff training, accurate customer data and new procedures for checking chatbot responses.
question.stem: Analyse why Harbour & Pine may be under pressure to adopt the proposed digital system.

table.title: Selected business data for Harbour & Pine

cells: Change in online sales revenue in the last 12 months
Percentage of online visitors who make a purchase
Average response time to an online customer enquiry
Customers surveyed who said personalised recommendations would make them more likely to buy

levels.descriptor: Shows limited knowledge of digital technology or innovation, with a simple point linked to Harbour & Pine. Analysis is absent or mainly asserted.

Shows sound understanding of a pressure for innovation or digital adoption and applies it to the data or context. Includes a developed chain showing how adoption could affect a business outcome, although analysis may be narrow or incomplete.

Shows strong, well-applied analysis of pressures for innovation and the value of adopting digital technology. Develops clear causal chains using relevant data and context, such as competitive pressure, changing customer expectations, conversion, service speed or effective implementation requirements.

indicative_content: Competitive pressure is high because rivals’ online sales grew by 14%, compared with Harbour & Pine’s 2%. If the gap persists, rivals may gain online customers and market share, pressuring Harbour & Pine to innovate rather than retain an undifferentiated website.

Only 3% of Harbour & Pine’s online visitors make a purchase, compared with 5% for rivals. Analysing previous purchases and browsing activity could enable relevant recommendations, increasing the likelihood that visitors find suitable products and convert into buyers.

Customer expectations are changing: 46% of surveyed customers state that personalised recommendations would make them more likely to buy. The proposed system could therefore add value through a more relevant customer experience and potentially higher sales.

An 18-hour enquiry response time is much slower than rivals’ two hours. A chatbot could answer routine questions immediately, improving service and allowing staff to concentrate on complex enquiries, which may improve customer satisfaction and reduce lost sales.

Buying technology alone would not guarantee value. Harbour & Pine needs accurate data, trained staff, procedures to check responses and escalation to people; otherwise poor recommendations or incorrect chatbot answers could damage customer trust.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Harbour & Pine faces competitive pressure to innovate because its online sales grew by only 2%, while national rivals achieved 14%. Rivals also convert 5% of online visitors into buyers, compared with Harbour & Pine’s 3%. If customers receive more relevant recommendations from competitors, they may be more likely to buy there, widening Harbour & Pine’s sales disadvantage. Using customer purchase and browsing data could personalise suggestions, helping visitors identify suitable homewares and increasing conversion.

There is also pressure to improve customer service digitally. Harbour & Pine takes 18 hours to answer an online enquiry, compared with two hours for rivals. An AI-supported chatbot could provide immediate answers to routine delivery questions, reducing customer frustration and freeing staff to deal with more complex issues. This could improve the online experience at a time when 46% of surveyed customers say personal recommendations would make them more likely to buy. However, value depends on implementation: inaccurate customer data or poorly checked chatbot responses could create irrelevant advice and reduce trust. Therefore, staff training and reliable escalation procedures are needed for the digital system to create the intended advantage.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Fresco Foods is a small UK producer of chilled meal kits sold to independent supermarkets. Its main ingredient packs must be used within 21 days of delivery. Fresco uses stock in first, first out order. It currently buys ingredient packs from a nearby supplier, LocalHarvest. Demand is normally 100 packs per day, but can rise to 140 packs per day during local food festivals. Fresco has £24,000 of cash reserves and must pay suppliers when deliveries arrive. Its chilled storage area can hold a maximum of 2,000 packs.
question.stem:
Figure 1 shows Fresco Foods' current inventory control chart information for ingredient packs when demand is at its normal level. LocalHarvest has a six-day lead time and has delivered on time in 98% of orders over the last year.

Fresco is considering changing to GlobalSource. GlobalSource charges a lower price but has a longer, less reliable lead time. Its minimum order quantity is 1,500 packs.

Evaluate the view that Fresco Foods should choose GlobalSource and reduce its buffer inventory to 100 packs because obtaining the lowest purchase price is the most important factor in inventory decisions.

table.title: Figure 1: Inventory control chart information and supplier data

cells: Inventory falls from 1,800 to 900 packs in 9 days; an order is placed at 900 packs; after a further 6 days, inventory reaches the 300-pack buffer and a delivery restores inventory to 1,800 packs.
£2.80 per pack; 98% of orders delivered on time
£2.45 per pack; 10-day lead time; 85% of orders delivered on time; minimum order quantity 1,500 packs
Packs have a 21-day shelf life; stock is issued first in, first out; chilled storage capacity is 2,000 packs

levels.descriptor: Shows limited relevant knowledge of inventory, suppliers or buffer stock. Application to Fresco is absent or superficial. Assertions are unsupported, with little or no analysis of consequences. A conclusion, if offered, is unsupported.

Shows some accurate understanding and some application to Fresco. Explains one or more consequences of supplier choice or changing inventory levels, such as cash tied up, stock availability or waste. Evaluation is present but is mostly unbalanced, generic or weakly justified.

Shows clear, accurate knowledge of the inventory control chart and relevant influences on inventory levels. Analyses linked consequences for Fresco using the supplied data, including supplier reliability, lead time, demand variation, holding stock and/or shelf life. Reaches a reasoned judgement, although the balance or conditions of the judgement may not be fully developed.

Shows thorough and consistently accurate knowledge, applied closely to Fresco's circumstances. Develops a balanced chain of analysis using the inventory control chart and supplier evidence, considering both operational service and cash, cost or waste consequences. Evaluation is well supported by the data and reaches a clear, context-dependent judgement about whether GlobalSource and a 100-pack buffer are appropriate.

indicative_content: An inventory control chart identifies the maximum inventory level, re-order level, buffer inventory, lead time and re-order quantity. Fresco currently orders at 900 packs so that, at normal use of 100 packs per day, six days of usage reduces stock to the 300-pack buffer when LocalHarvest delivers.
GlobalSource's lower price saves £0.35 per pack. On its 1,500-pack minimum order, this is a £525 saving compared with LocalHarvest, which could reduce cash outflows when stock is purchased.

A 10-day GlobalSource lead time means Fresco must place orders earlier than with LocalHarvest. At normal demand, 10 days of usage is 1,000 packs, so a 100-pack buffer would give far less protection against a late delivery than the existing 300-pack buffer.

During a food festival, demand can reach 140 packs per day. Over GlobalSource's 10-day lead time, usage could be 1,400 packs before allowing for any buffer. This makes a reduced 100-pack buffer particularly risky and may lead to stock-outs, missed supermarket orders and poorer customer service.

GlobalSource delivered on time for 85% of orders, compared with 98% for LocalHarvest. The lower reliability increases the case for holding a buffer rather than reducing it, because a late delivery could stop Fresco producing meal kits.

Holding more inventory ties up cash, needs chilled storage and creates waste risk if packs expire. However, the present maximum of 1,800 packs is below the 2,000-pack capacity, and the normal 15-day cycle with first in, first out rotation is compatible with the 21-day shelf life.

The lowest purchase price is not necessarily the lowest overall cost. A lower price could be outweighed by lost sales, disruption or emergency sourcing if GlobalSource is late, whereas LocalHarvest's shorter and more reliable lead time supports lower-risk operations.

A supported judgement may favour retaining LocalHarvest, or using GlobalSource only if Fresco raises its re-order level and maintains an adequate buffer. The preferred decision depends especially on whether festival demand is predictable and whether GlobalSource can improve delivery reliability.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Fresco should not automatically choose GlobalSource simply because its price is lower. GlobalSource would reduce the purchase price by £0.35 per pack. Since its minimum order is 1,500 packs, Fresco would save £525 on each order. This could be valuable because inventory ties up working capital and Fresco has only £24,000 in cash reserves.

However, the current inventory control chart is designed around LocalHarvest's six-day lead time. At normal usage, stock falls by 600 packs during those six days, from the 900-pack re-order level to the 300-pack buffer. This gives Fresco protection if demand is slightly higher than expected or a delivery is late.

GlobalSource has a 10-day lead time and is less reliable, with only 85% of deliveries arriving on time. At normal demand, Fresco would use 1,000 packs during this lead time. A buffer of only 100 packs would leave little protection. The risk is much greater during food festivals, when 10 days of usage could be 1,400 packs. A late GlobalSource delivery could therefore cause Fresco to run out of ingredient packs, preventing production and risking lost supermarket orders.

Fresco should also consider waste. More inventory increases chilled-storage costs and the risk that packs exceed their 21-day shelf life. Nevertheless, the present maximum level of 1,800 packs is below the 2,000-pack storage limit. With first in, first out rotation and normal demand, the existing chart cycle can use stock within the shelf-life period. Therefore, reducing inventory is not essential on storage or expiry grounds.

Overall, GlobalSource may be attractive if its price saving is important and Fresco can reliably forecast demand. However, reducing the buffer to 100 packs is not justified while GlobalSource has a longer and less reliable lead time, especially before food festivals. Fresco should retain LocalHarvest, or only move to GlobalSource after increasing its re-order level and retaining a buffer large enough to protect customer service.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice. Hearth & Home is a UK manufacturer of made-to-order kitchen units. It is considering buying an automated cutting machine to replace part of its manual cutting process. The directors want to improve the business's performance but are concerned about the effect on both immediate results and future competitiveness.
question.stem: Analyse whether buying the automated cutting machine is likely to improve Hearth & Home's short- and long-term performance.

table.title: Data for Hearth & Home's proposed automated cutting machine

cells: £180,000, paid immediately from the business's cash reserves
Four weeks; no kitchen units can be produced during this period
Sales revenue is expected to fall by £90,000 during the four-week installation period
£72,000 lower labour and material costs each year
The machine could increase annual output from 2,400 to 3,000 kitchen units
The supplier states that cutting errors should fall from 8% of units to 3% of units after staff training
Six experienced cutters would need retraining; two have said they may leave if their role changes

levels.descriptor: Detailed, applied analysis of both short- and long-term performance. The response develops clear chains of reasoning from the data and makes relevant connections between immediate disruption or cash use and later costs, capacity or quality. It recognises that the outcome depends on relevant conditions, such as successful installation, training or demand for extra output.

Some applied analysis of short- and/or long-term performance. The response uses relevant data and explains one or more likely effects, although chains of reasoning may be incomplete or the comparison between time periods may be uneven.
Limited understanding of short- or long-term performance, with simple assertions or undeveloped use of the case material. Analysis is largely descriptive.

indicative_content: In the short term, the £180,000 immediate cash payment and £90,000 expected revenue loss during installation could weaken performance because the business has fewer cash reserves while production stops.
Once installed, annual labour and material savings of £72,000 could improve longer-term financial performance, provided the machine operates as expected and savings are not offset by other costs.
Increasing output from 2,400 to 3,000 units could support long-term growth if sufficient customers want the additional kitchen units; unused capacity would reduce the benefit.
A fall in cutting errors from 8% to 3% could improve quality and reduce waste, supporting future customer satisfaction and the business's ability to compete.
If experienced cutters leave rather than complete retraining, disruption and lost knowledge could delay the expected quality improvement or reduce the benefits of the investment.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
The investment could weaken Hearth & Home's short-term performance. It must pay £180,000 immediately from cash reserves and production will stop for four weeks. This is expected to reduce sales revenue by £90,000, so the business may have less cash available while it is unable to fulfil orders. If customers cannot wait for their kitchen units, some may buy from rivals, making the immediate effect more damaging than the revenue figure alone suggests.

However, long-term performance may improve. The machine is expected to reduce labour and material costs by £72,000 each year. It could also raise output from 2,400 to 3,000 units, allowing the business to sell more kitchens if demand exists. In addition, reducing cutting errors from 8% to 3% could mean less waste and more reliable quality, which may encourage customers to return or recommend the business.

The long-term gains are not certain. Two experienced cutters may leave if their roles change, and the quality improvement depends on successful staff training. Therefore, the machine is more likely to improve long-term performance than short-term performance, but only if Hearth & Home can manage the installation disruption, retain or replace skilled staff, and sell the additional output.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice. Northfield Cyclewear Ltd sells cycling clothing online in the UK. In 2025, the directors reduced prices on selected products to attract new customers and spent more on digital advertising and staff training. Sales volumes increased, but several suppliers increased the prices charged for technical fabrics. The figures below have been prepared using the same accounting basis in both years, and there were no significant one-off items. The directors are deciding whether to continue the lower-price and higher-marketing approach in 2026.
question.stem: Evaluate whether Northfield Cyclewear Ltd should continue its lower-price and higher-marketing approach in 2026. Use the income-statement information provided to support a justified judgement.

table.title: Northfield Cyclewear Ltd: income statements for years ended 31 December (£000)

levels.descriptor: Shows limited understanding of an income statement, with simple use of one or more figures. A conclusion may be asserted but is unsupported or inconsistent with the evidence.

Explains relevant changes in income-statement performance and applies them to Northfield Cyclewear. Analysis shows some links between pricing, costs or operating expenses and profit. A judgement is given, but it is not fully balanced or developed.

Provides a well-developed, balanced evaluation using accurate comparisons from the income statements. Analysis clearly distinguishes revenue, gross profit and operating profit, considers the strategic explanation and limitations of the evidence, and reaches a well-justified judgement contingent on relevant conditions.

indicative_content: Revenue increased by £300,000, or 12.5%, which suggests that lower prices and/or increased marketing may have attracted customers.

Cost of sales increased by £315,000, more than the increase in revenue. Consequently, gross profit fell by £15,000 and gross profit margin fell from 40% (£960,000/£2,400,000) to 35% (£945,000/£2,700,000). This may reflect lower selling prices and higher fabric input costs.
Marketing, distribution and administrative expenses increased by £135,000. This contributed to operating profit falling from £420,000 to £270,000; operating profit margin fell from 17.5% to 10%.
Profit for the year fell by £120,000, from £288,000 to £168,000. Continuing the approach unchanged could further weaken returns available to retain in the business or distribute to owners.

The extra marketing and training may be an investment that builds brand awareness, staff capability and repeat demand. If these create future sales at improved prices or lower unit costs, the lower current operating profit could be acceptable.

The income statement reports profit over a period, not cash generated. It cannot alone establish whether the business has sufficient cash to fund continuing marketing, pay suppliers or meet finance costs.

A suitable judgement may be to modify rather than automatically continue or stop the strategy: retain marketing that demonstrably generates profitable repeat sales, negotiate supplier prices or improve productivity, and review whether prices can rise without losing too much demand.

The conclusion depends on whether management can restore gross margin and whether the additional marketing produces future revenue growth that exceeds its cost. Comparing further periods and cash-flow information would improve the decision.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Northfield should not continue the approach unchanged. Although revenue rose by £300,000, from £2.4m to £2.7m, this did not translate into higher gross profit. Cost of sales rose by £315,000, so gross profit fell slightly from £960,000 to £945,000. Gross profit margin therefore fell from 40% to 35%. This suggests that the lower prices and higher fabric costs have reduced the amount earned from each £1 of sales.

The fall is more serious at operating-profit level. Marketing, distribution and administrative expenses rose by £135,000, contributing to operating profit falling from £420,000 to £270,000. Operating profit margin fell from 17.5% to 10%, while profit for the year fell from £288,000 to £168,000. If the business repeats the same decisions without improving prices, purchasing costs or efficiency, it may generate more sales but less profit for owners.

However, stopping the strategy immediately could be short-sighted. The increased marketing and training may have helped to raise sales volumes and could create repeat customers or more capable staff. If this investment allows Northfield to increase prices later, secure cheaper fabric supplies or spread fixed operating costs across more sales, profit could recover in future years.

Overall, Northfield should continue only a revised version of the approach. It should measure which marketing activity produces profitable sales and seek to restore gross margin through supplier negotiations, productivity improvements or selective price increases. The income statement gives a strong warning because both gross and operating profit have fallen, but it does not show cash generated. Directors should also examine cash-flow information before committing to further spending.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice. Northshore Kitchens Ltd makes fitted kitchens. Its directors are comparing its performance with UrbanHome Designs Ltd, a competitor. Northshore has recently bought computer-controlled cutting equipment, whereas UrbanHome uses older equipment that is largely written down in its accounts. The directors are considering whether Northshore should delay further investment because its return on capital employed (ROCE) is lower.
question.stem: Using the data, analyse the limitations of using ratio analysis to judge whether Northshore Kitchens Ltd is performing less well than UrbanHome Designs Ltd.

table.title: Selected financial information for the year ended 31 March 2025

cells: Investment in new production equipment during the year

levels.descriptor: Shows limited understanding that ratios have limitations. Makes a simple, relevant point about the data, with little or no developed link to the judgement about performance.
Shows sound understanding of at least one limitation of ratio analysis and applies it to Northshore and/or UrbanHome. Includes some analysis of why the ratios may not give a fully valid comparison.

Shows well-developed analysis of multiple limitations, applied closely to the data. Explains clearly why the lower ratios do not by themselves establish that Northshore is performing less well, including the effect of investment timing and/or differing asset values.

indicative_content: ROCE is affected by both operating profit and capital employed. Northshore's £1.8 million investment increases its capital employed before the equipment has necessarily generated its full profit benefit, so its 12% ROCE may be temporarily lower.

UrbanHome's nine-year-old equipment may have a low book value because it is largely written down. This reduces its recorded capital employed and can make its 18% ROCE appear stronger, even if its underlying operations are not more efficient.

Ratios do not explain the cause of a difference. Northshore's 9% operating profit margin and UrbanHome's 11% margin could reflect differences in pricing, product mix, input costs, productivity or overheads; further information is needed before deciding which business is better managed.

A higher ratio is not automatically preferable. UrbanHome's higher ROCE could be associated with underinvestment in ageing equipment, while Northshore's investment may support future productivity or profit.
The comparison is for one year only. Trend data would be needed to determine whether Northshore's lower ratios are a short-term result of an investment cycle or a persistent weakness.
Ratios should be considered alongside strategic context and other aspects of performance, rather than being treated as a complete judgement.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Northshore's lower ROCE of 12%, compared with UrbanHome's 18%, does not necessarily mean it is performing less well. ROCE is based on operating profit relative to capital employed. Northshore has invested £1.8 million in new equipment, which will increase capital employed immediately, but the profit or productivity gains may take time to develop. Its ROCE could therefore be temporarily reduced by investment that improves future performance.

The comparison may also be distorted by asset age and accounting values. UrbanHome's equipment is nine years old and largely written down, so its recorded capital employed may be low. A lower denominator can increase ROCE, meaning its 18% figure may partly reflect old asset values rather than superior operating performance. In contrast, Northshore's one-year-old equipment is likely to have a higher recorded value.

Similarly, UrbanHome's higher operating profit margin of 11% does not explain why it is higher than Northshore's 9%. The difference could result from price, product mix, input costs, productivity or overheads. The directors would need more information and trend data before concluding that Northshore is less successful. Therefore, the ratios are useful starting points, but they are insufficient on their own to justify delaying further investment.

question.context: Northshore Kitchens Ltd is introducing computer-controlled cutting machines at its factory in Leeds. The business has identified that several experienced machine operators lack the digital skills needed to use the new equipment. It plans to pair these operators with trained supervisors for coaching during production shifts and offer clear progression towards senior technician roles.
question.stem: Explain how talent development could benefit Northshore Kitchens Ltd.

points.descriptor: Identifies a relevant feature of talent development.
accept: Talent development is the systematic development of employees' current and future capabilities.
It can include coaching, mentoring, work-based learning or career progression.
It develops potential as well as skills needed for a present role.

points.descriptor: Applies talent development to Northshore Kitchens Ltd's new technology.
accept: Coaching from trained supervisors can develop operators' digital skills for the computer-controlled cutting machines.
The senior technician progression route can develop employees for future skilled roles.
Development addresses the capability gap created by the new machinery.

points.descriptor: Explains a benefit through improved capability and work behaviour.
accept: Operators who can use the machines properly are more likely to use the equipment effectively during production.
Coaching during shifts allows employees to practise the new skills in the real factory setting.
Developing digital capability can help Northshore implement the technology change.

points.descriptor: Explains a further benefit linked to retention or future capability.

Preparing employees for senior technician roles supports continuity if skilled staff are needed in future.
The benefit depends on supervisors, processes and opportunities allowing operators to apply their learning; attendance or coaching alone does not prove improved performance.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Talent development is the planned improvement of employees' skills and potential for current and future roles. At Northshore Kitchens, supervisors could coach experienced operators during production so that they develop the digital skills needed to operate the computer-controlled cutting machines. This should help the business use its new technology more effectively because employees can apply the skills in their normal work. In addition, progression towards senior technician roles may encourage operators to remain with Northshore, helping it retain people with the capability needed in future.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Harbourline Furniture makes fitted wardrobes in Bristol. Assembly workers currently stay on one task throughout each shift. They are also considering moving assembly workers between measuring, cutting and fitting tasks every two weeks.
question.stem: Explain how flexible working and job rotation could benefit Harbourline Furniture.

points.descriptor: Explains flexible working as giving employees some choice over when, where or how long they work.
accept: Flexible working may include flexitime, remote working, compressed hours or job sharing.
Employees have greater control over their working arrangements.

points.descriptor: Applies flexible working to Harbourline Furniture: allowing design staff to select start and finish times around core hours could improve work-life balance and help the business retain or recruit office-based designers.
accept: It could reduce turnover among design staff.
It could make Harbourline more attractive to potential design employees.

points.descriptor: Explains job rotation as moving employees between tasks or roles at a similar level for set periods.
accept: Workers change from one similar-level task to another.
Job rotation can reduce boredom and broaden employees' skills.

points.descriptor: Applies job rotation to Harbourline Furniture: rotating assembly workers between measuring, cutting and fitting could give more workers the skills to cover absences and reduce repetitive work.
accept: A worker trained on several assembly tasks could cover a colleague who is absent.
Changing tasks every two weeks may make assembly work less monotonous.

mark_scheme.model_answer:
Flexible working gives employees some choice over when, where or how long they work. At Harbourline, letting design staff choose start and finish times within core hours could improve work-life balance, helping the business retain designers and attract new applicants.

Job rotation means moving employees between similar-level tasks for set periods. Rotating assembly workers between measuring, cutting and fitting could reduce boredom and develop wider skills, so more employees can cover absences.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice. Harbour Homeware operates three kitchenware shops in Devon. The business has found it difficult to retain sales advisers, and managers want to introduce one motivation method for all 24 advisers. The advisers carry out similar customer-service and stock-display tasks, but their personal circumstances differ. The managing director wants the method chosen to increase effort and persistence at work without reducing service quality.
question.stem: Using the data, analyse how Harbour Homeware should take account of differences between its employees when choosing financial and non-financial motivation methods.

table.title: Information about Harbour Homeware's sales advisers

cells: Most said that being able to choose shifts around college would matter more than a higher hourly rate.
Most said they wanted greater responsibility for planning displays and solving customer problems.
Most said that earning more money was important, but managers report that they still need support to learn the product range.

levels.descriptor: Shows limited knowledge of a financial or non-financial motivation method. Application to Harbour Homeware may be asserted or incomplete, with little explanation of how employees could respond differently.

Shows clear understanding of how at least one employee group or job-related factor could influence the choice of a motivation method. Includes relevant application and a logical chain from the method to motivation and likely behaviour or performance.

Shows well-developed analysis of differences between employee groups and makes a supported judgement about selecting methods. Analyses more than one relevant influence or explains why one uniform method may be unsuitable, recognising that motivation alone may not improve performance where capability, training or resources constrain it.

indicative_content: The nine student advisers may value flexible working because it gives them more control over fitting work around college. Better work-life balance could increase retention and willingness to work agreed shifts; a higher hourly rate may be less effective for this group if the timing of work remains unsuitable.

The experienced advisers' preference for responsibility suggests empowerment may provide intrinsic motivation through achievement, responsibility and recognition. Allowing them to resolve customer problems or plan displays could increase effort and speed up decisions, but training and trust are needed to reduce inconsistent decisions or mistakes.

A sales bonus is an extrinsic financial method that may encourage new advisers to make sales. However, their need to learn the product range means weak capability could limit customer service or sales even if they are motivated; training and support are also needed.

A single method is unlikely to motivate every adviser equally because individuals can respond differently to the same reward or job design. Harbour Homeware could use different methods for different groups rather than assuming pay will solve retention and performance problems.
If the bonus measures only sales volume, advisers may focus on quick sales rather than appropriate advice and service quality. The design of the incentive therefore matters.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Harbour Homeware should not assume that one method will motivate all 24 advisers. For the nine students, flexible working may be more appropriate than a higher rate of pay. If they can choose shifts that fit around college, work may be easier to sustain alongside study. This could improve their willingness to remain with the business and reduce staff turnover.

For the experienced full-time advisers, empowerment may be more motivating. Giving them responsibility for displays and customer problems can provide achievement and recognition, which may encourage greater effort. It could also allow customer issues to be solved more quickly. However, managers need to trust employees and provide suitable training, otherwise decisions may be inconsistent.

A monthly sales bonus may motivate new advisers through extra pay, but it should not be the only response. They still need to learn the product range, so limited capability could prevent good performance even when they want to earn the bonus. Harbour Homeware should therefore combine training with the bonus and avoid using a single motivation method for every employee group.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice question. ParcelPath Ltd is a UK online retailer that dispatches household goods from a warehouse in Birmingham. Late dispatches and picking errors have increased over the last six months. The operations manager proposes a Taylor-style approach: split order picking into tightly defined tasks, specify the quickest approved method for each task and introduce a payment of £0.18 for every correctly completed order above each employee's daily target. The manager believes that clearer task design and an economic incentive will increase effort and productivity.
question.stem: Evaluate whether ParcelPath Ltd should introduce the proposed Taylor-style approach in its warehouse.

table.title: ParcelPath warehouse data

cells: Average orders picked per employee per day
Employee survey: staff saying they understand the daily target
Employee survey: staff saying scanners regularly lose connection
Employee survey: staff wanting more variety or responsibility in their role
Employee survey: staff saying additional pay would encourage them to work faster
New starters in the last three months
18 employees; 12 have not yet completed scanner training

levels.descriptor: Shows limited knowledge of Taylor-style management and/or makes simple comments about ParcelPath. May identify that payment per correctly completed order could encourage employees to work faster. Judgement, if present, is asserted rather than supported.

Shows clear understanding and applies it to ParcelPath. Explains how tightly defined tasks and payment above target could influence effort and output, and considers at least one relevant limitation, such as errors, employee differences or inadequate scanner training. Includes a judgement, although this may be conditional or not fully developed.

Shows thorough, balanced analysis of the proposed approach in the context of the data. Develops clear chains from task design and economic incentives to motivation, behaviour and performance, while recognising that motivation does not automatically create performance. Evaluates important constraints and unintended consequences, reaches a well-supported, contextual judgement, and may recommend conditions or changes to the proposal.

indicative_content: Taylor-style management in this context uses tightly designed tasks and an economic incentive. The £0.18 payment for correctly completed orders above target could motivate some employees through external financial reward, especially as 61% say extra pay would encourage faster work.

Clearer approved methods may reduce uncertainty and help employees work consistently. This could raise orders picked per day from 96 and help improve the on-time dispatch rate from 82% towards the 95% target.

The incentive is linked to correctly completed orders, which may reduce the risk that employees simply work faster and ignore accuracy. However, employees may still focus on the measured target rather than other useful behaviour, and poorly designed incentives can create unintended behaviour.

The evidence suggests a system constraint: 38% report scanner connection problems and 12 of 18 new starters have not completed scanner training. Employees may be motivated by pay but still be unable to work quickly or accurately because they lack reliable resources or capability.

The 46% wanting more variety or responsibility may react negatively to more tightly defined tasks. A single approach may not motivate all employees, since people respond differently to rewards and job design.

ParcelPath should address scanner reliability and training before judging the approach unsuccessful. A trial, with monitoring of both on-time dispatches and errors, could test whether the payment and task design improve performance without worsening quality.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
ParcelPath could benefit from the proposal because it combines clear task design with an economic incentive. If employees know the quickest approved method for each picking task, there may be less confusion about how work should be completed. In addition, 61% of staff say that extra pay would encourage them to work faster. The £0.18 payment for correctly completed orders above target could therefore increase effort and help raise average output above 96 orders per employee per day. If more orders are picked promptly, the on-time dispatch rate could move closer to the 95% target.

However, the approach may not solve the main causes of weak performance. Motivation is not the same as performance. For example, 38% of employees report unreliable scanner connections, and 12 of the 18 new starters have not completed scanner training. Even an employee who wants the extra payment may be unable to pick orders quickly or accurately without functioning equipment and the necessary capability. Introducing the scheme before fixing these issues could cause employees to see targets as unfair.

There is also a risk that tightly defined tasks reduce motivation for some staff. Nearly half of employees want more variety or responsibility. These employees may value interest or responsibility more than a small financial reward, so a more controlled job design could reduce their effort or increase dissatisfaction. Although linking payment to correctly completed orders should protect quality, employees may still concentrate on the measured target and overlook other aspects of warehouse work.

Overall, ParcelPath should not introduce the full approach immediately across the warehouse. It should first improve scanner reliability and complete training for new starters. It could then run a short trial of clearer task methods and the accuracy-linked payment, monitoring both dispatch speed and picking errors. This is more likely to show whether the approach improves performance rather than merely increasing pressure on employees.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice question. Northway Homewares operates a warehouse in Leeds supplying online orders. The 48 warehouse employees pick, pack and dispatch customer orders. The operations manager is considering replacing a monthly attendance bonus with a package of flexible start and finish times, job rotation between picking and packing, and a chance for experienced employees to act as shift coordinators. The manager says this approach will motivate employees by meeting different needs, using Maslow's hierarchy of needs. However, the warehouse has recently had several scanner faults and two experienced staff have left.
question.stem: Evaluate whether Northway Homewares should introduce the proposed motivation package using Maslow's hierarchy of needs. Use the data provided to support a justified judgement.

table.title: Northway Homewares employee survey and operating data

cells: Employees saying the attendance bonus is important to them
Employees saying flexible working would improve their work-life balance
Employees saying they would like greater responsibility at work
Employees saying repetitive tasks are a reason they may leave
Late orders linked by supervisors to scanner faults
New employees who have worked at Northway for under three months

levels.descriptor: A well-developed evaluation that accurately uses Maslow's hierarchy as a model of differing employee needs and applies it closely to the data. Analysis explains how the package could affect motivation and behaviour, while considering relevant limitations and other constraints on performance. A clear, contextual and justified judgement is reached.

A reasonable analysis of how one or more elements of the package could motivate employees, with some use of the Northway data. There is some consideration of a limitation or alternative factor, and a judgement is given, although it may be conditional or not fully developed.

Basic knowledge of motivation or Maslow's hierarchy, with limited application to Northway. The response may identify benefits of flexible working, job rotation or responsibility, but explanation, use of data and/or judgement is limited.

indicative_content: Maslow's hierarchy is a model that organises different categories of human need; therefore, Northway should not assume that every employee will be motivated by the same reward.

Flexible working may help meet needs connected with employees' circumstances outside work: 31 of 48 employees say it would improve work-life balance. This could improve persistence and reduce labour turnover.

Job rotation may reduce boredom and build a wider range of skills, which is relevant because 29 of 48 employees identify repetitive work as a possible reason for leaving. However, rotation requires training time and may reduce short-run productivity.

Shift-coordinator opportunities could provide responsibility, achievement and recognition for some experienced employees. This may raise motivation, but only 26 of 48 say they want greater responsibility, so the effect is unlikely to be universal.
Removing the attendance bonus may demotivate the 14 employees who regard it as important. Retaining some form of financial reward, or introducing the package gradually, could reduce this risk.
Motivation is not the same as performance. Scanner faults account for 4 percentage points of the 9% late-order rate, so improved motivation alone will not solve the late-dispatch problem.
Twelve employees are new and may need training and clear support before they can benefit from job rotation or coordinator responsibility.

A justified conclusion may support a trial of the package alongside repairs to scanners and training, rather than fully replacing the bonus immediately. The final decision depends on employee responses and whether operational constraints are addressed.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Northway's package could be more effective than relying only on an attendance bonus because Maslow's hierarchy treats employees as having different categories of need. Flexible working may be valuable for employees whose motivation is affected by their wider circumstances: 31 out of 48 say it would improve work-life balance. If this reduces conflict between work and home commitments, employees may be more willing to remain with Northway and maintain effort.

Job rotation and coordinator roles could also increase intrinsic motivation. Rotation may reduce the boredom identified by 29 employees and give staff broader skills. Coordinator roles offer responsibility and recognition, which may motivate some employees through achievement. This is relevant as 26 employees want more responsibility. In turn, lower boredom and greater responsibility could reduce the risk of employees leaving.

However, Maslow's hierarchy is a model rather than a rule: employees will not necessarily respond in the same way. Removing the attendance bonus could reduce motivation for the 14 employees who say it is important. Also, the package may not improve delivery performance quickly. Twelve employees are new, so rotation and extra responsibility need training, while scanner faults explain 4 percentage points of the 9% late-order rate. Highly motivated staff still cannot dispatch orders efficiently when essential equipment fails.

Overall, Northway should introduce the package on a trial basis, rather than immediately remove the bonus for all staff. It should repair scanners and provide training at the same time. This is likely to meet a wider range of employee needs, but retaining or adapting a financial reward would recognise that some staff may value it more than flexibility or responsibility.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Northshore Kitchens Ltd makes fitted kitchen units in Leeds. Its 48 production employees work in small assembly teams. Output per employee has fallen and the business has received more late-delivery complaints. The operations manager, Priya Shah, is considering replacing some individual, repetitive tasks with team-based roles. Each team would plan its daily work, check finished units and nominate a team member to present improvement ideas to managers. Priya believes this approach reflects Herzberg's two-factor theory.
question.stem: Evaluate whether Northshore Kitchens Ltd should introduce Priya Shah's proposed team-based roles to improve employee performance. Use Herzberg's two-factor theory and the data provided.

table.title: Employee survey and operations data at Northshore Kitchens Ltd

cells: Employees who say they would value more responsibility or recognition for good work
Employees who report that faulty cutting equipment delays their work at least weekly
Employees who say their current tasks are repetitive
Average units completed per employee each week, six months ago
Average units completed per employee each week, now
Cost of training teams to plan work and carry out quality checks
Estimated time before all teams can work independently

levels.descriptor: Shows accurate understanding of Herzberg's distinction between hygiene conditions and motivating factors. Develops balanced, contextual analysis of the proposed roles using the data, including limitations caused by operational constraints, and reaches a clear, justified judgement.

Shows some relevant understanding of Herzberg's theory and applies it to Northshore Kitchens. Gives developed analysis of at least one benefit or limitation, with some use of the data. A judgement is present but may be unsupported or not fully balanced.

Shows limited knowledge of motivation or Herzberg's theory. Makes simple, generic assertions about responsibility, recognition, teamwork, pay or productivity, with little application, analysis or judgement.

indicative_content: Herzberg distinguishes between hygiene conditions and motivating factors. Improving motivating factors, rather than only removing dissatisfaction, may increase effort and persistence.

The team-based roles could provide responsibility: teams would plan daily work and check quality. Presenting improvement ideas may also provide recognition. This may make work more meaningful and reduce the effect of repetitive tasks reported by 35 of 48 employees.

The proposal is supported by survey evidence: 31 of 48 employees say they would value more responsibility or recognition. Higher motivation could encourage greater care and effort, potentially improving output and reducing late deliveries.

However, faulty cutting equipment is a separate performance constraint. Twenty-two of 48 employees report weekly delays, so motivated teams may still be unable to raise output while equipment prevents work. The fall from 18 to 15 units per employee may therefore not be mainly a motivation problem.

Training costs £24,000 and teams need three months before working independently. During this period, productivity could fall further or quality checks could be inconsistent if employees lack the capability to take on new responsibilities.
Employees may respond differently to the same job design. The survey does not prove that responsibility or recognition will cause higher performance, and motivation is not identical to performance.

A justified conclusion may support a phased introduction only if Northshore also repairs or replaces the cutting equipment and provides training; otherwise the operational bottleneck makes the full investment risky.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Herzberg's two-factor theory separates hygiene conditions from motivating factors. Priya's proposal is likely to add motivating factors because employees would have greater responsibility for planning work and checking quality, while presenting ideas to managers could provide recognition. This could make employees more willing to put sustained effort into their work. It is relevant that 31 of the 48 employees say they would value more responsibility or recognition. Also, 35 employees describe their tasks as repetitive, so broader team roles may reduce boredom. Greater care in quality checks could reduce errors and help Northshore improve late deliveries.

However, motivation may not be the main reason why output has fallen from 18 to 15 units per employee each week. Twenty-two employees report that faulty cutting equipment delays them at least weekly. Even a highly motivated team cannot complete units when equipment prevents production. This is an operational constraint, so introducing team roles alone may not improve performance. The business would also pay £24,000 for training and wait three months before teams can work independently, creating a risk of disruption in the short term.

Overall, Northshore should not rely on the proposed roles by themselves. The approach could improve motivation for many employees, but its effect on performance is uncertain while equipment remains unreliable. A phased trial with training and repairs to the cutting equipment would be the strongest decision, because it addresses both motivation and the resource constraint.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

Units organised around what the business sells.

Separate regional teams for NorthStar's UK shop locations.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Harbour Homewares is a growing UK retailer with 18 shops. Each shop has one shop manager who directly supervises 12 sales assistants. points.descriptor: Identifies that span of control is the number of employees directly managed by a manager.
accept: A correct definition of span of control.
The number of direct reports a manager has.

points.descriptor: Applies span of control to Harbour Homewares: the shop manager’s span could fall from 12 sales assistants to three team leaders, while each team leader would supervise four sales assistants.
accept: Shop managers would have fewer direct reports.
Team leaders would each manage four assistants.
The manager’s span becomes narrower.

points.descriptor: Identifies that hierarchy is the number of levels of authority or reporting within a business.
accept: A correct definition of hierarchy.
Layers of management or formal authority.

accept: There would be another management layer.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Span of control means the number of direct reports a manager supervises. At present, each shop manager directly manages 12 sales assistants. questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Harbour Brew is a chain of 18 coffee shops across the South West. Currently, the head office approves all staff rotas, local supplier orders and customer refund decisions. The owners are considering allowing each shop manager to make these decisions within agreed spending limits, while head office continues to set company-wide standards and monitor performance.
question.stem: Explain how delegation could help Harbour Brew to move towards a more decentralised approach to decision-making.

points.descriptor: Identifies delegation as giving a manager authority to make defined decisions or carry out specified work, while accountability remains within the business.
accept: Delegation is passing authority for particular tasks or decisions to another employee.
Delegation allows managers to make decisions within limits set by senior managers.

points.descriptor: Applies delegation to Harbour Brew by explaining that shop managers could be given authority over rotas, supplier orders or customer refunds within agreed spending limits.
accept: Shop managers could approve refunds without waiting for head office.
Shop managers could alter rotas to deal with busy periods.
Shop managers could place local supplier orders within a budget.

points.descriptor: Explains that delegating these decisions would decentralise decision-making because authority would move from head office to shop-level managers.
accept: Decisions would be made closer to individual coffee shops rather than centrally at head office.
Shop managers would have more local decision authority.

points.descriptor: Explains a likely benefit to Harbour Brew, such as quicker responses to customer complaints or changing demand, while head office can retain overall control through standards, spending limits and performance monitoring.
accept: Customers may receive refunds more quickly, improving service.
Managers could adjust rotas promptly when a shop becomes busy.
Head office can still maintain control by setting limits and monitoring shop performance.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Delegation is when authority for defined decisions is passed to another manager, although the business retains overall accountability. Harbour Brew could delegate authority to shop managers to change staff rotas, order from local suppliers and approve refunds within agreed spending limits. This would make the business more decentralised because decisions would be taken in individual shops rather than being approved by head office. For example, a manager could respond immediately to a customer complaint with a refund, while head office still controls standards and monitors performance.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Harbour Homeware Ltd sells kitchen products online. Its stated values include treating customers honestly and reducing waste. Employee voice through team meetings.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Hearth & Grain is a growing bakery business in Leeds. mark_scheme.model_answer: A power culture is where influence is concentrated around a central person or small group. Hearth & Grain shows this because Sana personally approves discounts, selects suppliers and handles staff problems. A role culture is based on defined responsibilities and formal procedures.
