Managers whose bonus is mainly determined by labour-cost performance

levels.descriptor: Shows limited knowledge of employee relations, employee voice or culture. Application to HarbourBrew may be general or based on an isolated item of data, with little explanation of consequences.

Explains how the forums could improve communication, representation or handling of concerns, and makes some relevant application to HarbourBrew. Analysis includes at least one developed link to employee relations or culture, although the chain of reasoning may be incomplete.

Provides clear, developed analysis of how representative consultation could strengthen employee relations and shape expected behaviours at HarbourBrew. Uses the data effectively and recognises how management incentives may reinforce or undermine the intended culture.

indicative_content: The forums give employees representative voice: concerns about rotas can be exchanged with managers before they become more serious disputes.
Written responses within ten working days may show employees that concerns are considered. This could build trust, improve relations and help explain the fall in formal grievances from 15 to 8.
Better employee relations may contribute to lower turnover, from 24% to 18%, because employees may feel listened to rather than leave after unresolved concerns.
If managers repeatedly listen to employee representatives and act on issues, this may create a culture where constructive challenge is expected and tolerated, rather than employees remaining silent.
The forums do not automatically create meaningful voice: 7 of the 46 issues did not receive a response within the stated time, which could weaken trust.

The culture promoted by the forums could conflict with the bonus system. Since 72% of managers are mainly rewarded for labour-cost performance, managers may prioritise cheaper rotas over responding to employee concerns, teaching employees that cost control matters more than challenge or wellbeing.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
The employee forums could improve employee relations by giving staff representatives a structured way to raise rota concerns with regional managers. This can improve the exchange of information and allow problems to be discussed before they become formal disputes. For example, formal grievances fell from 15 to 8 in the six months after the forums began. If employees believe that managers will listen and respond, relationships may become less confrontational. This may also help explain why employee turnover fell from 24% to 18%, as employees who feel represented may be less likely to leave.

The forums could also influence culture because repeated management behaviour teaches employees what is genuinely expected. Where employees can challenge decisions and receive a written reply, HarbourBrew may develop a norm that constructive challenge is accepted. However, the effect may be limited. Only 39 of 46 issues received a response within ten working days, so some employees may conclude that their voice is not consistently valued. In addition, 72% of managers are mainly rewarded for keeping labour costs below target. If this leads managers to dismiss rota concerns in order to reduce staffing costs, the lived culture may become one of silence and cost control, despite the directors’ stated aim of constructive challenge.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice. Northstar Kitchens Ltd makes fitted kitchens for independent retailers. Its new managing director wants the business to compete by reducing installation errors and responding more quickly when delivery risks are identified. At present, team leaders are rewarded mainly for completing the highest number of installations each week. Employees can submit concerns through an online form, but managers do not always reply. The managing director plans to change the culture so that employees are expected to raise risks and work with other teams to solve them.
question.stem: Analyse why Northstar Kitchens may need to change its culture and one problem it could face when making this change.

table.title: Selected workforce information at Northstar Kitchens

cells: Employees who agree that they can raise delivery or safety concerns without negative consequences
Employees who say they received a response after submitting a concern online
Installation errors in the last 12 months
Employees leaving the business in the last 12 months

levels.descriptor: Clear and developed analysis of both a reason for cultural change and a relevant problem of achieving it, consistently applied to Northstar. Shows linked consequences for behaviour and business performance.
Some analysis of a reason for, and/or a problem with, changing culture, with relevant application to Northstar. Chains of reasoning may be incomplete or uneven.
Limited knowledge of culture change with simple application to the case. Response may identify a reason or problem without explaining its consequences.

indicative_content: Northstar's new strategy requires employees to identify and raise delivery or safety risks, so a culture that rewards only the volume of completed installations may conflict with this aim.

Only 28% of employees feel able to raise concerns without negative consequences and only 22% receive a response. This suggests that the lived culture may discourage voice, meaning delivery risks and causes of installation errors may remain undiscovered.
A change towards listening to concerns and cross-team problem solving could improve information sharing and help reduce the 96 installation errors, supporting the new strategy.

Cultural change may be resisted because established values and habits are deeply held. Team leaders may continue to prioritise weekly installation numbers because this is what the existing reward system recognises.

If employees believe that raising concerns is still ignored or penalised, they may not trust the proposed change. The business may therefore take a long time to establish new expected behaviours, and employees who reject the new approach may leave.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Northstar needs to change its culture because its new strategy depends on employees raising delivery and safety risks early. Currently, team leaders are rewarded mainly for completing the largest number of installations, which may teach employees that speed matters more than reporting possible problems. This is reinforced by only 28% of employees feeling safe to raise concerns. If risks are not raised, the business may fail to find the causes of its 96 installation errors. A culture that genuinely values employee voice and joint problem solving could provide managers with better information, allowing errors to be addressed and helping Northstar respond faster.

However, changing the culture could be difficult because existing habits and incentives are already established. Team leaders may resist a change if they believe that spending time discussing risks will reduce their weekly installation totals. Also, employees have seen that only 22% of online concerns receive a response, so they may doubt that management will act differently. Unless Northstar changes what it rewards and responds to concerns consistently, staff may continue to stay silent and the intended cultural change could take a long time to become normal behaviour.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice. Northgate Home Systems Ltd designs and installs smart heating controls for UK housebuilders. It employs 84 people. The managing director currently approves product changes, pricing and installation-process changes. Departments have separate procedures and employees normally pass requests upwards through their line manager. Following delays in responding to housebuilders’ requests for bespoke controls, the managing director is considering replacing this approach with multidisciplinary project teams. Each team would include engineers, installers, sales staff and a purchasing employee, and would have authority to solve a client problem without waiting for the managing director’s approval. Team members would be selected for their expertise and would move to another project when their work is complete.
question.stem: Evaluate whether Northgate Home Systems Ltd should introduce a task culture.

table.title: Northgate Home Systems Ltd: operational information

cells: Average time from client request to agreed solution
Client requests completed after the promised date
Product or installation changes awaiting managing director approval
Employees who say departments share useful information quickly
Number of major client projects expected in the next 12 months

levels.descriptor: Shows limited knowledge of Handy’s culture types and makes generic assertions about Northgate. May identify task culture as involving teams or projects, but explanation and judgement are undeveloped.

Shows clear knowledge and application of Handy’s culture types. Analyses how a task culture could affect Northgate’s decisions or performance, with some consideration of a limitation or alternative approach. Reaches a conclusion, though it may not be fully supported by the evidence.

Shows thorough, well-applied analysis of Handy’s culture types. Develops balanced chains of reasoning using the data, considering why task culture may suit some work but not all of Northgate’s activities. Makes a well-supported, contextual judgement about whether and how the business should introduce task culture.

indicative_content: A task culture brings people together around expertise and project or problem delivery. Northgate’s proposed teams combine engineering, installation, sales and purchasing expertise, so they could resolve bespoke client requests more quickly.

Project teams with authority to act could reduce the 22 changes awaiting the managing director’s approval. This may reduce the current 18-working-day response time and help lower the 31% of client requests completed late.

Northgate currently displays features consistent with power culture because influence is concentrated around the managing director, and role culture because departments use separate procedures and requests move through line managers. These approaches can provide control and clear responsibilities, but may slow cross-functional responses.

The low 29% result for rapid information sharing suggests that simply creating teams will not automatically solve coordination problems. Team members need genuine authority and effective information sharing rather than having every important decision returned to the managing director.

Task culture could be appropriate for the 14 major client projects, where varied specialist knowledge is needed. However, Northgate may still need defined procedures and responsibilities for routine installation, safety or repeated activities; a complete replacement of all role-based practices may create inconsistency.

Handy’s types are ideal patterns. Northgate may contain different cultures across teams, so management should use evidence from project performance and employee experience rather than assume that naming the culture guarantees improvement.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Northgate should introduce task culture for its major bespoke client projects, but it should not attempt to replace every existing way of working immediately.

A task culture organises people around expertise and solving a particular problem. Northgate’s proposed teams would bring together engineers, installers, sales staff and purchasing employees. This is likely to suit bespoke controls because a client request may require technical, supply and installation decisions at the same time. At present, only 29% of employees believe useful information is shared quickly between departments. A cross-functional team could share that knowledge directly, rather than each department passing information upwards and across separate procedures.

The change could also improve responsiveness. Northgate has 22 changes waiting for the managing director’s approval and takes an average of 18 working days to agree a solution. This suggests features of a power culture, since influence is concentrated around the managing director. Giving expert project teams authority could remove this bottleneck. If solutions are agreed faster, Northgate may reduce the 31% of client requests completed after the promised date, helping it manage the 14 major projects expected next year.

However, task culture is not automatically the best culture for all activities. The present departmental procedures have role-culture features: responsibilities and procedures are clearly defined. These may still be valuable for routine work, where consistency is important. Also, if teams lack clear boundaries, they may make different decisions for similar clients. The 29% information-sharing result also means that management must ensure that teams genuinely cooperate; merely calling a group a project team would not guarantee better coordination.

Overall, Northgate should introduce task culture on the 14 major client projects, where combining specialist expertise is most likely to speed problem solving. It should retain clear procedures for routine work and set limits on the decisions teams can make. This blended approach is more justified than a complete cultural replacement because it addresses approval delays while retaining the consistency that defined responsibilities can provide.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice question. Northline Homeware Ltd assembles flat-pack furniture at a UK factory. Orders have increased, but output per employee has remained below the factory’s target for the last four months. Employees report that some workstations lack reliable tools and that teams are sometimes short-staffed. The operations director proposes introducing tightly specified assembly tasks, with supervisors monitoring the quickest method. Employees who exceed their daily output target would receive a cash bonus. The director states: “A business can achieve high employee performance mainly by paying workers for higher output.” Some employees have asked for greater responsibility and recognition, while others say that predictable pay and secure working conditions matter most to them.
question.stem:
Evaluate the view that Northline Homeware Ltd can achieve high employee performance mainly by paying workers for higher output.

In your answer, use Taylor’s scientific management, Maslow’s hierarchy of needs and Herzberg’s two-factor theory.

levels.descriptor: Shows limited knowledge of motivation, with little or no accurate use of the named theories. Application to Northline is absent or very general. Makes simple assertions about pay or performance, with little developed reasoning or judgement.

Shows some accurate knowledge of one or more named theories. Includes some relevant application to Northline, such as bonuses, output targets or working conditions. Analysis is partially developed but tends to assume that motivation automatically creates performance. Judgement is limited or unsupported.

Shows clear knowledge of Taylor, Maslow and/or Herzberg, with relevant application to the business. Explains how output-related pay and task design could affect effort and behaviour. Also identifies at least one relevant limitation, such as employee differences or resource constraints. Reaches a judgement, although it may not be fully balanced or sustained.

Shows well-developed and mostly balanced analysis using the named theories. Applies arguments closely to Northline’s specified tasks, cash bonus, employee concerns and operational difficulties. Explains why pay may improve effort for some employees but may not address all needs or causes of weak performance. Reaches a supported judgement that considers conditions and relative importance.

Shows sustained, perceptive and balanced evaluation of the claim. Integrates Taylor, Maslow and Herzberg accurately as contrasting lenses rather than treating them as universal laws. Uses the Northline context consistently to assess causal links between rewards, motivation and performance, including capability, tools, staffing and process constraints. Reaches a clear, nuanced and well-justified overall judgement about whether output-related pay should be the main approach.

indicative_content: Taylor’s scientific management supports the director’s proposal: tightly specified tasks, monitoring the quickest method and financial incentives may encourage employees to increase effort and follow an efficient process.

A cash bonus for exceeding output targets is an extrinsic reward. It may be particularly effective where assembly work is measurable and employees believe that extra effort can lead directly to extra pay.

Taylor’s approach may be less effective if targets encourage unintended behaviour, for example prioritising speed over care, or if employees cannot achieve targets because tools are unreliable or teams are short-staffed.

Maslow’s hierarchy suggests employees may have different categories of needs. Some Northline employees may value predictable pay and secure working conditions, whereas others may respond more to responsibility or recognition. A single bonus scheme may therefore not motivate everyone equally.

Herzberg’s two-factor theory distinguishes hygiene conditions from motivating factors. Reliable tools, adequate staffing, predictable pay and secure conditions may prevent dissatisfaction, but greater responsibility and recognition may be more likely to create positive motivation for some workers.
Motivation is not identical to performance. Even highly motivated assemblers may be unable to raise output if they lack equipment, staffing, capability, clear priorities or an effective process.

Northline could combine fair and predictable pay with output bonuses, reliable tools, staffing improvements, recognition and greater responsibility. This may address a broader range of employee needs and operational constraints.
The most appropriate policy depends on evidence from Northline, including whether low output results mainly from low effort, poor job design, insufficient resources or a mixture of causes.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Paying employees for higher output could help Northline improve performance, but it is unlikely to be sufficient as the main solution on its own.

Taylor’s scientific management supports the operations director’s proposal. Assembly work can be broken into tightly specified tasks, and supervisors can identify and monitor an efficient method. If employees receive a cash bonus for exceeding a daily target, the link between additional effort and reward may be clear. This could raise effort and persistence, particularly because output in a furniture assembly factory is relatively easy to measure. It may also reduce variation in how tasks are completed, helping Northline meet its output target.

However, Taylor’s approach assumes that financial incentives and task control will produce the desired behaviour. Northline’s employees are already reporting unreliable tools and short staffing. A motivated employee may work harder for a bonus but still be unable to assemble more furniture when equipment delays the task or a team lacks enough people. Therefore, the business could wrongly conclude that low output is caused by low motivation when the main constraint is resources or process design. In addition, a poorly designed output target could encourage employees to focus on speed rather than careful assembly.

Maslow’s hierarchy suggests that employees will not all be motivated by the same factor. The employees seeking predictable pay and secure working conditions may value these needs more than a variable bonus. By contrast, employees asking for greater responsibility and recognition may respond less strongly to cash alone. Consequently, paying for output may motivate part of the workforce, but it may not create consistent effort across all teams. A combination of fair predictable pay, secure conditions, recognition and opportunities for responsibility may be more effective.

Herzberg’s two-factor theory also questions whether a bonus should be Northline’s main policy. Reliable tools, sufficient staffing and predictable pay may be hygiene conditions: improving them may reduce dissatisfaction, but they may not necessarily create strong positive motivation. The requests for recognition and responsibility point towards motivating factors. Giving trained employees responsibility for checking quality or improving their workstation could provide achievement and recognition, potentially encouraging more sustained commitment than a daily payment alone.

Overall, output-related pay could be useful at Northline because the work is measurable and Taylor’s approach may increase short-term effort. Nevertheless, the director’s claim is too strong. Performance depends not only on motivation but also on tools, staffing, capability and process design. Northline should first fix the operational barriers, then use a carefully designed bonus alongside predictable pay, recognition and appropriate responsibility. This broader approach is more likely to improve both output and the quality of assembly over time.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice. Harbour Bowl Ltd operates six casual dining restaurants in coastal towns. In January 2025, the business reduced restaurant staffing levels to control costs. Managers also introduced a social-media campaign promoting faster service and family meal deals. The directors want to assess whether the business's overall performance has improved.
question.stem: Using the data, analyse whether Harbour Bowl Ltd's overall performance has improved following the staffing reduction and marketing campaign.

table.title: Selected performance data for Harbour Bowl Ltd

cells: Labour cost as a percentage of sales revenue

levels.descriptor: Shows limited analysis using one or more figures from the data. May identify an improvement or deterioration, with a simple or incomplete link between functional areas.

Shows developed analysis of linked operations, HR and/or marketing evidence. Explains how changes in one area may affect another and reaches an implied or stated view of performance, although the judgement may be uneven.

Shows well-developed, balanced analysis using relevant operations, HR and marketing data together. Explains plausible causal chains and trade-offs, recognises that short-term gains may conflict with longer-term performance, and reaches a justified judgement on overall performance.

indicative_content: Marketing performance appears stronger: monthly meals sold increased from 18,000 to 20,700 and local market share rose from 12% to 14%. The social-media campaign and meal deals may have attracted customers from competitors.
The staffing reduction may have helped reduce labour cost as a percentage of sales revenue from 31% to 27%, improving cost control in the short term.

Operations performance has weakened: fewer employees per restaurant may have reduced capacity at busy times, contributing to waiting times increasing from 11 to 18 minutes and meal errors rising from 1.8% to 4.6%.

HR data may help explain the operational deterioration. Labour turnover rose from 3% to 9%, so less experienced employees and repeated recruitment could reduce service consistency and increase errors.

The marketing-led increase in demand may itself have placed additional pressure on restaurants with fewer staff. Therefore, higher sales and market share do not necessarily show that the business can meet demand effectively.

Customer satisfaction fell from 82% to 71%. If poor waiting times and errors continue, dissatisfied customers may not return, reducing retention and potentially reversing the sales and market-share gains.

Overall performance has improved in terms of sales, market share and labour-cost control, but the evidence suggests this may not be sustainable unless Harbour Bowl resolves the people and capacity constraints causing poorer service.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Harbour Bowl has achieved some short-term improvements. Monthly meals sold increased by 2,700, from 18,000 to 20,700, while market share rose from 12% to 14%. This suggests the family meal deals and social-media campaign have increased demand. In addition, labour cost as a percentage of sales revenue fell from 31% to 27%, so reducing staff may have improved cost control.

However, the data indicates that operations and HR performance have worsened. Average staffing fell from 24 to 20 employees per restaurant at the same time as meals sold increased. This combination may have created a capacity bottleneck, helping to explain why customer waiting time rose from 11 to 18 minutes and meal errors increased from 1.8% to 4.6%.

Higher labour turnover, rising from 3% to 9%, may be contributing to these operational problems. New or less experienced staff may make more errors or work less efficiently. Poorer service is likely to have affected customers, as satisfaction fell from 82% to 71%. If customers do not return because of long waits or incorrect meals, the current increase in market share may be temporary.

Overall, Harbour Bowl's sales, market share and labour-cost performance have improved, but its overall performance is not clearly stronger because the growth appears to be straining staffing and service capacity. The improvement is unlikely to be sustainable unless the business reduces turnover or increases its ability to serve the higher level of demand.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Northmoor Bikes, a UK manufacturer, imports gear systems from Japan. The UK government introduces a new charge on imported gear systems to support UK component manufacturers.
question.stem: Identify the international trade policy described.

options.label: A
options.text: A tariff

options.label: B
options.text: A quota

options.label: C
options.text: A subsidy

options.label: D
options.text: A trading bloc

option_rationale: A is correct because a tariff is a tax or charge imposed on imports.
B is incorrect because a quota restricts the quantity of a product that may be imported, rather than imposing a charge.
C is incorrect because a subsidy is financial support for an activity or producer, rather than a charge on imported goods.
D is incorrect because a trading bloc is a group of economies that reduces trade barriers between its members.
mark_scheme.model_answer: : A tariff

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Northern Crumb is a UK biscuit business that has exported its products to Lydora. Previously, open trade meant that its biscuits entered Lydora without an import tariff. The Lydoran government has now introduced an 18% tariff on imported biscuits. Northern Crumb is considering franchising its brand to local Lydoran bakery businesses, which would make and sell Northern Crumb biscuits locally using its agreed business format.
question.stem: Explain one reason why protectionism in Lydora may encourage Northern Crumb to use franchising rather than continue exporting biscuits from the UK.

points.descriptor: Identifies that a tariff is a tax on imports and is a protectionist trade barrier.
accept: A tariff raises the cost of foreign goods entering a country.
Protectionism restricts or makes imports less competitive.

points.descriptor: Applies the tariff to explain that Northern Crumb's UK-made biscuits would become more expensive to sell in Lydora.
accept: The 18% tariff increases the cost of imported Northern Crumb biscuits.
Northern Crumb may have to raise prices or accept a lower margin on exports to Lydora.

points.descriptor: Identifies that franchising allows another business to use an agreed brand and business format under contract.
accept: A local bakery could operate using Northern Crumb's brand and methods.
Franchising is contractual replication of a business format or brand.

points.descriptor: Applies franchising to explain that biscuits made by Lydoran franchisees would not be imported from the UK, so the import tariff on finished biscuits could be avoided, helping Northern Crumb remain competitive in Lydora.
accept: Local production through franchisees could avoid the tariff on imported finished biscuits.
Avoiding the tariff may allow a lower selling price or protect Northern Crumb's margin in Lydora.

mark_scheme.model_answer: The 18% tariff is a tax on imported biscuits, so it increases the cost of Northern Crumb's products sent from the UK to Lydora. This could force the business to increase its price or reduce its profit margin. Franchising would allow local Lydoran bakeries to use Northern Crumb's brand and business format to make biscuits locally. As the finished biscuits would not be imported from the UK, the tariff could be avoided, helping the brand remain competitive.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: PeakTrail Ltd is a UK producer of low-cost hiking equipment. It is considering selling through online retailers in Noria, an emerging economy where port facilities and mobile-payment networks have recently improved. The directors believe that increased links between countries could make this expansion possible.
question.stem: Explain how globalisation could create an opportunity for PeakTrail Ltd in an emerging economy such as Noria. In your answer, explain both globalisation and an emerging economy.

points.descriptor: Explains globalisation as increasing integration of business or economic activity across national borders.
accept: Increasing cross-border links between markets, production, finance, information or business networks.
Businesses becoming more connected internationally.

points.descriptor: Explains an emerging economy as an economy undergoing substantial development and becoming more integrated with wider markets.
accept: A developing and increasingly internationally connected economy.
An economy experiencing significant development; do not require it to be described as poor.

points.descriptor: Applies globalisation to PeakTrail Ltd by explaining that stronger international links could allow the UK business to sell to, coordinate with, or use online retailers in Noria.
accept: Cross-border online retailing could give PeakTrail access to Noria's customers.
Improved international business links could help PeakTrail distribute products from the UK to Noria.

points.descriptor: Applies the characteristics of an emerging economy to explain the opportunity for PeakTrail Ltd, such as improved infrastructure or integration making the Noria market more accessible.
accept: Improved ports could make delivery into Noria easier.
Mobile-payment networks could make online purchases from PeakTrail's retailers easier.
Development and wider market integration could make Noria a more accessible new market.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Globalisation is the increasing integration of business activity across national borders. It could allow PeakTrail to use online retailers in Noria to reach customers outside the UK. An emerging economy is one undergoing substantial development and greater integration with wider markets. Noria's improved ports and mobile-payment networks could make it easier for PeakTrail's products to be delivered and bought online, creating a new sales opportunity.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Northfield Sauces Ltd makes premium cooking sauces at its factory in Yorkshire. It wants to start selling in Canada without opening a factory there. The business owns the recipes and its brand name.
question.stem: Explain how Northfield Sauces Ltd could use both exporting and licensing to sell its sauces in Canada.

points.descriptor: Explains exporting as selling goods made in one country to customers or businesses in another country.
accept: Selling domestically produced sauces from the UK into a foreign market.
Supplying products made in the UK to Canada.

points.descriptor: Applies exporting to Northfield Sauces Ltd: it could produce sauces in its Yorkshire factory and send them to Canadian retailers or a Canadian distributor.
accept: Shipping sauces made in Yorkshire to Canada.
Selling its UK-made sauces through Canadian shops or a distributor.

points.descriptor: Explains licensing as giving another business contractual permission to use specified intellectual property or business rights.
accept: Allowing another firm to use its recipes and/or brand under an agreement.
Giving a Canadian firm the right to use Northfield's brand or sauce recipes.

points.descriptor: Applies licensing to Northfield Sauces Ltd: it could permit a Canadian food producer to make and sell sauces using its recipes and brand, rather than Northfield opening a Canadian factory.
accept: A Canadian producer could make branded sauces using Northfield's recipes.
The firm could license its brand and recipes to a Canadian business, avoiding the need to build its own factory there.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Northfield could export by making its sauces in Yorkshire and shipping them to Canadian retailers or a distributor. Alternatively, it could license its recipes and brand to a Canadian food producer. That producer would then have contractual permission to make and sell Northfield-branded sauces in Canada, so Northfield would not need to open its own factory there.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Oak & Frame Ltd is a UK furniture business. It currently makes all of its flat-pack furniture in Leeds. The directors are considering buying and operating an assembly plant in Poland, where it would assemble products for European customers.
question.stem: Explain how direct investment could allow Oak & Frame Ltd to offshore its assembly operations.

points.descriptor: Identifies direct investment as establishing or acquiring lasting business operations in another country.
accept: FDI involves buying or setting up an overseas operation.
The business would invest in a plant it owns or controls in Poland.

points.descriptor: Explains that offshoring involves moving an activity, such as assembly, from the UK to another country.
accept: Assembly would be relocated from Leeds to Poland.
Production activity would take place overseas rather than in the UK.

points.descriptor: Applies the point to Oak & Frame Ltd by explaining that it could buy and operate the Polish assembly plant rather than merely sell furniture there.
accept: Oak & Frame would establish or acquire the proposed Polish plant.
The firm would control assembly for its European customers from Poland.

points.descriptor: Explains that ownership or control gained through direct investment enables Oak & Frame Ltd to organise and manage the offshored assembly activity.
accept: Direct investment gives greater control over the overseas assembly operation.
Owning the plant allows the business to coordinate its assembly operations in Poland.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Direct investment would involve Oak & Frame Ltd establishing or acquiring a lasting operation in Poland, such as the proposed assembly plant. This would offshore assembly because the activity currently carried out in Leeds would be moved to another country. As Oak & Frame would own or control the Polish plant, it could manage the assembly operation for European customers from Poland.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice. BrewCycle Ltd owns coffee shops in the UK, Spain and Japan. It controls the shops in each country rather than simply exporting coffee to them. Spanish customers prefer sweeter iced drinks, while Japanese rules require different recycling labels on takeaway cups. The directors want every shop to use the same cup design, menu layout and advertising campaign because ordering larger quantities centrally could reduce unit costs.
question.stem: Explain why BrewCycle Ltd is a multinational and how it should balance local responsiveness with cost-reduction pressure in its international operations.

points.descriptor: Identifies why BrewCycle is a multinational.
accept: It owns or controls business operations in more than one country.
It has controlled coffee-shop operations in the UK, Spain and Japan.

points.descriptor: Explains local responsiveness as adapting aspects of the offer or operations to conditions in each country.
accept: Adapting products, marketing or operations to local customer, legal or cultural conditions.
Changing the offer or processes where local requirements differ.

points.descriptor: Applies local responsiveness to BrewCycle.
accept: It could offer sweeter iced drinks in Spain.
It must use recycling labels that meet Japanese rules.

points.descriptor: Explains the cost-reduction benefit of standardisation and applies it to BrewCycle.
accept: Using common cups, menu layouts or advertising can reduce duplication and allow bulk purchasing, lowering unit costs.
It could standardise elements that do not conflict with local needs, while adapting drinks and legally required labels.
Central ordering of shared cup designs or campaigns could reduce BrewCycle's costs.

mark_scheme.model_answer: BrewCycle is a multinational because it owns and controls coffee-shop operations in more than one country: the UK, Spain and Japan. As a multinational, it should adapt where local conditions affect customer value or legal compliance. For example, sweeter iced drinks may better meet Spanish customer preferences, and Japanese recycling labels must meet local rules. However, it can standardise cup designs, menu layouts or advertising where this does not prevent adaptation. Central bulk ordering would reduce duplication and lower unit costs, so BrewCycle should combine local changes where needed with common global activities where possible.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice. PeakBite is a UK producer of oat-and-fruit snack bars. Its directors are considering exporting to Lydora, where it would sell through a national supermarket chain. PeakBite would keep production in the UK and use a local distributor in Lydora. The directors want to judge whether Lydora is an attractive market before committing to the launch.
question.stem: Analyse the attractiveness of Lydora as a market for PeakBite’s snack bars.

table.title: Selected market information for Lydora

cells: Annual growth of packaged snack-bar market
62% of surveyed supermarket shoppers said they would consider buying a fruit-and-oat snack bar
The three largest brands have a combined 78% market share
A 6% tariff is charged on snack bars imported into Lydora
The proposed distributor can supply 1,100 supermarkets, but charges PeakBite 18% of sales revenue
The Lydoran currency fell by 12% against sterling during the past year

levels.descriptor: Shows clear, developed analysis of market attractiveness using relevant data. Explains how two or more factors could affect PeakBite’s sales potential, costs or risk, and reaches a supported overall view.
Shows some analysis of market attractiveness, applied to PeakBite and supported by at least one item of data. Chains of reasoning may be uneven or the overall judgement may be limited.
Shows basic knowledge of factors affecting market attractiveness, with limited application to the data. Response may identify a relevant advantage or disadvantage without explaining its effect fully.

indicative_content: The £240 million market and 9% annual growth suggest potential for sales and future revenue growth. The 62% consumer-research result may indicate customer interest in PeakBite’s product type.
The three leading brands already hold 78% of the market, so PeakBite may find it difficult and costly to gain supermarket visibility and persuade customers to switch brands.

The 6% import tariff raises the cost of UK-produced bars sold in Lydora. The 18% distributor charge further reduces the revenue PeakBite retains, which may reduce profit unless it raises prices or accepts lower margins.
Access to 1,100 supermarkets could give PeakBite wide distribution and make market entry easier, but the falling Lydoran currency means sales revenue converted into sterling may be worth less.
Overall attractiveness depends on whether the market-growth and distribution opportunity are sufficient to outweigh competition, import costs, distributor charges and currency risk.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Lydora has some attractive features for PeakBite. The snack-bar market is worth £240 million and is growing by 9% each year. This gives PeakBite access to a sizeable market in which demand may continue to increase. In addition, 62% of surveyed supermarket shoppers would consider a fruit-and-oat bar, suggesting that there may be customer interest in PeakBite’s product. The distributor’s access to 1,100 supermarkets could also allow the business to reach customers quickly without investing in its own retail network.

However, market entry could be difficult and less profitable than the market size initially suggests. The largest three brands hold 78% of sales, so customers may already be loyal to established competitors. PeakBite could need substantial promotion or lower prices to win market share. As the bars are made in the UK, the 6% import tariff will increase costs. PeakBite must also give the distributor 18% of sales revenue. These costs may reduce its margin or force it to increase prices, making it harder to compete. The 12% fall in Lydora’s currency also creates risk because revenue converted back into sterling may fall.

Overall, Lydora is potentially attractive because it is large, growing and offers broad supermarket access, but PeakBite should be cautious. Its attractiveness will depend on whether expected demand is strong enough to overcome high competition, entry costs and currency risk.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Northshore Clothing sells school uniforms. It introduces safer dyeing processes, publishes information about factory working conditions and agrees fairer payment terms with small suppliers, even though these actions increase its costs.
question.stem: Which statement best identifies corporate social responsibility (CSR)?

options.label: A
options.text: A business taking responsibility for the wider effects of its decisions on stakeholders and the environment.

options.label: B
options.text: A business making charitable donations while ignoring the effects of its main operations.

options.label: C
options.text: A business meeting only the minimum legal requirements in every decision.

options.label: D
options.text: A business choosing actions only when they are certain to increase profit.

option_rationale: A is correct because CSR involves recognising and managing the wider social, environmental and stakeholder consequences of business decisions.
B is wrong because charitable giving alone is not CSR if the business does not act responsibly in its core operations.
C is wrong because legal compliance is a minimum requirement, whereas CSR can involve action beyond legal duties.
D is wrong because responsible actions may involve costs or restrict profitable opportunities and are not defined by guaranteed profit.
mark_scheme.model_answer: A

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context:
Harbour & Hearth is a UK homewares retailer with 38 shops and an online store. It sells candles, cushions and tableware. The business has made an operating profit in each of the past five years, but its directors are concerned about criticism of its supply chain.

One of Harbour & Hearth’s candle suppliers, BrightWax Ltd, has offered to reduce its price from £4.80 to £4.20 per candle if Harbour & Hearth agrees to pay invoices 90 days after delivery rather than its current 30 days. BrightWax is a small business and has told Harbour & Hearth that the longer payment period would make it harder to pay its workers and buy materials.

The directors are considering a new CSR approach. They would keep payment to BrightWax at 30 days, introduce annual independent checks of key suppliers’ working conditions, and publish the results. This would cost Harbour & Hearth £180,000 per year. The business would also donate £50,000 each year to local homelessness charities. Alternatively, the directors could accept BrightWax’s lower price and make only the £50,000 charity donation.

Harbour & Hearth estimates that accepting the lower price would increase annual operating profit by £240,000. A customer survey of 600 shoppers found that 68% said they would be more likely to trust a retailer that reports on supplier working conditions. However, only 22% said they would pay higher prices for homewares because of this.
question.stem: Evaluate whether Harbour & Hearth should adopt the proposed CSR approach of maintaining 30-day supplier payments, checking and reporting on supplier working conditions, and donating to local charities. Use Carroll’s CSR framework in your answer.

levels.descriptor: Shows limited knowledge of one or more aspects of CSR, possibly identifying charity or legal behaviour. Application to Harbour & Hearth is weak or generic. Judgement, if present, is asserted rather than supported.

Explains relevant dimensions of Carroll’s CSR framework and applies them to Harbour & Hearth. Analyses some stakeholder or financial consequences of the proposed approach, with some recognition of a trade-off. A conclusion is reached but is not fully developed or conditional.

Provides a well-developed evaluation using Carroll’s economic, legal, ethical and/or philanthropic responsibilities accurately. Analyses the tensions between profitability, supplier treatment, accountability and community support using the case evidence. Reaches a clear, justified and contextual judgement, considering the relative importance of alternatives and/or conditions affecting the decision.

indicative_content: Carroll’s framework distinguishes economic responsibility, legal responsibility, ethical responsibility and philanthropic responsibility; charitable giving is only one part of CSR.

Maintaining 30-day payment terms could meet an ethical responsibility towards BrightWax because the supplier has stated that 90-day terms could affect its ability to pay workers and buy materials. Legal compliance alone may not address this fairness issue.

Independent checks and published results could improve accountability for working conditions. This may build trust, supported by the finding that 68% of surveyed shoppers would be more likely to trust a retailer that reports on supplier conditions.

The proposed approach has an economic cost: supplier checks and reporting cost £180,000 and charity donations cost £50,000 annually. Accepting the lower supplier price would instead increase operating profit by £240,000, so directors must consider financial viability as well as wider responsibilities.

The 22% willing to pay higher prices suggests that greater trust may not translate directly into sufficient extra revenue. Therefore, reputation benefits are uncertain and should not be assumed to recover the cost.

The £50,000 charity donation is philanthropic, but it would not compensate for imposing payment terms that may harm BrightWax. Core supplier behaviour is more significant than peripheral charitable activity.

A supported judgement may favour the proposed approach because ethical supply-chain treatment and transparent reporting address direct stakeholder impacts and potential long-term trust. However, this depends on Harbour & Hearth being able to absorb the annual costs without damaging its economic viability, and on the checks leading to meaningful improvements rather than reporting alone.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Harbour & Hearth should adopt the proposed approach, provided that the £230,000 annual cost does not threaten its ability to remain financially viable.

Carroll’s CSR framework includes economic, legal, ethical and philanthropic responsibilities. Economically, accepting BrightWax’s lower price would increase annual operating profit by £240,000. This could provide funds for investment and help Harbour & Hearth continue operating successfully. The proposed approach instead costs £180,000 for supplier checks and reporting, plus £50,000 in donations. Therefore, the directors cannot ignore the economic responsibility of generating viable returns.

However, the lower-price option could be ethically weak even if a 90-day payment term is lawful. BrightWax has explained that delayed payment would make it harder to pay workers and purchase materials. Keeping 30-day terms would treat a smaller, dependent supplier more fairly and reduces the risk that Harbour & Hearth improves its own profit by transferring financial pressure elsewhere. This is an ethical responsibility beyond simply meeting minimum legal requirements.

The supplier checks and published results could also strengthen accountability. Reporting gives customers evidence about working conditions rather than asking them to trust a vague CSR claim. This may improve reputation, since 68% of surveyed customers say they would be more likely to trust a retailer that reports on supplier conditions. Yet the commercial benefit is uncertain: only 22% would pay higher prices, so Harbour & Hearth should not assume that the scheme will quickly pay for itself.

The £50,000 donation is philanthropic responsibility because it is a voluntary contribution to the local community. Nevertheless, charity alone would be a weak CSR strategy if Harbour & Hearth accepted payment terms that potentially harmed BrightWax. Donations do not offset poor treatment in the business’s core supply chain.

Overall, Harbour & Hearth should prioritise fair payment terms and credible supply-chain checks because these address the direct effects of its buying decisions on suppliers and workers, while potentially building long-term trust. The donation should be retained only if the business can fund it alongside the checks without undermining economic viability. If profits were too low to sustain all elements, maintaining 30-day supplier payment and meaningful supplier oversight should take priority over the charitable donation.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Northmoor Foods Ltd makes chilled prepared meals for supermarkets. It is considering a £1.2 million investment in an automated packing line. The finance director estimates that the project has a positive NPV of £140,000 using expected sales forecasts. The new line would replace some repetitive manual packing tasks, but no compulsory redundancies are planned because affected employees could be retrained for quality-control and maintenance roles.
question.stem: Analyse the importance to Northmoor Foods Ltd of non-financial factors when deciding whether to invest in the automated packing line.

table.title: Non-financial information about the proposed automated packing line

cells: Supermarkets have asked Northmoor to improve traceability and reduce plastic waste. The line would print a traceability code on every pack and use 18% less plastic packaging.
Thirty packing employees would need retraining. A staff survey found that 11 of the 30 employees are concerned that automation could reduce their future job security.
The line would require a six-week installation period. During this period, packing capacity would be 25% lower than normal.
The supplier has operated the same type of line at other food businesses for three years. Northmoor would need to maintain food-safety standards throughout installation and operation.

levels.descriptor: A well-developed analysis of two or more relevant non-financial factors, clearly applied to Northmoor. The response explains linked effects on the investment decision and reaches a supported overall view about why these factors matter alongside the positive NPV.

Some analysis of relevant non-financial factor(s), with application to Northmoor. Chains of reasoning are present but may be uneven, or the overall significance for the decision is only partly developed.

Basic knowledge of non-financial factors, with limited application to the business. Assertions may identify an advantage or disadvantage but contain little explanation of its effect on the investment decision.

indicative_content: The automated line supports Northmoor's strategic position because improved traceability may help it meet supermarket requirements. This could protect or strengthen customer relationships, so the investment may be worthwhile even though NPV is a forecast rather than a certainty.

Using 18% less plastic may improve Northmoor's environmental performance and appeal to supermarkets or consumers concerned about packaging. This may provide a longer-term reputational benefit not fully captured in the NPV forecast.

Retraining 30 employees could retain staff knowledge and provide the quality-control and maintenance skills needed to operate the line. However, concern among 11 employees about job security could lower morale or increase labour turnover, disrupting implementation.

A six-week period at 25% lower capacity could make it harder to meet supermarket orders. Lost sales or poorer reliability could damage relationships, meaning managers should plan stock, overtime or phased installation before proceeding.

Food-safety performance is vital for a chilled-meal producer. If the installation or new process weakens standards, reputational damage and lost supermarket contracts could outweigh the expected financial gain.

The line has been used by other food businesses for three years, which may reduce operational uncertainty. However, Northmoor should still assess whether the equipment fits its own workforce, site and food-safety processes.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Non-financial factors are important because the positive NPV of £140,000 is based on forecasts and does not show every consequence of the decision. For example, the line would print a traceability code on every pack. As supermarkets have asked for better traceability, this investment could help Northmoor retain contracts and strengthen its reputation as a reliable supplier. It also uses 18% less plastic, which may support supermarkets' environmental expectations. These strategic and reputational gains could make the investment attractive even if the financial forecast changes.

However, employees could affect whether the benefits are achieved. Thirty workers require retraining and 11 are worried about job security. If this concern reduces morale or causes experienced staff to leave, Northmoor could face disruption while introducing the line. Conversely, successful retraining could provide the quality-control and maintenance skills needed to operate it effectively.

The six-week installation period also matters because capacity will be 25% lower. If Northmoor cannot supply supermarkets during this time, it could lose sales or damage customer relationships. Overall, Northmoor should not rely only on NPV: the investment appears strategically beneficial, but it should first manage employee communication, training and the temporary capacity reduction.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice question. Harbour Homeware Ltd is a UK retailer of kitchen accessories. It sells online and to independent shops on credit. The directors are considering whether its short-term financial position is improving before taking out further borrowing.
question.stem: Analyse what the data suggest about Harbour Homeware Ltd's ability to meet its short-term obligations compared with the previous year and with its competitor, Cedar Kitchenware Ltd.

table.title: Short-term financial data

cells: Inventory as a proportion of current assets
Receivables overdue by more than 60 days

levels.descriptor: Detailed, applied analysis of the change over time and the competitor comparison. The response reaches a supported judgement about short-term obligations, recognising that the apparently stronger ratio may be weakened by the quality and likely speed of converting current assets into cash.

Some developed analysis using relevant data. The response explains what one or both ratio comparisons could mean for Harbour Homeware's ability to meet short-term obligations, although coverage of asset quality, the competitor or limitations may be uneven.
Basic, relevant statements about the ratios or financial position, with limited explanation and/or limited use of the business data.

indicative_content: Harbour Homeware's current asset-to-current liability ratio increased from 1.2:1 in 2024 to 1.4:1 in 2025. This suggests a larger amount of current assets relative to each £1 of short-term obligations, which could improve its capacity to meet bills due soon.
The 2025 ratio of 1.4:1 is higher than Cedar Kitchenware's 1.3:1. On this measure, Harbour Homeware appears to have a slightly stronger short-term financial position than its competitor.

The ratio alone may overstate Harbour Homeware's liquidity. Inventory makes up 75% of its current assets in 2025, compared with 50% at Cedar. Inventory is not the same as cash and may not be converted into cash quickly enough to settle obligations.

Harbour Homeware's overdue receivables rose from £18,000 to £42,000. Credit sales recorded as receivables have not yet become cash, so delayed customer payment could create cash pressure despite the improved ratio.

Therefore, the increase in the ratio is a positive sign, but the growing reliance on inventory and overdue receivables means the directors should not assume that all current assets are readily available to pay short-term liabilities. Further borrowing could increase financial risk if cash conversion remains slow.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Harbour Homeware's current asset-to-current liability ratio has risen from 1.2:1 in 2024 to 1.4:1 in 2025. This means that it has more current assets relative to its £300,000 of current liabilities than previously, so it may be better able to meet obligations that fall due in the short term. Its 2025 ratio is also above Cedar Kitchenware's 1.3:1, suggesting Harbour has a marginally stronger position on this measure.

However, the comparison needs careful interpretation. In 2025, 75% of Harbour's current assets are inventory, compared with only 50% for Cedar. Inventory is an asset but is not cash; if stock sells slowly, Harbour may struggle to turn enough of its current assets into cash when bills are due. In addition, its receivables overdue by more than 60 days increased to £42,000, well above Cedar's £12,000. These overdue amounts may delay cash inflows.

Overall, the ratio trend is favourable, but Harbour's higher inventory proportion and overdue receivables make its short-term position less secure than the 1.4:1 ratio alone suggests. The directors should consider cash conversion as well as the ratio before adding further borrowing.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Northshore Cycle Co sells bicycles and accessories through a shop and website. Demand for a new electric-bike accessory has increased after it was featured by a cycling influencer. The directors are considering a £100,000 four-year bank loan to buy enough of the accessory for the expected demand. The loan would be received immediately and then used to pay the supplier immediately. The supplier will not offer credit.
question.stem:
Evaluate whether Northshore Cycle Co should take the £100,000 bank loan to buy the new accessory stock.

Use the statement of financial position and the additional information to support your judgement.

table.title: Northshore Cycle Co: financial and operating information

cells: Statement of financial position at 31 March 2025: Cash
Available in the business bank account
£75,000 has been in stock for more than six months
Book value of shop fittings, tools and delivery vans
£90,000 is due within the next 30 days
Repayable over the next five years
Expected to generate £155,000 cash and card sales within six months; no customer credit will be offered
Other costs of the proposed sales
Expected to be paid in cash during the six months
Four-year loan; £9,000 interest is payable during the first year

levels.descriptor: Shows limited knowledge of a statement of financial position and makes simple, largely unsupported comments about the loan or the figures. Application to Northshore Cycle Co is limited. A judgement may be asserted but is not justified.

Shows sound understanding that the statement of financial position is a snapshot of assets, liabilities and equity. Applies relevant figures to explain benefits and/or risks of the loan, with some developed analysis. Reaches a judgement, although this may be conditional or not fully weighed against the limitations of the data.

Shows thorough understanding and uses the financial-position data selectively and accurately to develop balanced analysis. Evaluates asset quality, the timing of liabilities and the effect of additional borrowing, recognising the limits of using a single snapshot. Reaches a clear, justified and appropriately conditional judgement.

indicative_content: A statement of financial position shows assets, liabilities and equity at one date. Northshore's £518,000 total assets are not the same as cash available to pay bills.
The business has only £32,000 cash, while £90,000 of trade payables is due within 30 days and its £18,000 overdraft can be demanded immediately. This creates a short-term liquidity risk.

Although current assets total £308,000, their quality is uncertain: £75,000 of inventory is slow-moving and £30,000 of receivables is overdue. These assets may not become cash quickly enough to settle current obligations.

The proposed loan initially increases both cash/assets and liabilities by £100,000. Once used to buy stock, cash is replaced by inventory, so it does not itself solve Northshore's immediate liquidity problem.

The accessory could generate £155,000 of cash and card sales within six months. After £100,000 stock cost and £15,000 other costs, it could provide £40,000 before interest, helping cash generation if the forecast is achieved.
The loan increases debt alongside the existing £132,000 bank loan and creates £9,000 first-year interest, increasing financial risk and reducing the benefit of the forecast sales.
The predicted sales are uncertain and the business already has slow-moving inventory. If demand is lower than expected, Northshore could hold more stock while debt and interest still have to be paid.

Book values of equipment and inventory may not equal the cash that could be raised from selling them. The directors should also use cash-flow forecasts, demand evidence and the timing of loan repayments before deciding.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Northshore should be cautious about taking the loan. A statement of financial position is a snapshot of its assets, liabilities and equity, and it suggests that the business has a liquidity problem despite having total assets of £518,000.

For example, Northshore has only £32,000 cash but must pay £90,000 of trade payables within 30 days. The £18,000 overdraft is also repayable on demand. Its £308,000 current assets may appear sufficient, but they are not all readily available cash: £75,000 of inventory has been unsold for more than six months and £30,000 of receivables is overdue. Therefore, the business may struggle to convert enough current assets into cash quickly.

The loan could be worthwhile if the sales forecast is reliable. The new stock is expected to generate £155,000 of cash and card sales within six months. After the £100,000 stock purchase and £15,000 other cash costs, this would provide £40,000 before interest. As customers will not buy on credit, successful sales would improve cash inflows rather than create further receivables.

However, borrowing £100,000 increases liabilities when Northshore already has a £132,000 bank loan. After the loan money is used immediately to buy stock, the business has more inventory rather than more cash. This is risky because it already holds slow-moving stock. In addition, £9,000 interest is payable in the first year even if demand for the accessory is weaker than forecast.

Overall, Northshore should take the loan only if it has convincing evidence that the accessory will sell rapidly and a cash-flow forecast showing that the £90,000 payable and overdraft can be met before the sales cash arrives. Without this evidence, it should not borrow, because the additional stock and debt could worsen its short-term liquidity position.

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice question. Northbank Outdoor Ltd sells camping equipment.

options.label: A
options.text: 0.08 times

options.label: C

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Harbour Homeware sells premium kitchen equipment. Its corporate objective is to build a strong reputation for quality over the next five years. However, senior managers have set a bonus for marketing managers based only on this quarter's sales revenue. Marketing plans a large discount campaign, while the operations department has requested funding for staff training and improved quality checks.
question.stem: Explain one risk to Harbour Homeware of short-termism causing functional objectives to be inconsistent.

points.descriptor: Identifies short-termism as prioritising immediate results over longer-term investment or competitiveness.
accept: A valid definition of short-termism.
Prioritising quarterly sales, profit or bonuses over future performance.

points.descriptor: Explains that functional objectives should support the overall corporate objective and be consistent across departments.
accept: Departmental goals should help achieve the business's longer-term quality reputation.
Marketing and operations need aligned objectives.

points.descriptor: Applies the inconsistency to Harbour Homeware: marketing's discount campaign is intended to increase this quarter's sales, whereas operations wants investment in training and quality checks.
accept: Reference to the sales-revenue bonus encouraging the marketing objective.
Reference to the requested funding for training or quality checks.

points.descriptor: Explains a resulting risk: diverting funds towards discounts rather than quality improvements could weaken product quality or the premium brand reputation, damaging longer-term competitiveness.
accept: Customers may no longer see the business as premium.
Lower investment in training or quality checks may reduce quality.
Short-term sales gains may harm the five-year reputation objective.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Short-termism means giving priority to immediate outcomes, such as this quarter's sales revenue, rather than long-term investment. Functional objectives should support the corporate objective, but Harbour Homeware's marketing team is encouraged to run discounts to meet its bonus target while operations wants funding for training and quality checks. If money is directed towards discounting instead, quality may not improve and customers may no longer view the business as premium. This could damage its aim of building a strong quality reputation over five years.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Refill & Root is a small UK haircare business. Its founders planned to target environmentally conscious customers with premium shampoo sold in refillable aluminium bottles. To support this longer-term direction, the business invested in bottle-cleaning equipment and trained staff to explain the refill system in store. After several months, customers began asking for smaller refill bottles suitable for taking on holidays. The founders then added a 100 ml refill range, although this had not been included in their original plan. This month, the marketing manager has arranged a three-day social-media campaign promoting the new travel-size range.
question.stem: Explain how Refill & Root demonstrates the difference between planned and emergent strategy, and between strategy and tactics.

points.descriptor: Identifies planned strategy as a deliberate longer-term set of choices made before action is taken.
accept: A planned strategy is decided in advance.
Planned strategy gives the business a long-term direction.

points.descriptor: Applies planned strategy to Refill & Root's decision to serve environmentally conscious customers through premium refillable haircare, supported by investment in equipment and staff training.
accept: The refillable aluminium-bottle positioning was part of the founders' original plan.
Buying cleaning equipment and training staff support the intended refill strategy.

points.descriptor: Explains emergent strategy as a change or adaptation that develops from new evidence or experience rather than being part of the original plan, applied to customer demand for travel-size bottles.
accept: The 100 ml range emerged after customers asked for it.
Customer feedback caused the business to adapt its original plan.

points.descriptor: Distinguishes tactics from strategy by explaining that the three-day social-media campaign is a specific short-term action used to implement or support the wider strategy.
accept: The social-media campaign is a tactic because it is a particular action.
The campaign promotes the travel-size range rather than defining the whole long-term direction.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Refill & Root's planned strategy was its original longer-term choice to target environmentally conscious customers with premium haircare in refillable aluminium bottles. Its investment in cleaning equipment and staff training helps implement this direction. The travel-size refill range is emergent strategy because it was developed in response to customer requests and was not in the original plan. In contrast, the three-day social-media campaign is a tactic: it is a specific short-term action used to promote the new range, rather than the overall strategic direction.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Northshore Roasters is a UK coffee business that plans to open three new cafés over the next two years. Its strategic plan includes allocating funds to premises, staff training and coffee-machine purchases. Managers know that forecasts may be wrong and that unexpected risks could affect the expansion.
question.stem: Explain one reason why Northshore Roasters should support its strategic plan with contingency planning.

points.descriptor: Shows knowledge that contingency planning supports a strategic plan by preparing the business for risk or unexpected circumstances.
accept: Contingency planning helps a business prepare for risks.
It provides support if circumstances do not develop as planned.
It recognises that forecasts used in plans may be wrong.

points.descriptor: Applies this to Northshore Roasters by referring to its planned expansion, new cafés, or its spending on premises, training or coffee machines.
accept: Northshore is opening three cafés.
The business is committing funds to premises, training and machines.
Its two-year expansion plan depends on forecasts.

points.descriptor: Explains that contingency planning can help the business adapt its plans when new evidence or changed circumstances mean the original plan is no longer suitable.
accept: Managers can review and adapt the expansion plan if evidence changes.
It reduces the risk of continuing with a plan based on incorrect forecasts.
The business can reassess its strategy if conditions change.

points.descriptor: Develops the application by linking adaptation to protecting the resources committed to the expansion or helping Northshore continue to pursue its longer-term objectives.
accept: This may prevent Northshore wasting funds committed to cafés, training or machines.
It can help the business make better use of scarce resources during the expansion.
It can help Northshore continue towards its planned growth despite unexpected risks.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Contingency planning would prepare Northshore Roasters for risks that could affect its two-year café expansion. Forecasts may be wrong, so managers could review and adapt the plan if unexpected circumstances make opening all three cafés unsuitable. This could protect the funds allocated to premises, staff training and coffee machines, helping the business use its scarce resources more effectively.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice. Northmoor Roasters is a UK coffee roaster that sells ethically sourced coffee through its website and to independent cafés. In January 2024, senior managers created a three-year strategic plan. The plan aimed to position the business as a premium, reliable supplier rather than competing mainly on price. It included investment in roasting equipment, staff training and a customer-ordering system. Marketing, operations and finance were each given targets linked to the plan. The directors review performance at the end of each year and may revise the plan if market conditions change.
question.stem: Analyse how strategic planning may have improved Northmoor Roasters' strategic performance.

table.title: Northmoor Roasters: selected performance data

cells: Orders delivered in full and on time
Capital invested in equipment, training and the ordering system

levels.descriptor: Shows limited understanding of strategic planning or performance measures. Makes a basic use of one item of Northmoor Roasters data, with little or no developed chain of reasoning.

Shows clear understanding of how planning can give direction, align activities or set targets for control. Applies relevant data to Northmoor Roasters and develops at least one linked analytical point about strategic performance.

Shows thorough, well-applied analysis of the relationship between strategic planning and performance. Uses several relevant measures to reach a supported judgement about the extent of improvement, recognising that not all targets were achieved and/or that plans need review as conditions change.

indicative_content: The strategic plan gave Northmoor a clear premium and reliable-supplier direction, allowing investment decisions to support this longer-term position rather than being isolated tactics.

Planning may have aligned operations, staff training and the ordering system with the aim of reliable service. This is supported by orders delivered in full and on time increasing from 82% to 94%, exceeding the 93% target.

Targets enable control because managers can compare actual results with planned results. Northmoor can identify success in repeat customer rate, which reached 70% against a 68% target, but also investigate why market share reached only 8% rather than 9%.

Performance improved, as revenue rose from £4.0 million to £4.5 million and operating profit rose from £320,000 to £350,000. However, both remained below their 2024 targets, so the plan cannot be judged wholly successful.

The £500,000 investment may have reduced short-term profit while building capabilities that improve service and repeat purchasing. Therefore, the strategy may take longer to deliver its full financial benefit.

Planning has limits because forecasts and targets may not reflect changing competition or customer demand. The directors should review and adapt the plan rather than treating a missed market-share target as automatic strategic failure.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Strategic planning may have improved Northmoor's performance because it gave the business a coherent direction: becoming a premium and reliable supplier rather than simply attempting to cut prices. The £500,000 investment in equipment, training and the ordering system could align operations and employees with this position. This appears effective because orders delivered in full and on time increased from 82% to 94%, above the 93% target. More reliable delivery may encourage cafés to reorder, helping the repeat customer rate rise from 58% to 70%, also above target.

Planning also provides targets for control. Managers can compare actual results with planned results and decide where changes are needed. For example, sales revenue increased from £4.0 million to £4.5 million and operating profit increased from £320,000 to £350,000, suggesting progress. However, both results were below target, and market share was only 8% against a 9% target. This means the strategic plan has improved several measures but has not yet fully achieved its intended competitive position.

Overall, the plan appears valuable because service reliability and repeat purchasing improved, which may produce financial benefits over a longer period. However, the directors should review why market share and financial targets were missed, since conditions or competition may have changed. Strategic planning is most useful when it is monitored and adapted, rather than followed rigidly.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: NimbleHome designs connected kitchen appliances. Its engineers have developed a specialist design process that integrates hardware, software and user testing. The process is used across several product ranges and rival firms have struggled to replicate it.
question.stem: Identify NimbleHome's core competence.

options.label: A
options.text: Its specialist design process combining hardware, software and user testing

options.label: B
options.text: The number of kitchen appliances it sold last year

options.label: C
options.text: A temporary reduction in the price of one appliance

options.label: D
options.text: A one-off social media campaign that attracted attention

option_rationale: A is correct because it is a difficult-to-copy combination of skills and capabilities that can support competitive advantage across product ranges.
B is wrong because sales volume is an outcome and does not itself identify a distinctive capability.
C is wrong because a temporary price reduction is an action, not a hard-to-copy skill, knowledge or capability.
D is wrong because a one-off campaign is unlikely to be an enduring capability that competitors cannot copy.
mark_scheme.model_answer: : A

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: BudgetBrew is a UK chain of coffee shops. It buys coffee beans and packaging in very large quantities, uses identical equipment in every branch and has simplified its menu. These choices reduce the cost of making each drink, allowing BudgetBrew to charge lower prices than many nearby independent coffee shops.
