To avoid competing only on price, BudgetBrew has also developed a mobile app that remembers customers’ usual orders and allows collection within five minutes.
question.stem: Explain how BudgetBrew could use a low-cost strategy and differentiation to compete with nearby independent coffee shops.

points.descriptor: Explains low-cost strategy as aiming to achieve lower operating or production costs than competitors, rather than simply setting a low selling price.
accept: Lower costs can enable lower prices or protect profit margins.
A business seeks a structural cost advantage over rivals.

points.descriptor: Applies low-cost strategy to BudgetBrew’s large-scale purchasing, standard equipment or simplified menu, which reduce the cost per drink and can allow lower prices.
accept: Buying beans and packaging in bulk reduces input costs.
Using the same equipment or a limited menu can reduce operating costs.
Lower costs allow BudgetBrew to undercut nearby independents.

points.descriptor: Explains differentiation as providing a valued feature or benefit that customers see as distinct from alternatives, encouraging preference and reducing reliance on price competition.
accept: Differentiation gives customers a reason to choose the business beyond low price.
A distinctive service or convenience feature can make demand less price sensitive.

points.descriptor: Applies differentiation to BudgetBrew’s app remembering usual orders and enabling five-minute collection, which offers convenience and may encourage customers to choose it over independent coffee shops.
accept: The app saves customers time.
Remembered orders create a more convenient customer experience.
Fast collection provides a valued distinction from nearby rivals.

mark_scheme.model_answer: BudgetBrew’s low-cost strategy is based on having lower costs than competitors, not just charging a low price. Bulk buying, identical equipment and a simplified menu can reduce the cost of each drink, so it can charge less than nearby independent coffee shops. Differentiation means offering customers a valued distinction from rivals. Its app remembers regular orders and allows quick collection, giving customers convenience and a reason to choose BudgetBrew that is not solely its lower price.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice question. Northshore Cycle Tours provides guided cycling holidays on traffic-free routes in the Yorkshire Dales. It targets experienced adult cyclists who want small groups, detailed route planning and high-quality local accommodation. Rather than offering the cheapest holidays, Northshore employs qualified guides, provides well-maintained e-bikes and gives customers a luggage-transfer service.
question.stem: Explain how Northshore Cycle Tours could use a focus strategy and non-price competition to compete successfully.

points.descriptor: Identifies that a focus strategy involves concentrating on a narrow, clearly defined customer segment rather than attempting to serve the whole market.
accept: Focus means targeting a specialist/niche market.
Focus is a narrow competitive scope.

points.descriptor: Applies focus strategy to Northshore by identifying experienced adult cyclists seeking specialist guided holidays in the Yorkshire Dales.
accept: It targets experienced cyclists.
It concentrates on customers wanting small-group cycling holidays.
It serves a niche of adult cycling tourists.

points.descriptor: Explains that non-price competition attracts customers through factors other than charging less, such as quality, service, convenience or expertise.
accept: Non-price competition is competing on quality or service rather than a lower price.
It uses valued features instead of relying on discounts.

points.descriptor: Applies non-price competition by explaining that qualified guides, e-bikes, route planning, luggage transfers or quality accommodation make the holiday more attractive to its target customers, even if Northshore is not the cheapest provider.
accept: Qualified guides can reassure cyclists and improve their experience.
Luggage transfers add convenience for cyclists.
Well-maintained e-bikes and detailed routes can distinguish Northshore from cheaper rivals.
High-quality accommodation can attract customers who value comfort.

mark_scheme.model_answer: A focus strategy means serving a narrow segment rather than the whole holiday market. Northshore focuses on experienced adult cyclists who want specialist, small-group tours in the Yorkshire Dales. It can then use non-price competition by offering qualified guides, reliable e-bikes and luggage transfers. These features improve quality and convenience, so its target customers may choose Northshore even when a rival offers a lower price.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: RiverBean Coffee operates 12 coffee shops in Yorkshire. It has developed a system that uses customer order data to predict demand at different times of day. Staff prepare popular items before busy periods and deliveries are routed between shops to reduce waste. RiverBean can usually serve customers more quickly than nearby independent coffee shops while keeping its food costs low.
question.stem: Explain how RiverBean Coffee could sustain a competitive advantage over nearby independent coffee shops.

points.descriptor: Identifies a relevant meaning of competitive advantage or a source of sustainable advantage.
accept: Competitive advantage is creating greater customer value or lower costs than rivals.
A capability that rivals cannot quickly copy can create sustainable competitive advantage.
Using data and processes can create a cost or service advantage.

points.descriptor: Applies RiverBean's order-data system to its operations.
accept: RiverBean uses order data to predict demand.
It prepares popular products before busy periods.
It routes deliveries between its 12 shops to reduce waste.

points.descriptor: Explains the customer value or cost effect created by the system.
accept: Faster service may make customers choose RiverBean rather than independent coffee shops.
Reduced waste and better delivery routing can lower RiverBean's food costs.
Lower costs could allow RiverBean to keep prices competitive or retain higher margins.

points.descriptor: Explains why the advantage may be sustained.
accept: The combined data, routines, staff experience and delivery network may take time for independent coffee shops to develop.
The advantage is harder to copy because it is an activity system rather than one easily copied product feature.
RiverBean can continue learning from customer data, helping it improve demand predictions over time.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Competitive advantage means offering customers superior value, or operating at a lower cost, compared with rivals. RiverBean uses order data to predict demand, so it can prepare popular items before busy periods and serve customers faster. This convenience may encourage customers to choose RiverBean rather than a nearby independent coffee shop. Its delivery routing and lower waste also reduce food costs, allowing competitive prices or higher margins. The advantage could be sustained because independent shops would need time to build comparable customer data, operating routines and a coordinated delivery network.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context:
Vela Grind is a UK online seller of whole-bean coffee. It currently sells a wide range of standard coffee beans to home coffee drinkers. Large supermarket brands sell comparable 250g bags at lower prices and have national distribution.

The directors are considering a new strategy. Vela Grind would concentrate on the narrower segment of home espresso enthusiasts. It would offer beans with detailed roast information, recipe guides for different espresso machines and a subscription service that lets customers alter delivery dates. The directors would stop trying to match supermarket prices and would charge a premium price. They believe this focus differentiation strategy would make the business less vulnerable to price competition.
question.stem: Using the data provided and your knowledge of Porter’s generic strategies, evaluate whether Vela Grind should adopt the proposed strategy.

table.title: Selected information for Vela Grind and competitors

cells: Home espresso enthusiasts, estimated at 12% of the online whole-bean market
68% said roast information and machine-specific guidance would make them more likely to buy; 22% said price would be their main reason for choosing coffee
Two trained roasters and a customer-service team already produce online brewing guides
National buying scale and established supermarket shelf space
One premium online coffee seller has introduced subscriptions, but does not provide machine-specific guidance
Supermarket brands could reduce prices further during promotions

levels.descriptor: Shows limited knowledge of a generic strategy and/or makes simple assertions about the proposal. Application to Vela Grind or the data is limited. Any judgement is unsupported or unclear.

Explains how a focus differentiation strategy could affect Vela Grind, with relevant use of the scenario. Includes some analysis of benefits and/or risks, and reaches a judgement, although the reasoning may be one-sided or not fully developed.

Provides a well-developed and balanced evaluation of the proposed focus differentiation strategy. Analysis clearly links Vela Grind’s target scope, customer value and capabilities to likely competitive effects, while considering limitations such as imitation, customer price sensitivity or implementation. Reaches a clear, justified judgement that is firmly based on the data.

indicative_content: A focus strategy serves a narrower customer segment; here, Vela Grind would target home espresso enthusiasts rather than all household coffee buyers.

Differentiation requires a benefit customers value. Detailed roast information, machine-specific guidance and flexible subscriptions could make the offer more useful and reduce customers’ willingness to switch solely on price.

The survey supports differentiation because 68% of espresso enthusiasts say the information and guidance would make them more likely to buy. Vela Grind’s trained roasters and existing customer-service guides provide capabilities that support the position.

Vela Grind should not attempt broad cost leadership: its direct cost is £3.10 per bag compared with £2.70 for supermarket brands, while supermarkets have national buying scale and can use price promotions.

The higher selling price of £8.50 could support a premium position, but 22% of the target group still identify price as their main choice factor. The market is also limited because espresso enthusiasts are estimated at only 12% of the online whole-bean market.

The strategy may be less durable if rivals copy subscriptions. However, a combined system of roaster expertise, machine-specific guidance and responsive service may be harder to copy than subscriptions alone.
The proposal is most appropriate if Vela Grind maintains a coherent focus on enthusiasts and continues investing in the capabilities customers value, rather than simply charging a higher price.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Vela Grind’s proposal is a focus differentiation strategy because it concentrates on the narrower group of home espresso enthusiasts and seeks to offer them benefits beyond the coffee itself. Detailed roast information and machine-specific recipes could create customer value by helping buyers obtain better results from their espresso machines. This is supported by the survey: 68% say these features would make them more likely to buy. Vela Grind already has two trained roasters and a team producing brewing guides, so its operations appear to support the differentiated position rather than the business merely claiming to be different. This could reduce price sensitivity and make the £8.50 price more acceptable.

The proposal is also more realistic than trying to become a broad cost leader. Vela Grind’s direct cost is £3.10 per bag, above the supermarket brands’ £2.70, and supermarkets have national buying scale. Vela Grind is therefore unlikely to win a price war, especially as supermarkets could reduce prices during promotions. Focusing on specialist customers allows Vela Grind to avoid competing directly for every household coffee buyer.

However, the strategy has risks. Espresso enthusiasts represent only 12% of the online whole-bean market, limiting potential sales. In addition, 22% of this target group still choose mainly on price, so some customers may switch to cheaper brands. A premium online seller has already copied subscriptions, showing that a single feature may not be difficult to imitate. Vela Grind must ensure that its combination of roaster expertise, useful guidance and service remains valuable and consistently delivered.

Overall, Vela Grind should adopt the strategy because its existing capabilities and the survey evidence make focus differentiation more credible than low-cost competition. Its success will depend on treating the guidance, expertise and flexible service as an integrated offer, rather than relying only on a higher price or a subscription feature that competitors can copy.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Willow & Tide is a UK-based producer of natural household cleaning products. It currently sells ready-to-use spray bottles through its website and independent retailers. The directors are considering launching concentrated refill pouches. Customers would add water at home and reuse an existing spray bottle. The directors want to decide whether to proceed with the launch in the next 12 months.
question.stem: Evaluate how useful a SWOT analysis would be to Willow & Tide’s directors when deciding whether to launch concentrated refill pouches. [9 marks]

table.title: Information available to Willow & Tide

cells: The factory has 20% unused production capacity. The operations manager estimates that pouch production can use this spare capacity, but a pouch-sealing machine would cost £85,000.
A survey of 600 existing online customers found that 62% said they would be likely or very likely to try a refill pouch. The survey did not include customers who buy through independent retailers.
Two national cleaning-product brands have announced refill ranges to be sold in supermarkets within six months.
Willow & Tide has an email database of 48,000 previous online customers. However, its sales revenue has fallen by 8% in the last year.
The directors require any new product range to make a positive contribution within its first year.

levels.descriptor: Shows limited understanding of SWOT analysis and/or makes general comments about the case. Application to Willow & Tide is brief or descriptive. A judgement may be asserted but is not supported.

Shows clear understanding that SWOT brings together internal strengths and weaknesses with external opportunities and threats. Applies relevant evidence to the refill-pouch decision and explains some implications. Considers at least one limitation or counter-argument, although the judgement may be incomplete or not fully prioritised.

Shows thorough, focused analysis of how a SWOT could connect Willow & Tide’s evidence, capabilities and external conditions to the launch decision. Evaluates the quality, significance or uncertainty of the evidence and the firm’s ability to act on it. Reaches a well-supported, justified judgement about the usefulness of SWOT, with clear prioritisation.

indicative_content: SWOT could organise internal evidence, such as the 20% unused capacity and the email database, alongside weaknesses including falling revenue and the £85,000 machinery requirement.

The customer survey may indicate an opportunity, but it is not automatically an exploitable opportunity: Willow & Tide must have sufficient finance and capability to buy the machine and generate a positive contribution in year one.

The announced supermarket launches are a threat because larger rivals may increase competition before Willow & Tide launches; alternatively, they may indicate growing interest in refills, but this does not guarantee demand for Willow & Tide.
A SWOT is more useful as a summary after evidence has been gathered than as a simple list. Directors need to judge the scale, timing and reliability of each factor.

The survey is limited because it covers only existing online customers, not independent-retailer customers, so treating its result as evidence of total market demand could lead to an unsound decision.

SWOT categories can be subjective and do not predict the future or rank factors automatically. The directors should prioritise whether the machine cost and likely contribution can be justified before committing to launch.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
A SWOT analysis would be useful because it would bring together Willow & Tide’s internal position and its external environment before the directors decide on the refill pouches. For example, the 20% unused factory capacity is a relevant strength, since it could allow production without expanding the whole factory. The email database of 48,000 previous online customers could also help the business promote a trial launch directly to customers who already know the brand.

However, these strengths need to be considered alongside weaknesses. The £85,000 pouch-sealing machine is a significant commitment, particularly as revenue has already fallen by 8%. Therefore, spare capacity does not by itself make the launch attractive: the business must be able to fund the machine and still achieve positive contribution in the first year. This shows why SWOT should link a capability to the specific decision rather than simply label spare capacity as a strength.

The survey result suggests an opportunity because 62% of existing online respondents say they are likely or very likely to try a pouch. Yet this evidence is uncertain because the survey excluded customers buying from independent retailers. The directors cannot assume that the result represents all potential demand. Similarly, national brands launching refill ranges could be a threat if competition arrives in supermarkets before Willow & Tide launches. It might also suggest that demand for refills is increasing, but Willow & Tide would need the resources to respond quickly.

Overall, SWOT would be useful as a way of synthesising the available evidence and identifying the main strategic issue: whether Willow & Tide’s customer access and spare capacity are sufficient to overcome the machinery cost and imminent competition. It should not determine the decision on its own, because it does not rank factors or prove future demand. The directors should give greatest weight to whether reliable sales evidence supports positive first-year contribution before approving the launch.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Harbour Bean is a small chain of independent coffee shops. A national coffee-shop brand is considering opening outlets in the same town.
question.stem: Which factor is most likely to be a barrier to entry for the national coffee-shop brand?

options.label: A
options.text: Customers can easily switch between coffee shops.

options.label: B
options.text: The national brand must invest heavily in suitable premises, equipment and staff before opening.

options.label: C
options.text: Harbour Bean offers coffee and cakes to its customers.

options.label: D
options.text: Several existing coffee shops compete for customers in the town.

option_rationale: A is wrong because easy customer switching reduces a barrier to entry rather than creating one.
B is correct because the substantial initial investment is a capital barrier that may deter potential entrants.
C is wrong because selling coffee and cakes describes the market offering, not a barrier that prevents entry.
D is wrong because this describes rivalry among existing competitors, rather than a specific barrier to entering the market.
mark_scheme.model_answer: B

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Harvest Bowl is a small UK producer of chilled salad bowls sold to large supermarket chains. Two supermarket chains account for 75% of Harvest Bowl’s sales and can choose from several similar salad-bowl producers. Harvest Bowl buys a specialist compostable bowl from one supplier because its machinery is designed only for that supplier’s bowl size.
question.stem: Explain how buyer power and supplier power could affect Harvest Bowl.

points.descriptor: Explains buyer power as the ability of customers to influence price or trading terms.
accept: Buyers can negotiate lower prices or demand better terms.
Customer bargaining power is correctly defined.

points.descriptor: Applies buyer power to Harvest Bowl: the two large supermarket chains represent most sales and have alternative producers available.
accept: The supermarkets may use their large share of Harvest Bowl’s sales to negotiate.
Supermarkets can switch to similar salad-bowl producers.

points.descriptor: Explains supplier power as the ability of suppliers to influence input prices or supply terms.
accept: A supplier can raise prices or impose less favourable conditions.
Supplier bargaining power is correctly defined.

points.descriptor: Applies supplier power to Harvest Bowl: it relies on one specialist bowl supplier and changing would be difficult because its machinery is designed for that bowl size.
accept: The supplier could increase the price of compostable bowls.
Harvest Bowl has high switching costs because its machinery fits the current supplier’s bowls.
Higher input costs or less favourable supply terms could reduce Harvest Bowl’s margin.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Buyer power is the ability of customers to influence the price or terms offered by a business. Harvest Bowl’s two supermarket customers account for 75% of its sales and can choose similar producers, so they may demand lower prices, putting pressure on Harvest Bowl’s margin. Supplier power is the ability of a supplier to influence prices or terms. Harvest Bowl depends on one specialist compostable-bowl supplier and would find it difficult to switch because of its machinery, so the supplier could raise input prices, increasing Harvest Bowl’s costs.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice question. NorthLine Rail operates passenger train services between several UK cities. It competes with other rail operators on some routes. Its customers can also choose to drive, use intercity coaches or attend business meetings by video call instead of travelling.
question.stem: Explain how rivalry and the threat of substitutes could affect NorthLine Rail.

points.descriptor: Explains rivalry as competitive pressure between existing businesses in the same market.
accept: Competition among existing rail operators.
Pressure created by firms already providing rail services.

points.descriptor: Applies rivalry to NorthLine Rail by explaining that competition from other rail operators may lead to pressure on fares or service quality.
accept: NorthLine may need to reduce ticket prices to retain passengers.
NorthLine may need to improve timetables, reliability or onboard service because rival rail operators compete for customers.

points.descriptor: Explains a substitute as a different solution that meets the same customer need.
accept: An alternative way for customers to make the journey or avoid travelling.
A different product or service that satisfies the need for transport or attending a meeting.

points.descriptor: Applies substitutes to NorthLine Rail by explaining that cars, coaches or video calls could reduce demand or limit the fares it can charge.
accept: Customers may drive or use coaches rather than buy NorthLine tickets, reducing passenger numbers.
Video meetings can replace some business journeys, reducing demand for rail travel.
NorthLine may be unable to increase fares substantially because customers can switch to driving, coaches or video calls.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Rivalry is competition between existing firms. NorthLine Rail may face other rail operators on some routes, so it may have to keep fares competitive or improve its service to attract passengers. A substitute is a different solution that meets the same customer need. Customers could drive, use a coach or hold a meeting by video call instead of using NorthLine Rail. This could reduce ticket demand and restrict the prices NorthLine can charge.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice. LoopLunch Ltd sells reusable insulated lunch containers in the UK. The directors must choose whether to position LoopLunch mainly as a low-price everyday product or as a premium, durable product with a five-year guarantee.
question.stem: Using the data, analyse how competitive pressures should influence LoopLunch Ltd’s choice of positioning strategy.

table.title: Selected market information for LoopLunch Ltd

cells: Three established reusable-container brands sell similar insulated containers for £18–£24. Their products are stocked by major supermarkets and online retailers.
Customers can use disposable food packaging costing about £1 per week, ordinary plastic containers costing £4–£7, or buy lunch from cafés near workplaces.
A specialist supplier produces the leak-proof seals required for insulated containers. It supplies most UK brands and charges LoopLunch £5.50 per seal set.
A premium container would retail at £32, use a stronger seal set and include a five-year guarantee. A low-price version would retail at £19 and have a one-year guarantee.

levels.descriptor: Shows limited understanding of a relevant competitive pressure or positioning choice. Application to LoopLunch may be asserted or generic, with little or no developed chain of reasoning.

Explains one or more relevant industry pressures using the data and develops some analysis of how these could affect LoopLunch’s positioning. Reasoning may be uneven or consider only one side of the choice.

Provides a clear, developed analysis of how relevant rivalry, substitutes, buyer alternatives or supplier power affect the practicality of low-price and/or premium positioning. Applies the evidence closely and uses logical chains to reach a supported conclusion about positioning.

indicative_content: The £18–£24 prices of established direct rivals create rivalry and make a £32 premium price difficult to sustain unless the stronger seal and five-year guarantee provide a meaningful reason for customers to choose LoopLunch.

Disposable packaging, low-cost plastic containers and buying lunch from cafés are substitutes because they can meet the need for carrying or obtaining lunch without buying LoopLunch. Their availability can make customers more price-sensitive and place a ceiling on LoopLunch’s price.

A £19 low-price position is close to direct competitors’ prices and may attract price-conscious buyers, but it may be hard to stand out when established brands already have access to supermarkets and online retailers.

The specialist seal supplier’s concentration gives it power over costs and terms. The £5.50 seal cost could constrain LoopLunch’s ability to compete on price, making a premium position that protects margin more appropriate.

Premium positioning is not automatically successful: cheap substitutes and rival products mean the guarantee and durability must be valued by customers, rather than being features customers will not pay extra for.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
LoopLunch should be cautious about positioning solely on a low price. Three established brands already charge £18–£24 and are available through major supermarkets and online retailers. Although LoopLunch’s £19 version would be within this range, customers may see little reason to switch from familiar brands. This rivalry could force LoopLunch to cut prices further or spend more on promotion, reducing the benefit of a low-price position.

There are also several substitutes. Disposable packaging, ordinary containers and cafés can all satisfy the customer’s need to carry or obtain lunch, even though they are not direct reusable-container brands. For example, plastic containers cost only £4–£7, so some buyers may regard a £32 product as too expensive. These alternatives increase buyer price sensitivity and could limit the price LoopLunch can charge.

However, the specialist supplier has power because it supplies most UK brands and the seal costs £5.50. This cost pressure makes competing mainly on price risky, as LoopLunch may have limited margin to absorb a lower selling price. A premium durable position could therefore be more defensible if customers value the stronger seal and five-year guarantee enough to justify £32. LoopLunch should use these features to differentiate clearly, while recognising that the availability of cheap substitutes means the premium benefit must be convincing.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice question. PedalLoop operates a small bicycle repair shop in Bristol. It is considering investing £180,000 to launch a monthly e-bike subscription service for commuters. Subscribers would pay £69 per month, receiving an e-bike, repairs and theft cover. The business would initially operate from one city-centre hub.
question.stem: Using Porter's Five Forces, evaluate whether PedalLoop should launch its e-bike subscription service.

table.title: Information on Bristol commuter travel and e-bike subscriptions

cells: Three established e-bike subscription firms already operate in Bristol. Their monthly prices range from £59 to £75. Two competitors advertise heavily online and offer a same-day replacement bike service.
PedalLoop estimates that a new operator needs at least £150,000 for bikes, software and a depot. However, e-bikes can be leased from specialist finance providers, reducing the initial cash needed.
A commuter survey of 300 local workers found that 42% normally use a bus, 31% drive and 18% cycle using their own bike. A monthly bus pass costs £56.

One UK distributor supplies the battery model compatible with PedalLoop's proposed e-bikes. It has stated that battery prices will rise by 12% next year. PedalLoop could use another battery system, but this would require replacing chargers at a cost of £24,000.

The survey found that 64% of respondents would compare at least three providers before subscribing. Customers can cancel a subscription with 30 days' notice. However, 38% said that included repairs would be important when choosing a provider.
Bristol City Council plans to add 20 km of segregated cycle lanes over the next two years, subject to final budget approval.

levels.descriptor: Shows limited knowledge of one or more of Porter's forces. Application to PedalLoop is generic or narrowly based on the data. Makes simple assertions about whether to launch, with little explanation of effects on prices, costs, demand or profitability.

Shows sound understanding of several relevant forces and applies them to PedalLoop using the case data. Explains how competitive pressures could affect revenue, costs or margins. A judgement is given but is not fully weighed, or considers only a limited range of changing conditions.

Shows thorough, well-selected application of Porter's Five Forces. Analyses interactions and trade-offs between forces using the data, including the significance of evidence such as prices, switching conditions or supplier costs. Reaches a clear, justified judgement about launch that is conditional where appropriate and recognises uncertainty or change over time.

indicative_content: Rivalry is likely to constrain PedalLoop's pricing because three established firms charge £59–£75 and two provide heavily promoted same-day replacement bikes. PedalLoop's £69 proposed price is within the market range, but it may need costly service differentiation rather than competing only on price.

Bus travel, car use and personally owned bikes are substitutes because they satisfy the commuting need without being direct e-bike subscription rivals. The £56 bus pass creates a lower-price alternative, potentially limiting demand or placing a ceiling on the subscription price.

Supplier power is strong because one distributor supplies the compatible battery and intends to increase prices by 12%. PedalLoop's alternative involves £24,000 of charger replacement costs, so it may face higher operating costs and reduced margins.

Buyer power is relatively strong: 64% would compare at least three providers and customers can leave with 30 days' notice. This makes it difficult to recover higher battery costs through price rises. Included repairs may reduce buyer power for the 38% who value that service.
Entry barriers are mixed. The need for around £150,000 creates a capital barrier, but leasing e-bikes reduces the cash barrier, so future entrants could increase rivalry.

The planned 20 km of cycle lanes could make e-bike commuting more attractive and increase demand, but approval is uncertain. A launch may be more attractive if PedalLoop can secure battery terms and provide a valued repair service before further entrants emerge.

A justified judgement may support a cautious launch, such as a limited pilot, rather than committing the full £180,000 immediately. This depends on securing supplier protection and demonstrating that repair quality differentiates the offer sufficiently from competitors and substitutes.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
PedalLoop faces significant pressure from buyers and existing rivals. Three established firms already charge between £59 and £75, so PedalLoop's proposed £69 price is not obviously cheaper. As 64% of potential customers would compare at least three providers and can cancel with 30 days' notice, customers can switch easily. This could force PedalLoop to spend on marketing or improve its service, reducing the margin earned from each subscription. However, the fact that 38% value included repairs gives PedalLoop an opportunity to use its existing repair expertise as a differentiator rather than simply cutting its price.

Supplier power is also a major risk. A single compatible battery distributor plans a 12% price rise. PedalLoop could change battery system, but replacing chargers would cost £24,000, so its alternatives are expensive. Higher battery costs may be difficult to pass on because bus travel costs only £56 per month and is a substitute for commuters. Cars, buses and personally owned bikes are substitutes because they meet the same travel need, even though they are not e-bike subscription competitors.

Entry barriers provide only partial protection. The estimated £150,000 start-up requirement may deter some firms, but leasing bikes lowers the cash needed for entry. Therefore, a successful market could attract more rivals. Conversely, the proposed 20 km of cycle lanes may increase the number of potential customers, although the plan is not yet certain.

Overall, PedalLoop should not immediately commit all £180,000 to a full launch. It should launch a smaller pilot only if it can negotiate a longer-term battery price agreement and use reliable repairs to attract customers who value the service. This cautious approach is justified because buyer, supplier and substitute pressures are currently strong, while the possible growth from new cycle lanes remains uncertain.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice question. Northgate Cycles Ltd makes electric bicycles in the UK. It is considering opening a second assembly site. The finance director believes that growth in total assets proves that Northgate's financial position is stronger and that it should take out further borrowing to fund the site.
question.stem: Evaluate the finance director's view that Northgate Cycles Ltd has a stronger financial position and should therefore take out further borrowing to open the second assembly site. Use the data provided and your knowledge of statements of financial position and comparisons of ratios over time and with competitors.

table.title: Northgate Cycles Ltd: selected statement of financial position data and ratios

levels.descriptor: Shows limited knowledge of assets, liabilities, equity, statements of financial position or ratios. Makes simple assertions about Northgate, with little or no use of the data. Evaluation is absent or unsupported.

Shows some accurate understanding of the statement of financial position as a snapshot of assets, liabilities and equity, and/or of comparing ratios. Applies some data from Northgate, but analysis is brief or one-sided. A judgement may be given but is not well supported.

Shows clear understanding and relevant application of the financial-position data. Analyses changes over time and/or comparisons with PedalPower, explaining implications for liquidity, debt, working capital or finance capacity. Reaches a supported judgement, although the evaluation may not fully consider the limitations of the evidence.

Shows thorough and well-focused understanding of how a statement of financial position and ratio comparisons can inform, but not determine, a financing decision. Develops sustained analysis of Northgate's asset quality, liability structure, liquidity and debt risk using precise data comparisons. Makes a balanced, context-based judgement that recognises the snapshot and valuation limitations of the evidence and identifies relevant further information, such as cash-flow timing and the ability to convert inventory and receivables into cash.

indicative_content: A statement of financial position is a snapshot at a single date showing assets, liabilities and equity; total assets equal total liabilities plus equity. It can show financial structure, but it does not show the timing of all cash movements.

Northgate's total assets increased from £2.80m to £3.85m. However, this alone does not prove greater financial strength because the rise includes non-cash assets such as non-current assets, inventory and receivables.

Cash fell from £0.08m to £0.05m while current liabilities rose from £0.80m to £1.25m. This may make meeting short-term obligations more difficult, particularly if inventory is slow-moving or customers pay receivables late.

Northgate's liquidity ratio fell from 1.25 to 1.16 and is below PedalPower's 1.60. This comparison suggests relatively greater short-term liquidity risk, although a ratio at one date can conceal the timing and quality of assets and liabilities.

Inventory rose by £0.25m and receivables rose by £0.23m. These are assets, but neither is the same as cash; their usefulness in meeting bills depends on how quickly and reliably they can be converted into cash.

Non-current liabilities rose from £0.70m to £1.35m while equity fell from £1.30m to £1.25m. The debt-to-equity ratio increased from 1.15 to 2.08, compared with PedalPower's 0.90, indicating a greater reliance on debt relative to equity.

Further borrowing could initially increase cash and assets, but it would also increase liabilities and could add to Northgate's financial risk. The decision should depend on expected cash generation and repayment capacity, not asset growth alone.

Book values of non-current assets may not equal their market values. The directors should also consider cash-flow information, the age and collectability of receivables, the saleability of inventory and the timing of debt repayments before deciding. The statement and ratios should be interpreted alongside operational information.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
The finance director has some evidence that Northgate has expanded. Total assets rose from £2.80m to £3.85m, and non-current assets increased by £0.60m. This could indicate that the business has invested in resources that may support a second assembly site. A statement of financial position also shows how the business is financed: in both years Northgate's assets are matched by liabilities and equity.

However, higher total assets do not necessarily mean that Northgate can comfortably take on more borrowing. A statement of financial position is a snapshot, and assets differ greatly in liquidity. Northgate's cash balance fell from £0.08m to £0.05m, despite the increase in total assets. At the same time, current liabilities increased from £0.80m to £1.25m. Therefore, Northgate may have less immediately available cash to meet short-term obligations.

The composition of the increase in current assets is also important. Inventory increased from £0.50m to £0.75m and receivables increased from £0.42m to £0.65m. These are assets, but they are not equivalent to cash. If bicycles are slow to sell or customers pay late, Northgate could experience cash pressure even though its reported assets have grown. This concern is supported by the liquidity ratio, which fell from 1.25 to 1.16. It is also lower than PedalPower's 1.60, suggesting that Northgate has a weaker short-term liquidity position than its competitor at the same date.

The financing trend also makes additional borrowing risky. Non-current liabilities almost doubled, from £0.70m to £1.35m, while equity fell slightly from £1.30m to £1.25m. Consequently, the debt-to-equity ratio rose from 1.15 to 2.08 and is much higher than PedalPower's 0.90. This suggests Northgate is increasingly reliant on debt rather than equity. Further borrowing would initially raise cash and total assets, but it would also raise liabilities and may increase pressure on the business to make repayments.

Overall, the director's conclusion is too confident. Asset growth may help Northgate expand, but the trend in cash, liquidity and debt relative to equity suggests that further borrowing could worsen financial risk. Northgate should only proceed if it has evidence that inventory can be sold promptly, receivables will be collected reliably and future cash inflows will cover the timing of its short-term obligations and debt repayments. It should use cash-flow and operational information alongside the statement of financial position and ratio comparisons before making the final decision.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Northway Grocers is an established UK supermarket chain. A member of its digital team develops a new customer app using the company’s existing technology, funding and store data.
question.stem: Which action is an example of intrapreneurship?

options.label: A
options.text: An employee develops the new app within Northway Grocers using the company’s resources.

options.label: B
options.text: An employee leaves Northway Grocers to set up an independent app business.

options.label: C
options.text: Northway Grocers buys shares in a technology company.

options.label: D
options.text: An employee follows an existing procedure to process customer refunds.

option_rationale: A is correct because it involves entrepreneurial activity by an employee within an established organisation, using its resources.
B is wrong because setting up an independent business is entrepreneurship rather than intrapreneurship.
C is wrong because purchasing shares is an investment decision, not entrepreneurial activity by an employee or team within the organisation.
D is wrong because carrying out an established routine does not involve developing a new product, process or business model.
mark_scheme.model_answer: A

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice question. Northmoor Kitchens produces fitted kitchen units. It has expanded production and now orders much larger quantities of timber each month.
question.stem: Which statement identifies a purchasing economy of scale for Northmoor Kitchens?

options.label: A
options.text: The business receives a lower price per sheet of timber because it places larger orders.

options.label: B
options.text: The business uses automated cutting machinery to produce more units per hour.

options.label: C
options.text: The business spreads the salary of its operations manager across a greater output.

options.label: D
options.text: The business increases its selling price because it has become better known.

option_rationale: A is correct because buying larger quantities can give the business greater bargaining power and reduce the unit price paid to suppliers.
B is wrong because this describes a technical economy of scale, arising from more efficient machinery or production technology.
C is wrong because this describes a managerial economy of scale, where management costs are spread across more output.
D is wrong because higher selling prices do not describe an economy of scale, which concerns lower average costs.
mark_scheme.model_answer: A

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Harbour Homewares Ltd supplies kitchen products to independent retailers. It has rapidly won new customers and sales have increased. The business has recruited many new staff and now has more departments to coordinate. It must also buy extra stock before its new retail customers pay their invoices, and its cash balance is falling.
question.stem: Explain how Harbour Homewares Ltd could experience diseconomies of scale and overtrading as it grows.

points.descriptor: Explains diseconomies of scale as rising average costs caused by a business becoming too large or complex to manage efficiently.
accept: Coordination or communication problems as the business grows can increase costs per unit.
A definition showing that increasing scale can make operations less efficient.

points.descriptor: Applies diseconomies of scale to Harbour Homewares Ltd.
accept: More departments and newly recruited staff may be harder to coordinate.
Poor communication or less experienced staff could lead to mistakes, delays or duplicated work, increasing average costs.

points.descriptor: Explains overtrading as growth creating working-capital pressure beyond the finance available.
accept: A business can have rising sales but insufficient cash to fund its expansion.
Expansion may require spending on stock before customer cash is received.

points.descriptor: Applies overtrading to Harbour Homewares Ltd.
accept: Harbour Homewares must purchase additional stock before retailers pay invoices.
Its falling cash balance could mean it cannot meet payments or continue funding its rapid growth.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Harbour Homewares may experience diseconomies of scale because its larger workforce and additional departments make communication and coordination more difficult. This could cause delays, errors or duplicated work, raising its average costs. It may also be overtrading because it needs to pay for extra stock before new retail customers pay their invoices. Therefore, despite higher sales, its falling cash balance may leave insufficient working capital to fund day-to-day payments and further growth.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice question. Northbay Homeware Ltd has taken over Oak & Hearth Ltd, a smaller retailer of kitchen products, to gain access to its loyal customers and specialist product range. Northbay expects to reduce costs by using one ordering system and sharing warehouses. However, Oak & Hearth’s managers use different stock-control software and several experienced buyers have said they may leave after the takeover.
question.stem: Explain one reason why Northbay Homeware Ltd’s takeover of Oak & Hearth Ltd may fail to create the business success Northbay expects.

points.descriptor: Identifies a valid takeover-specific reason why expected success may not be achieved.
accept: Northbay may overpay for Oak & Hearth.
Expected cost savings or additional sales may not materialise.
The two businesses’ systems or operations may be difficult or costly to integrate.
A clash of cultures or management approaches may occur.
Key Oak & Hearth staff or customers may leave after the takeover.

points.descriptor: Explains the chosen reason using relevant business knowledge.
accept: Overpayment means the acquisition cost may exceed the value of future benefits received.
Integrating different systems can require additional spending, training and management time.
A management or culture clash can reduce cooperation and decision-making quality.
Losing experienced staff can remove specialist knowledge and supplier relationships.
Losing customers reduces the additional revenue expected from buying the business.

points.descriptor: Applies the explanation to Northbay’s takeover of Oak & Hearth.
accept: Uses the different stock-control software or planned single ordering system.
Uses Oak & Hearth’s experienced buyers potentially leaving.
Uses Northbay’s aim to share warehouses or access Oak & Hearth’s customers and specialist range.

points.descriptor: Develops a clear consequence showing why the takeover may not create the expected success.
accept: Integration costs and disruption could be greater than the savings from one ordering system and shared warehouses.
If experienced buyers leave, Northbay may struggle to source the specialist range, weakening customer loyalty.
Lower sales or higher costs would reduce profit and mean the anticipated benefits of the takeover are not achieved.

mark_scheme.model_answer: One reason is that Northbay may find it difficult and expensive to integrate Oak & Hearth’s stock-control software with its own ordering system. Northbay expects cost savings from using one system and sharing warehouses, but software changes may require training, technical support and management time. This could disrupt ordering or create stock shortages. The extra costs and lost sales could exceed the expected savings, so the takeover may not increase profit as Northbay planned.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice question. TrailBrew Ltd makes reusable insulated drinks bottles for independent UK cafés. The business has won a 12-month supply contract with a national café chain. The contract will substantially increase sales, but the café chain will pay 60 days after delivery. TrailBrew must purchase materials and make the bottles before receiving this cash.
question.stem: Analyse the likely impact of TrailBrew Ltd’s planned growth on its functional areas.

table.title: TrailBrew Ltd: current position and forecast after winning the contract

levels.descriptor: Shows limited relevant understanding of growth and identifies one or more possible effects on a functional area. Application to TrailBrew is absent or general, and chains of reasoning are undeveloped.
Shows sound understanding of how growth can affect functional areas, with clear application to TrailBrew’s data. Gives at least one developed chain of reasoning explaining a likely consequence.

Shows thorough, well-applied analysis of the linked effects of TrailBrew’s growth on multiple functional areas. Chains of reasoning are developed and use relevant data to explain significant operational, people, financial or systems consequences.

indicative_content: Operations/production will face a capacity constraint because forecast sales of 140,000 bottles exceed factory capacity of 100,000. TrailBrew may need additional capacity or changes to operations; otherwise it may be unable to meet the new contract, despite higher demand.

The finance function will face increased working-capital pressure. Materials inventory is forecast to rise from £90,000 to £210,000, while the new customer pays after 60 days rather than 30 days. Cash is tied up in stock and unpaid sales before cash is received, creating a financing pressure.

Human resources will need to recruit and integrate 10 additional production employees, increasing the workforce from 18 to 28. Rapid recruitment may reduce average experience or make coordination more difficult, which could affect production quality or efficiency.
Management and systems may need to become more robust as higher output, more employees, more inventory and a large customer contract create greater organisational complexity.
The higher revenue forecast does not automatically mean the growth is successful: the business must have sufficient cash, capacity and management capability to support the increase in activity.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
TrailBrew’s operations function is likely to face an immediate capacity problem. Forecast bottle sales are 140,000, but the factory can make only 100,000 bottles each year. Therefore, the business cannot meet all expected demand using its current capacity. It may need to obtain additional capacity or alter its operations. If it fails to do so, it could lose sales or damage its relationship with the café chain, so the revenue forecast of £2.1m may not be achieved.

The finance function will also experience pressure on working capital. Materials inventory is expected to increase by £120,000, from £90,000 to £210,000, so more cash will be spent before bottles are sold. In addition, the café chain pays in 60 days, compared with TrailBrew’s current 30-day terms. This means TrailBrew could have to pay for materials, wages and increased production before receiving cash from the contract. Consequently, sales growth could create a cash gap and require additional finance, even if the contract increases revenue.

There will also be an impact on human resources and management systems. The production workforce rises from 18 to 28 employees, which is a large increase in a small business. Recruiting and integrating staff quickly may dilute experience and create more coordination between people and processes. If systems and supervision do not develop with the workforce, efficiency or quality could fall. Therefore, TrailBrew’s growth affects operations, finance and people simultaneously; higher sales alone do not guarantee sustainable growth.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Harbour & Hearth sells kitchenware and has begun offering a related range of table linens. Both ranges use the same warehouse, delivery vehicles and online marketing team.
question.stem: Which statement identifies an economy of scope for Harbour & Hearth?

options.label: A
options.text: The business lowers the cost of both product ranges by sharing its warehouse, delivery vehicles and marketing team.

options.label: B
options.text: The business reduces its average cost per kitchen pan by producing a larger quantity of the same pan.

options.label: C
options.text: The business lowers unit costs because its existing warehouse is used closer to full capacity.

options.label: D
options.text: The business increases average costs because coordinating its larger operation becomes more difficult.

option_rationale: A is correct because economies of scope arise when related products share resources, reducing the cost of providing the combined range.
B is wrong because this describes an economy of scale: lower average cost from increasing output of one product.
C is wrong because fuller use of existing capacity is a utilisation effect, not necessarily an economy of scope.
D is wrong because this describes a diseconomy of scale caused by greater coordination difficulty.
mark_scheme.model_answer: A

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Northline Coffee Roasters sells coffee beans and coffee equipment to independent cafés across Yorkshire. It has a warehouse in Leeds and a fleet of delivery vans. Peak Bakes makes premium chilled pastries and sells mainly to offices, gyms and co-working spaces in the same region. It has an online ordering system and a list of regular business customers. The owners are considering combining the two businesses.
question.stem: Explain how combining Northline Coffee Roasters and Peak Bakes could create synergy.

points.descriptor: Identifies synergy as an additional gain from combining businesses, where the result is greater than the businesses could achieve separately.
accept: A clear definition of synergy as an extra benefit created by combining businesses.
A statement that the two businesses may achieve more together than separately.

points.descriptor: Explains that duplicated resources or costs could be removed.
accept: Northline's Leeds warehouse or delivery vans could also be used for Peak Bakes products.
The businesses could share administration, ordering or delivery resources, reducing duplicated costs.

points.descriptor: Explains that the businesses could sell to each other's customers.
accept: Northline could offer Peak Bakes pastries to independent cafés.
Peak Bakes could offer Northline coffee to its office, gym or co-working customers.
The combined customer lists could create additional sales opportunities.

points.descriptor: Explains how complementary capabilities could improve the offer or operation.
accept: Northline's café relationships and Peak Bakes' chilled-pastry expertise could allow a wider food-and-drink offer.
Peak Bakes' online ordering system could be used to sell Northline's coffee products to more business customers.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Synergy is an additional gain created when two businesses are combined and can achieve more than they could separately. Northline's warehouse and delivery vans could distribute Peak Bakes pastries as well as coffee, so the firms may avoid running separate delivery operations. Northline could sell pastries to its independent café customers, while Peak Bakes could offer coffee to offices and gyms. Also, Peak Bakes' online ordering system could help Northline reach more business customers.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Northfield Bikes sells its existing commuter bicycles to customers in the UK.
question.stem: Which action is an example of market penetration for Northfield Bikes?

options.label: A
options.text: Offer a loyalty discount to encourage more UK customers to buy its existing commuter bicycles.

options.label: B
options.text: Start selling its existing commuter bicycles in Ireland.

options.label: C
options.text: Launch a new range of electric scooters for its UK customers.

options.label: D
options.text: Buy a UK company that produces camping equipment and sell its products.

option_rationale: A is correct because it aims to increase sales of an existing product in an existing market.
B is market development because the bicycles are existing products but Ireland is a new market for the business.
C is product development because electric scooters are a new product sold to an existing market.
D is diversification because it involves new products in a new market, regardless of buying another business as the growth method.
mark_scheme.model_answer: A

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Hearth & Field is a UK bakery that sells its standard range of loaves and pastries through supermarkets across England and Wales. The business plans to begin supplying the same standard range to supermarkets in the Republic of Ireland. It also plans to create a new gluten-free pastry range for its current supermarket customers in England and Wales.
question.stem: Explain how Hearth & Field’s two plans represent market development and product development.

points.descriptor: Identifies market development as selling an existing product in a new market.
accept: An existing product is introduced to a new market.
Growth using current products with new customers or a new geographical market.

points.descriptor: Applies market development to Hearth & Field supplying its existing standard loaves and pastries in the Republic of Ireland, which is a new market for the business.
accept: Selling the same bakery range in Ireland is market development.
Ireland is a new geographical/customer market while the products remain unchanged.

points.descriptor: Identifies product development as introducing a new product to an existing market.
accept: A business creates a new product for its current customers.
Growth through new products sold in existing markets.

points.descriptor: Applies product development to Hearth & Field launching gluten-free pastries for its existing supermarket customers in England and Wales.
accept: The gluten-free pastry range is new, but it is sold to the bakery's current UK market.
England and Wales remain existing markets while the product range changes.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Market development means taking existing products into a market that is new to the business. Hearth & Field is using market development because it will sell its current loaves and pastries in the Republic of Ireland, where it does not currently supply supermarkets. Product development means introducing a new product to an existing market. Its gluten-free pastry range is product development because it is a new product for existing supermarket customers in England and Wales.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Harbour & Hearth is a UK business that sells handmade candles through its shops and website. It plans to begin selling electric bicycles to commuters in several UK cities. The business has not sold bicycles before and has no experience of the cycling market.
question.stem: Explain why Harbour & Hearth's plan to sell electric bicycles is diversification.

points.descriptor: Identifies diversification as a growth direction involving a new product and a new market for the business.
accept: Diversification means selling new products in new markets.
A strategy involving both product and market newness.

points.descriptor: Applies product newness: electric bicycles are a new product for Harbour & Hearth.
accept: The business currently sells candles, not bicycles.
Electric bicycles are outside its existing product range.

points.descriptor: Applies market newness: commuters/cycling customers are a new market for Harbour & Hearth.
accept: Its existing candle buyers differ from commuters buying electric bicycles.
The cycling market is new to the business.

points.descriptor: Explains that the move will require new knowledge or capabilities because the business is entering an unfamiliar product-market area.
accept: It may need knowledge of bicycle suppliers, safety requirements or commuter customer needs.
It will need different staff skills, marketing or operations from those used for candles.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Diversification is growth through a new product in a new market. Electric bicycles are new to Harbour & Hearth because it currently sells handmade candles. Commuters buying bicycles are also a new market, so the business may need new knowledge of cycling customers, suppliers and product safety.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Northshore Roasters is a UK coffee business with 18 cafés in northern England. Its main customers are commuters and students. Sales from its existing café drinks have risen by only 1% in the past year. The business has £180,000 available for expansion and wants to increase revenue without taking risks that could threaten its existing cafés.
question.stem:
Northshore Roasters is considering two growth options.

Analyse which option is likely to be more suitable for Northshore Roasters.

table.title: Information on Northshore Roasters' growth options

cells: Option A: sell bottled cold-brew coffee through UK supermarkets
A new product for Northshore Roasters, sold to UK consumers rather than only through its cafés. The business already has a small production kitchen and a recognised local brand.
The UK bottled cold-brew market is forecast to grow by 12% next year. Supermarkets require suppliers to provide reliable large-scale deliveries.
Option B: open cafés in Belgium
Northshore Roasters would sell its existing café drinks in a new country. It has no outlets, managers or supplier contracts outside the UK.
The Belgian café market is forecast to grow by 3% next year. Several established coffee chains already operate in the proposed city.

levels.descriptor: Analyses both options using accurate understanding of product and market newness. Makes developed, contextual chains of reasoning about market attractiveness, capabilities and risk, leading to a supported judgement about suitability.

Shows some analysis of one or both options. Applies relevant information from the data, with a logical but partly developed explanation of how influences such as growth, competition, resources or unfamiliarity affect the choice.
Shows limited understanding of a relevant growth direction or influence on choice. Response is mainly descriptive, generic or has weak application to Northshore Roasters.

indicative_content: Option A is product development because Northshore Roasters would offer a new bottled cold-brew product to its existing UK market. The 12% market growth could create a stronger revenue opportunity than its café drinks, which grew by only 1%.

Northshore Roasters' production kitchen and local brand may be transferable capabilities for Option A, reducing the capability gap and use of its £180,000 expansion funds. However, supplying supermarkets reliably at scale may require distribution capacity that it does not currently possess, creating operational risk.

Option B is market development because it takes existing café drinks into a new geographical market. It may require less product knowledge than developing bottled cold brew, but Belgium is a new market for the business, so unfamiliar customer preferences, managers and supplier contracts increase the information and capability gap.

Belgium's 3% market growth and established chains may restrict sales and make it difficult for Northshore Roasters to recover the cost of new outlets. This matters because it has limited funds and wishes to avoid risks to its existing cafés.

A justified conclusion may favour Option A because its faster-growing market and related production capability could make it more suitable, provided the business can secure dependable supermarket distribution. A different conclusion is valid if it is well supported by the operational demands of product development.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Option A is product development: Northshore Roasters would introduce bottled cold-brew, a new product, to UK consumers, an existing market. This could be suitable because the bottled cold-brew market is expected to grow by 12%, compared with only 1% growth in its current café drinks. Therefore, demand for the new product could increase revenue more quickly than relying on its cafés.

In addition, Northshore Roasters already has a production kitchen and a local brand. These related capabilities may reduce the cost and uncertainty of developing the product, which is important as it has only £180,000 available. However, supermarkets expect reliable high-volume deliveries. If the kitchen and distribution system cannot meet this requirement, the business could lose contracts or need to spend heavily, reducing the benefit of the higher-growth market.

Option B is market development because the business would sell its existing drinks in a new country. Although it would not need to develop a new product, it has no Belgian managers, outlets or supplier contracts. This unfamiliarity increases the capability gap. The market is also growing by only 3% and established chains are already present, so Northshore Roasters may struggle to gain enough customers to cover the costs of entering Belgium.

Overall, Option A is likely to be more suitable because it offers access to faster market growth while using some existing capabilities. Its suitability depends on whether Northshore Roasters can arrange reliable supermarket distribution within its available funds.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice question. EcoHome Refill is a UK business selling concentrated laundry and washing-up liquid refills through its website. Its customers buy reusable bottles once and then order refills. Sales have grown slowly because several large supermarkets now sell similar refill products. EcoHome is considering selling a new range of dishwasher-cleaning tablets to its existing UK online customers. The tablets would be sold in compostable packaging and could be ordered alongside its current refills. The directors believe the proposal could increase spending by existing customers, but they are concerned about the cost and the business's lack of experience of making tablets.
question.stem: Using the Ansoff matrix and the data provided, evaluate whether EcoHome Refill should launch the dishwasher-cleaning tablets.

table.title: Information for EcoHome Refill

cells: EcoHome has 48,000 active UK online customers. Its current laundry and washing-up refills generated £2.4 million revenue last year.
In a survey of 600 existing customers, 68% said that they regularly use a dishwasher. Of these customers, 55% said they would be likely to try EcoHome dishwasher tablets.
UK sales of dishwasher tablets are forecast to grow by 2% in the next year. Three large brands together hold 75% of this market and use price promotions frequently.

EcoHome has £180,000 available for the launch. Developing the tablet formula and obtaining packaging approval would cost £120,000. EcoHome has expertise in refill liquids but has never manufactured tablets.
EcoHome could instead offer a 10% loyalty discount on existing refills to encourage current customers to order more frequently. This would cost an estimated £45,000 in reduced revenue.

levels.descriptor: Shows accurate understanding of the Ansoff matrix and applies it consistently to EcoHome. Develops balanced, linked analysis of benefits and drawbacks using the data, considers a relevant alternative, and reaches a clear, well-supported judgement that is conditional where appropriate.

Shows some sound understanding of the Ansoff matrix. Makes relevant application to EcoHome and explains one or more consequences, though analysis may be uneven or less developed. A judgement is given but may be asserted or only partly supported.

Shows limited knowledge of growth directions and/or makes simple statements about the proposal. Application to EcoHome is limited and analysis is mostly descriptive. A conclusion may be absent or unsupported.

indicative_content: Launching dishwasher-cleaning tablets is product development because EcoHome would sell a new product to its existing UK customer market. It is not market development, because the target customers are not new to EcoHome.

The proposal may be attractive because EcoHome can market to 48,000 active customers and can bundle tablets with existing online orders. This could reduce the cost and difficulty of reaching buyers compared with entering a wholly new market.

Survey evidence suggests possible demand: 68% of customers regularly use a dishwasher and 55% of these customers say they are likely to try the tablets. However, stated intention in a survey may not become actual repeat purchases.

The strategy requires product capabilities EcoHome does not currently possess, since it has experience in liquid refills rather than tablet manufacture. This unfamiliarity may increase development, quality-control and supply risks.
The £120,000 development and approval cost would leave only £60,000 from the £180,000 available for marketing, production problems or delays. This weakens the financial flexibility of the launch.
Competition is strong, with three large brands holding 75% of the market and using price promotions. Market growth of only 2% may make it difficult to win sufficient sales without reducing prices.

Market penetration through a 10% loyalty discount would use existing products in an existing market. It has lower capability uncertainty and a lower estimated cost of £45,000, but discounts may reduce revenue and may not overcome strong competition.
A justified decision could be to proceed only after small-scale testing or after securing manufacturing expertise, rather than committing the full launch budget immediately.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
The proposed launch is product development on the Ansoff matrix because EcoHome would offer dishwasher-cleaning tablets, which are new to the business, to its existing UK online customers. This could be a sensible growth direction because EcoHome already has 48,000 active customers and could promote the tablets alongside refill orders. Customers would not need to be acquired through an entirely new sales channel. Also, 68% of surveyed customers use a dishwasher and 55% of this group say they are likely to try the product, suggesting that there may be a relevant customer need.

However, product development creates an important capability gap. EcoHome understands liquid refills but has never made tablets, so it may face problems with product quality, formulation or packaging approval. The £120,000 development and approval cost would use two-thirds of its £180,000 available funds, leaving only £60,000 to deal with marketing or unexpected production problems. This matters because three large brands already hold 75% of the market and use frequent price promotions. In a market growing by only 2%, EcoHome may struggle to gain repeat sales without spending heavily on promotion or cutting its price.

An alternative is market penetration: offering a loyalty discount on existing refills to encourage current customers to buy more often. This uses EcoHome's established products and capabilities and has an estimated cost of £45,000. However, the discount could reduce revenue and may not create a significant advantage against rivals selling similar refill products.

Overall, EcoHome should not commit immediately to a full tablet launch simply because it is product development. The existing customer base and survey results make the idea promising, but the limited remaining finance and lack of tablet expertise make execution risky. EcoHome should launch only if it can first test demand with a small batch or obtain reliable tablet-manufacturing expertise; otherwise, lower-risk market penetration is the more suitable short-term option.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Northfield Bakery has built a strong local reputation and wants to increase its sales over the next two years.
question.stem: Which action would be an example of organic growth for Northfield Bakery?

options.label: A
options.text: Opening two new Northfield Bakery shops using retained profit.

options.label: B
options.text: Buying a local competitor and taking control of its shops.

options.label: C
options.text: Creating a jointly owned delivery company with a supermarket.

options.label: D
options.text: Signing an agreement with an independent café to sell Northfield Bakery products.

option_rationale: A is correct because opening new shops using its own funds is internal expansion of the business.
B is wrong because purchasing a competitor is an acquisition, which is external growth.
C is wrong because a jointly owned business with another organisation is a joint venture.
D is wrong because cooperation with an independent business without combining ownership is a strategic alliance.
mark_scheme.model_answer: A

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Harbour Homewares Ltd sells kitchen equipment through 18 shops in the UK. It has acquired CookPro Ltd, a smaller competitor with six profitable shops in northern England. Following the acquisition, Harbour Homewares plans to close its own loss-making furniture division and sell the division’s warehouse.
question.stem: Explain how Harbour Homewares Ltd is using external growth and retrenchment in this situation.

points.descriptor: Identifies or defines external growth as expanding through combining with, or taking control of, an existing business.
accept: External growth involves acquiring or merging with an existing business.
Growth by buying another business rather than developing internally.

points.descriptor: Applies external growth to Harbour Homewares acquiring CookPro, giving it immediate control of CookPro’s six northern shops and/or its existing customers.
accept: Buying CookPro gives Harbour Homewares an immediate presence in northern England.
The acquisition gives it CookPro’s shops rather than having to open all six itself.

points.descriptor: Identifies or defines retrenchment as strategically reducing or refocusing a business by closing, selling or withdrawing from activities, assets or capacity.
accept: Retrenchment is reducing the scope of a business.
It can involve closing a division and disposing of assets.

points.descriptor: Applies retrenchment to the closure of the loss-making furniture division and sale of its warehouse, which can concentrate resources on stronger kitchen-equipment operations and/or release funds.
accept: Closing the furniture division removes an unprofitable activity.
Selling the warehouse may release capital for the kitchen-equipment business or integration of CookPro.
The business is refocusing on its core kitchen-equipment activity.

mark_scheme.model_answer:
External growth is expansion by acquiring or combining with an existing business. Harbour Homewares has used external growth by acquiring CookPro, so it immediately gains CookPro’s six northern shops rather than building this presence from scratch.

Retrenchment is a strategic reduction or refocusing of business activities. Harbour Homewares is closing its loss-making furniture division and selling its warehouse. This could release funds and allow managers to focus on the stronger kitchen-equipment business.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Northshore Bakes Ltd makes premium biscuits and sells them through independent food shops. It is considering working with GreenBean Coffee Ltd, which has a strong network of café customers but no biscuit range. The two businesses plan to create a new company, owned and controlled equally by both firms, to supply biscuit-and-coffee gift boxes to cafés.
question.stem: Explain how the planned arrangement could be a joint venture rather than a merger for Northshore Bakes Ltd and GreenBean Coffee Ltd.

points.descriptor: Identifies a joint venture as an activity or new organisation that is jointly owned or controlled by two or more businesses.
accept: A jointly owned business created by separate firms.
Both firms share control of a new activity.
A separately governed activity owned by partners.

points.descriptor: Applies the definition by explaining that Northshore Bakes Ltd and GreenBean Coffee Ltd would each own and control the new gift-box company equally.
