accept: The two firms have equal ownership of the new company.
They would share decisions about the gift-box operation.
Both businesses retain joint control of the new venture.

points.descriptor: Identifies a merger as a combination of organisations under an agreed ownership or control structure.
accept: A merger combines two businesses.
The organisations would combine ownership or control.
The two firms would become one combined organisation.

points.descriptor: Explains the difference in this case: the firms are creating a jointly controlled gift-box activity, rather than combining Northshore Bakes Ltd and GreenBean Coffee Ltd themselves into one organisation.
accept: The original biscuit and coffee businesses can remain separate while the new company is jointly controlled.
This is not a merger because the whole two firms are not combining.
The arrangement concerns a specific gift-box business rather than full combination of both organisations.

mark_scheme.model_answer: A joint venture is a separately governed activity that is owned or controlled jointly by partner businesses. Here, Northshore Bakes Ltd and GreenBean Coffee Ltd would each own and control the new gift-box company equally. In contrast, a merger combines the organisations themselves under an agreed ownership or control structure. The planned arrangement is therefore a joint venture because the two existing firms can remain separate while cooperating through the new company.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Hearth & Grain Ltd is a UK producer of packaged bread and pastries, selling mainly through supermarkets. It is considering buying Millstone Flour Ltd, which supplies flour to bakeries; FreshStop Stores, a chain of local food shops; and Bakewell Foods, another producer of packaged bread and pastries.
question.stem: Explain how the proposed purchases could provide Hearth & Grain Ltd with backward vertical integration, forward vertical integration and horizontal integration.

points.descriptor: Identifies backward vertical integration as taking control of an earlier stage of the value chain, such as a supplier of inputs.
accept: Buying Millstone Flour Ltd is backward vertical integration because it supplies flour, an input used by Hearth & Grain.
Backward integration means moving towards suppliers.

points.descriptor: Identifies forward vertical integration as taking control of a later, customer-facing distribution or retail stage.
accept: Buying FreshStop Stores is forward vertical integration because the shops sell food to final customers.
Forward integration means moving towards distribution or retailing.

points.descriptor: Identifies horizontal integration as combining with a business at the same stage of the value chain, commonly a competitor.
accept: Buying Bakewell Foods is horizontal integration because both firms produce packaged bread and pastries.
Horizontal integration involves acquiring a competitor operating at the same production stage.

points.descriptor: Applies the distinction accurately to Hearth & Grain's proposed purchases.
accept: Millstone is upstream, FreshStop is downstream and Bakewell operates alongside Hearth & Grain at the production stage.
The purchases differ because one is a supplier, one is a retailer and one makes similar products.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Millstone Flour would be backward vertical integration because Hearth & Grain would take control of a supplier earlier in its value chain. FreshStop Stores would be forward vertical integration because Hearth & Grain would gain a retail route to final customers. Bakewell Foods would be horizontal integration because it produces similar packaged bread and pastries at the same stage as Hearth & Grain.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Harbour Drinks Ltd produces canned soft drinks. It has bought 100% of BrightSteps, a chain of children’s shoe shops. The two businesses have no direct product or value-chain link. Harbour Drinks has also agreed to promote its drinks through FitRoute, an independent fitness-app business. FitRoute remains independently owned and neither business has bought shares in the other.
question.stem: Explain why Harbour Drinks’ purchase of BrightSteps is conglomerate integration, whereas its arrangement with FitRoute is an alliance.

points.descriptor: Explains conglomerate integration and applies it to the purchase of BrightSteps.
accept: Conglomerate integration is combining businesses with limited direct product or value-chain relationship (1), applied because a soft-drink producer and children’s shoe retailer operate in unrelated activities (1).
Accept reference to diversification through buying an unrelated business, provided the application to Harbour Drinks and BrightSteps is clear.

points.descriptor: Explains an alliance and applies it to the arrangement with FitRoute.
accept: An alliance is cooperation between independent businesses without a full ownership combination (1), applied because Harbour Drinks and FitRoute cooperate on promotion while FitRoute remains independently owned and neither has bought shares in the other (1).
Accept strategic alliance or a partnership arrangement where both firms retain independence.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Harbour Drinks’ purchase of BrightSteps is conglomerate integration because it has obtained control of a business with no direct product or value-chain connection to canned drinks. Children’s shoes and soft drinks are unrelated activities. The FitRoute arrangement is an alliance because the two independent businesses are cooperating to promote Harbour Drinks’ products, but FitRoute remains separately owned and there is no ownership combination.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context:
Northline Cycles is a UK business that sells mid-priced commuter bicycles and cycling accessories through its website and 18 shops in major cities. Its core bicycle designs have remained largely unchanged for three years. Northline has a 6% share of the UK commuter-bike market. The UK market is forecast to grow by 1% next year, and several larger rivals are offering interest-free credit and discounts. Northline's customer research suggests that 42% of its existing customers would consider buying accessories more often if it offered a loyalty scheme and faster online delivery.

The directors are considering three growth directions. First, they could focus on market penetration in the UK by spending £1.2 million on a loyalty scheme, targeted digital advertising and improving delivery. Secondly, they could introduce a new range of electric bicycles to existing UK customers. This would require £3.5 million for design, specialist components and staff training. Thirdly, Northline could sell its existing bicycles in Denmark through an online-only launch. Denmark has a growing commuter-cycling market, but Northline has no brand awareness there and would need to comply with local consumer and product rules.

Northline has £2 million available for investment. Its objective is to increase annual revenue within two years while avoiding a level of risk that could threaten its existing UK operations.
question.stem: Evaluate the view that Northline Cycles should choose market penetration rather than other growth directions.

levels.descriptor: Shows limited knowledge of growth strategies, with simple assertions about Northline. May identify market penetration or another Ansoff direction, but explanation and judgement are absent or very limited.

Shows some accurate knowledge of market penetration and/or other growth directions. Applies some points to Northline and gives partially developed analysis of benefits or drawbacks. A judgement may be stated but is unsupported or one-sided.

Shows clear understanding of market penetration and distinguishes it from at least one alternative direction. Develops chains of reasoning using Northline's circumstances, including relevant influences on the choice of markets and products. Reaches a supported judgement, although evaluation may be uneven.

Shows thorough and accurate understanding of the Ansoff framework, while recognising that the framework alone does not determine the best choice. Analyses market penetration and credible alternatives in a well-applied way, considering factors such as market conditions, competition, customer demand, resources, capabilities and risk. Makes a well-supported, contextual judgement with some qualification.

Shows a comprehensive and well-integrated evaluation. Uses the Ansoff framework accurately to compare the strategic directions without treating risk as automatic. Develops sustained, contextual analysis of the market, product, financial and capability evidence. Delivers a convincing and nuanced final judgement that weighs conditions and priorities, explaining when market penetration would or would not be the strongest choice for Northline.

indicative_content: Market penetration means increasing sales of Northline's existing bicycles and accessories in its existing UK market. The proposed loyalty scheme, targeted advertising and faster delivery fit this direction.

The 42% of existing customers interested in more frequent accessory purchases suggests that penetration could increase repeat purchases. Faster delivery may also improve convenience and customer loyalty, helping Northline compete without changing its core product range.

Market penetration may be difficult because UK commuter-bike market growth is only 1%, Northline already faces larger competitors and rivals offer credit and discounts. Advertising expenditure may mostly shift sales from competitors and could reduce profit if Northline has to match promotions.

Product development would mean selling new electric bicycles to Northline's existing UK market. It could respond to changing customer needs and provide a differentiated offer, but it requires new design knowledge, specialist components and staff training. Its £3.5 million cost exceeds Northline's £2 million available investment, increasing financial pressure.

Market development would mean selling Northline's existing products in Denmark, a new market for the business. The growing commuter-cycling market could offer more attractive demand than the slow-growing UK market, but lack of brand awareness and unfamiliar consumer and product rules create information, marketing and compliance requirements.

The choice should depend on Northline's objective of revenue growth within two years and its risk capacity. Market penetration has lower product and market unfamiliarity and costs £1.2 million, leaving financial capacity, but it may not generate sufficient growth in a mature and competitive market.

Ansoff classifies the direction of growth but does not itself establish financial viability or guarantee success. Northline needs evidence on expected sales, margins, competitor reactions and the likely effectiveness of its loyalty scheme before committing.

A justified conclusion may favour a staged market-penetration strategy because it fits the available finance, existing customer evidence and risk objective. However, this should be reviewed if the UK market remains constrained; Northline might then build capability for a later, carefully researched electric-bike launch or Danish market development.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Market penetration would involve Northline selling more of its existing bicycles and accessories to customers in its existing UK market. Its proposed loyalty scheme, targeted digital advertising and faster delivery are therefore market-penetration actions. This strategy has a strong short-term case because Northline has only £2 million available but penetration costs £1.2 million. It is also supported by customer research: 42% of existing customers say they may buy accessories more often if a loyalty scheme and faster delivery are introduced. If this intention becomes actual repeat purchasing, Northline can raise revenue with products, suppliers and UK customer needs that it already understands.

Market penetration may also be less disruptive than the alternatives. Northline would not need to develop electric-bike design expertise, source specialist components or learn Danish regulations. This matters because its objective is to grow revenue within two years without putting its UK operations at serious risk. Using existing shops, website and customer data could make the campaign quicker to implement than launching a new product or entering a new country.

However, penetration is not necessarily the best route. The UK commuter-bike market is expected to grow by only 1%, so Northline may find it difficult to generate substantial additional demand. It has only a 6% market share, but larger competitors are offering interest-free credit and discounts. They could respond to Northline's advertising or loyalty scheme with stronger promotions. In that case, Northline may need to spend more on incentives or lower prices, reducing margins even if sales rise. The 42% research result is encouraging, but it measures consideration rather than a commitment to spend more.

Product development through electric bicycles could offer a better response if customer needs are moving towards electric transport. Northline would sell a new product to an existing market, potentially using its established brand and shops to promote the range. This could differentiate the business from rivals competing mainly through discounts. Nevertheless, the £3.5 million requirement exceeds available investment by £1.5 million. Raising finance could increase risk, while weak expertise in specialist components and staff training could cause delays or quality problems. Consequently, the potential revenue opportunity may be unsuitable for Northline at present.

Market development into Denmark could be attractive because the commuter-cycling market is growing, unlike the UK market. Selling existing bicycles online would avoid some cost of opening shops and would use Northline's current product range. Yet Denmark is a new market from Northline's perspective. It has no brand awareness there and would need knowledge of local customer preferences and consumer and product rules. A growing market is not sufficient if Northline lacks the marketing and compliance capability to gain sales quickly.

Overall, Northline should initially choose market penetration, since it is affordable, can be implemented relatively quickly and is supported by evidence of possible increased accessory purchases from existing customers. This conclusion depends on the business setting clear targets for repeat purchases and contribution after promotion costs, rather than assuming the loyalty scheme will work. If penetration fails to deliver sufficient growth in the slow UK market, Northline should investigate the Danish opportunity or build capability for electric bicycles. Therefore, market penetration is the best immediate choice, but it is not automatically the best long-term growth direction.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: BrightBench Furniture is planning the launch of a new collection. Its project manager is reviewing the timing of activity G, which is to photograph the finished products for the online catalogue.
question.stem:
Calculate the total float for activity G. Show your working.

For activity G:
- earliest start time = 6 days
- duration = 3 days
- latest finish time = 13 days

points.descriptor: Uses the total-float calculation with the three relevant timings.
accept: Any correct substitution of latest finish time, duration and earliest start time, for example 13 - 3 - 6.
Any valid intermediate sequence using the supplied figures that leads to the correct answer.

points.descriptor: Correctly calculates 13 - 3 = 10, or an equivalent valid intermediate step.
accept: 10 as the latest permissible start time.
A correct equivalent sequence, such as 13 - (3 + 6) = 4.

points.descriptor: States that the total float is 4 days.
accept: 4 days.
Four days.

mark_scheme.model_answer:
Total float = latest finish time - duration - earliest start time
= 13 - 3 - 6
= 4 days

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Northfield Kitchens is planning the launch of a new showroom. Its managers use a network diagram to schedule activities such as fitting displays, staff training and installing signage.
question.stem: Identify the critical path in Northfield Kitchens' project network.

options.label: A
options.text: The sequence of dependent activities that determines the earliest possible project completion time

options.label: B
options.text: The activity in the project with the highest cost

options.label: C
options.text: All activities that can be delayed without affecting the project completion date

options.label: D
options.text: The sequence of activities with the greatest number of workers assigned

option_rationale: A is correct because the critical path is the sequence of dependent activities whose total duration determines the earliest project completion time.
B is wrong because an activity can be costly without being schedule-critical.
C is wrong because activities that can be delayed without affecting completion have float and are not necessarily on the critical path.
D is wrong because the number of workers assigned does not define the critical path.
mark_scheme.model_answer: . The correct answer is A.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice. Northgate Kitchens Ltd is fitting out a new production unit and wants it ready before a retailer’s delivery deadline. The project manager has prepared a network of activities. Activity A must be completed before either B or C can begin. Activity D can begin only when both B and C are complete. A supplier has offered pre-assembled electrical control panels, reducing the time needed for activity B.
question.stem: Analyse the likely effects on Northgate Kitchens Ltd’s project network of accepting the supplier’s offer and reducing activity B from 4 days to 2 days.

table.title: Project activity data
columns: Duration if supplier offer is accepted (days)

cells: Test and hand over the unit

levels.descriptor: Shows limited understanding of a network amendment, with a relevant calculation or simple statement about a route, critical activity or completion time. Application to Northgate Kitchens Ltd is limited.

Explains how reducing B changes the timing of the two dependency routes and identifies a relevant consequence for the project. Uses some accurate application to the activity data, although analysis of float, management priorities or risks may be incomplete.

Provides a developed analysis of the amended network. Accurately compares the routes, explains that the critical path changes and draws out well-applied implications for management action, deadline risk or resource decisions. Recognises that the revised network should be used alongside practical constraints such as quality or resource availability.

indicative_content: Before the amendment, route A-B-D takes 2 + 4 + 2 = 8 days, whereas A-C-D takes 2 + 3 + 2 = 7 days. Therefore A-B-D is initially the critical path.
After B is reduced to 2 days, route A-B-D takes 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 days, but route A-C-D remains 7 days. The revised project duration is therefore 7 days and the critical path moves to A-C-D.

B is no longer schedule-critical after the amendment. The A-B-D route has 1 day of float relative to the 7-day project duration, so a delay of up to 1 day on that route would not delay handover, assuming the stated dependencies remain unchanged.
Management attention should shift towards activity C, ventilation fitting, because any delay to C is now more likely to delay testing, handover and the retailer deadline.

The supplier offer can reduce the planned completion time by 1 day, but Northgate should consider whether pre-assembled panels create extra cost, quality checks or supplier-delivery risks. A network diagram does not by itself show whether technicians or equipment are available to complete C on time.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Accepting the offer changes the network because the duration of B falls from 4 days to 2 days. Originally, A-B-D took 8 days (2 + 4 + 2), compared with 7 days for A-C-D (2 + 3 + 2), so B was on the critical path.

Once B takes 2 days, A-B-D takes only 6 days. However, A-C-D still takes 7 days, so the project’s revised minimum completion time is 7 days and the critical path becomes A-C-D. This gives Northgate one day less planned project time than before, which may improve its chance of meeting the retailer’s deadline.

The amendment also changes management priorities. B is no longer critical and the A-B-D route has 1 day of float, whereas a delay to ventilation activity C would now delay D and the final handover. Northgate should therefore monitor C closely and ensure labour and equipment are available for it. The supplier offer may still involve a higher purchase cost or a risk that panels arrive late or require extra quality checks, so the manager should update the network and assess these practical issues rather than assuming the shorter B duration guarantees an earlier opening.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice. Harbour & Hearth Ltd is opening a second café in Bristol. The opening is booked for a local food festival in 18 working days. The operations manager has prepared a network analysis for the fit-out project. The business has one project team and may use temporary contractors if needed.
question.stem:
Evaluate whether Harbour & Hearth Ltd should pay for temporary contractors to reduce the duration of activity C from 6 working days to 3 working days.

Use the network data and information provided to support your answer.

table.title: Fit-out project network data

cells: Must be completed before B and C can begin.
Order and receive kitchen equipment; after A
The supplier has confirmed that this duration cannot be reduced.
Temporary contractors could reduce this to 3 days for £2,400.
Install kitchen equipment; after B and C
Requires both equipment delivery and completed wiring.
Can be carried out by the café manager while other work continues.
Final safety inspection and opening preparation; after D and E
The food festival opening date cannot be moved.

levels.descriptor: Detailed, well-focused evaluation of the contractor decision. The response accurately uses the network relationships to identify the relevant critical path and reaches a clear, justified judgement that considers schedule effects alongside cost, resource feasibility and risk.

Reasonable analysis applied to Harbour & Hearth. The response explains at least one likely effect of shortening activity C and offers a judgement, although network reasoning, balance or justification may be incomplete.

Limited relevant knowledge or simple application. The response may identify that contractors make wiring quicker or cost money, but has little developed analysis of dependencies, the project duration or a supported conclusion.

indicative_content: The original routes to F are A-B-D-F, taking 3 + 7 + 4 + 2 = 16 working days, and A-C-D-F, taking 3 + 6 + 4 + 2 = 15 working days. Staff training, A-E-F, takes 10 working days. Therefore A-B-D-F is the critical path and the project is scheduled to finish in 16 working days.

Activity C is not initially critical: the route containing C is one working day shorter than the critical route. Reducing C from six to three days reduces A-C-D-F to 12 working days but does not reduce the overall 16-day completion time, because B still delays D.

Paying £2,400 solely to achieve an earlier opening is unlikely to be justified, as the project already has a two-working-day margin before the fixed 18-day festival deadline and the contractors do not shorten the critical path.

The contractors could still reduce risk. If electrical wiring is delayed by more than one day, its float is used up and the C route could become critical, so completing it earlier creates a larger buffer against disruption.

Using temporary contractors may create resource or quality risks if they need supervision, do not meet the required standard, or interfere with other work. Network analysis does not itself establish whether suitable contractors are available or whether the shortened duration is realistic.

A justified conclusion could be that Harbour & Hearth should not normally pay for the contractors because C is non-critical and £2,400 does not shorten the planned project. However, it may be worthwhile if the manager considers electrical work highly uncertain or judges that avoiding any threat to the festival opening is worth the cost.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Harbour & Hearth should probably not pay £2,400 for temporary contractors solely to shorten activity C. The longest route is A-B-D-F: 3 + 7 + 4 + 2, or 16 working days. By contrast, A-C-D-F takes 15 working days. This means that B, rather than C, is currently restricting the start of D, so reducing C from six days to three days would not bring forward the planned completion date. The project would still take 16 working days, leaving two working days before the festival opening.

There is, however, a risk-based reason to use contractors. C has only one working day of float initially. If the electrical installation were delayed by more than one day, it could become critical and delay the whole project. Reducing C to three days would increase the buffer on that route, which could protect the opening date if wiring is uncertain.

Overall, the business should not pay for contractors if the aim is simply a faster opening, since the critical path includes the fixed seven-day equipment delivery and the £2,400 would not reduce the project duration. It should consider the cost only if electrical work has a substantial risk of delay and the financial or reputational cost of missing the food festival is likely to exceed £2,400. The manager should also check contractor availability and quality before relying on the revised duration.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Northmoor Kitchens Ltd supplies made-to-order kitchen units to independent retailers across the UK. It plans to replace paper job sheets with a tablet-based production scheduling system. Managers expect the system to give sales staff and the factory the same live information about order progress, reducing missed delivery dates.
question.stem:
Table 1 contains information collected by Northmoor Kitchens before the proposed change.

Analyse the barriers Northmoor Kitchens may face when introducing the tablet-based production scheduling system.

table.title: Table 1: Information about the proposed scheduling system

cells: Twenty-four factory employees have used paper job sheets for at least eight years. Several employees have said that they are worried managers will use the tablets to monitor the speed of their work.
Only six of the twenty-four factory employees have previously used a tablet at work. The business has arranged one two-hour training session for each employee before launch.
Paper job sheets are passed between cutting, assembly and packaging teams at the end of each shift. The new system requires employees to update each job on a tablet as soon as a task is completed.
The system will be introduced during Northmoor Kitchens' busiest month, when the factory is working to meet a high volume of retailer orders.

levels.descriptor: Shows well-developed analysis of two or more relevant barriers in the context of Northmoor Kitchens. Clear chains explain how barriers could affect employee behaviour and the implementation or use of the new system.
Shows some analysis of at least one relevant barrier, with application to Northmoor Kitchens. Chains of reasoning may be present but are incomplete or uneven.
Shows limited knowledge of barriers to change, with a simple point or assertion and little or no developed application to Northmoor Kitchens.

indicative_content: Employees may resist the change because they fear that tablets will be used to monitor their work rate. This uncertainty can reduce willingness to update jobs accurately, so the promised live information may be unreliable.

Most factory employees have no experience of tablets at work, while training is limited to one two-hour session. Employees may lack confidence or make errors when updating jobs, slowing adoption and disrupting production schedules.

The proposed system requires an immediate update after each task, replacing an established end-of-shift paper handover routine. Employees may continue using familiar paper processes, creating duplicate or missing information.

Introducing the system in the busiest month may leave managers and employees with little time to resolve problems or practise the new routine. Production pressure could encourage staff to bypass the tablets in order to complete orders quickly.
The barriers are restraining forces on the change. They are not necessarily irrational: concerns about monitoring and workload may identify risks that management needs to address.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Northmoor Kitchens may face employee resistance because several factory employees believe that managers could use the tablets to monitor the speed of their work. This fear may make employees less willing to use the system fully. For example, they might delay or avoid updating a job after each task. As a result, the live progress information seen by sales staff could be inaccurate, so the business may still miss delivery dates despite buying the new system.

A further barrier is limited capability. Only six of the twenty-four employees have used a tablet at work, but each employee will receive only one two-hour training session. Employees who are not confident with the tablets may enter updates incorrectly or need help from supervisors. This could slow production and make staff more likely to return to familiar paper job sheets.

The change also disrupts a routine that employees have followed for years: passing paper sheets between teams at the end of a shift. Asking employees to update a tablet immediately after every task changes how they work throughout the day. Introducing this during the busiest month increases the barrier because employees may prioritise completing retailer orders over learning the new process. Therefore, existing routines, lack of capability and concern about monitoring could all limit adoption unless Northmoor prepares employees and provides continuing support.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Northgate Furnishings has appointed a new managing director, who decides to introduce a different company structure and a new strategy focused on online sales.
question.stem: Identify the internal cause of change for Northgate Furnishings.

options.label: A
options.text: The appointment of a new managing director

options.label: B
options.text: A rival retailer reducing its prices

options.label: C
options.text: A change in customer preferences towards sustainable furniture

options.label: D
options.text: New legislation on product safety

option_rationale: A is correct because new leadership arises within the business and can prompt organisational change.
B is wrong because competitor pricing is an external pressure on the business.
C is wrong because changing customer tastes are an external cause of change.
D is wrong because legislation is imposed from outside the business and is an external cause of change.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Harbour Homeware sells kitchen equipment through 18 UK shops. Following a sharp fall in shop sales, the business will close six shops, merge its online and store-management teams, and remove two layers of management. Some affected employees may be made redundant.
question.stem: Explain why Harbour Homeware’s planned restructuring is an example of disruptive rather than incremental change.

points.descriptor: Identifies disruptive change as a sudden, large-scale break from existing ways of working.
accept: A valid definition of disruptive change.
Recognition that disruptive change involves major, rather than small gradual, change.

points.descriptor: Identifies restructuring as a major alteration to how a business is organised.
accept: A valid definition of restructuring.
Reference to changes such as closing sites, merging departments or delayering.

points.descriptor: Applies the explanation to Harbour Homeware closing six shops and merging its online and store-management teams.
accept: Closing six of the 18 shops changes the business’s operating structure.
Merging teams changes how work and management are organised.

points.descriptor: Applies the explanation by showing that removing two management layers and possible redundancies create a rapid, significant break for employees, rather than a series of small adjustments.
accept: Delayering creates a major structural change.
Potential redundancies increase disruption and uncertainty for employees.
The changes are substantial rather than gradual.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Disruptive change is a sudden, large-scale departure from existing ways of working, whereas incremental change consists of small gradual adjustments. Harbour Homeware is restructuring because it is changing its organisation by closing six shops, merging teams and removing two layers of management. These changes may also lead to redundancies, so they create a significant and rapid disruption for employees rather than an incremental change.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Northfield Homeware has 12 shops and a head office. Its managing director plans to remove one layer of area managers so that shop managers report directly to the operations director. At the same time, the business will introduce an intranet where shop employees can record customer feedback, view stock information and share successful display ideas. Previously, this information was held in separate shop files or known only by experienced employees.
question.stem: Explain how delayering and improved knowledge and information management could help Northfield Homeware.

points.descriptor: Shows knowledge of delayering.
accept: Delayering is the removal of one or more levels of management from an organisational hierarchy.
It reduces the number of management layers.

points.descriptor: Applies delayering to Northfield Homeware.
accept: Removing the area-manager layer means shop managers report directly to the operations director.
It could speed communication or decisions between shops and the operations director.
It may reduce management costs at Northfield Homeware.

points.descriptor: Shows knowledge of knowledge and information management.
accept: It is the capture, storage, sharing and use of business data, records and employees' experience.
It involves using systems and routines, such as databases or an intranet, to share what the business knows.

points.descriptor: Applies knowledge and information management to Northfield Homeware.
accept: The intranet allows customer feedback, stock information and successful display ideas to be shared between shops.
Shop employees can use experience previously held only by long-serving staff, reducing duplicated effort.
Shared stock information and customer feedback can support better shop decisions.

mark_scheme.model_answer:
Delayering removes a management level. By removing its area managers, Northfield Homeware could allow shop managers to communicate directly with the operations director, potentially speeding up decisions.

Knowledge and information management involves capturing, sharing and using information and employees' experience. The intranet could make customer feedback, stock data and successful display ideas available to all shops, rather than leaving this knowledge in separate files or with experienced employees.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: HarbourPrint Ltd produces printed brochures for local retailers. For five years, its managers have continued to invest mainly in large-volume print runs, despite customers increasingly wanting short runs, rapid amendments and digital marketing services. A major client has now cancelled its contract after an online campaign sent customers a misleading link. HarbourPrint's directors need to respond immediately to protect customers and the firm's reputation.
question.stem: Explain how HarbourPrint Ltd may be experiencing strategic drift and why it now needs crisis management.

points.descriptor: Identifies strategic drift as a growing mismatch between a business's strategy and changes in its environment or customer needs.
accept: A strategy that changes too slowly as the market changes.
A weakening fit between strategy and the external environment.

points.descriptor: Applies strategic drift to HarbourPrint Ltd.
accept: Its focus on large-volume print runs does not match demand for short runs, quick changes and digital marketing.
It has continued with its existing strategy while customer requirements have changed.

points.descriptor: Identifies crisis management as rapid action to respond to and limit harm from a sudden serious threat to operations, reputation, finances or survival.
accept: Preparing for and responding quickly to a serious unexpected event.
Containing damage and maintaining critical operations after a crisis.

points.descriptor: Applies crisis management to the cancelled contract and misleading online link.
accept: Directors should quickly assess the misleading link, communicate clearly with affected customers and correct or remove it to protect reputation.
They should assign responsibility and take immediate action to contain reputational damage and reduce further client losses.

mark_scheme.model_answer: Strategic drift occurs when a firm's strategy becomes increasingly poorly matched to changes in its market. HarbourPrint has kept investing in large-volume printing even though customers now want short print runs, rapid changes and digital marketing, so its strategy is no longer fitting customer needs. Crisis management is the rapid response to a serious event that threatens a business. The misleading online link and cancelled contract require HarbourPrint to assess the problem quickly, communicate with affected customers and correct the link to limit further reputational damage.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Harbour Homewares Ltd operates 18 UK shops and an online store. It plans to replace separate shop stock records and staff spreadsheets with one cloud-based stock-management system. The new system should show stock availability across all channels and reduce missed online orders. The managing director wants every site to use the system within four months. A trial in two shops is possible, but would delay the full launch by six weeks.
question.stem:
Harbour Homewares has used Lewin’s force field analysis to identify influences on its proposed stock-management system.

Evaluate whether Harbour Homewares should use Lewin’s force field analysis before deciding how to introduce the new system.

table.title: Harbour Homewares’ initial force field analysis

cells: Online customers increasingly expect accurate stock information
Shop managers believe staff will need substantial training
The business estimates that missed online orders cost £180,000 each year
Some experienced employees prefer their existing spreadsheets
A cloud-system supplier can provide implementation support
The system will require staff to enter stock movements during busy periods
Competitors already offer click-and-collect with live stock availability
A full launch within four months may disrupt the Christmas trading period

levels.descriptor: A well-developed evaluation that accurately uses force field analysis and applies both supporting and resisting forces to Harbour Homewares. Analysis explains how the relative strength of forces should influence implementation choices. A supported, contextual judgement is reached, recognising that the framework informs rather than determines the decision.

A clear response with some accurate understanding of force field analysis and relevant application to the proposed system. There is some analysis of supporting and/or resisting forces and an attempt at a judgement, although it may be unbalanced or insufficiently developed.

Limited knowledge of change or force field analysis, with basic and/or generic application. Points may identify advantages or disadvantages of the system, but analysis and judgement are weak or absent.

indicative_content: Lewin’s force field analysis identifies driving forces for change and restraining forces that may obstruct it; managers can assess their relative importance and consider strengthening drivers or reducing restraints.
Strong drivers include customer expectations for accurate information, estimated annual lost sales of £180,000, and competitors’ live stock availability. These suggest a credible need to change.

The strongest restraint is possible disruption during Christmas trading, rated 5. A rushed four-month rollout could reduce service at a critical sales period, so the business should not treat the existence of strong drivers as proof that immediate full implementation is best.

Training needs and extra data-entry during busy periods are significant restraints. Training, redesigned processes and adequate staffing could reduce these barriers; otherwise employees may continue using spreadsheets and the system may be installed without being adopted.

Supplier support is a useful driver, but its strength is lower than some restraints. The business should establish whether supplier support includes training, troubleshooting and support during peak trading.
A two-shop pilot could test workload, staff capability and the accuracy of stock records before wider rollout. It delays full implementation, but may reduce the risk and cost of failure.

The ratings are subjective and may change over time. Employees’ concerns may reveal genuine operational problems, so management should gather further evidence rather than dismiss resistance as dislike of change.

Overall, force field analysis should be used as a starting point, but Harbour Homewares should combine it with a pilot and actions to reduce training and workload barriers before committing to a full rollout.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Lewin’s force field analysis would be useful because it makes Harbour Homewares consider both the reasons for changing and the barriers to successful adoption. The strongest drivers are customer expectations and competition: if stock information is inaccurate, the business may continue to lose part of the estimated £180,000 of online orders each year. This suggests that retaining the current separate records could weaken its competitiveness.

However, the analysis also shows that implementation risk is substantial. Christmas disruption is rated 5, and a full launch in four months could damage service when sales are likely to be important. In addition, staff need training and may find entering stock movements difficult during busy periods. If these restraints are not addressed, employees could keep using spreadsheets, meaning the new technology is present but not used consistently. Management could reduce these restraints through training, simpler processes and sufficient staff cover.

The business should therefore use the analysis, but not regard the force ratings as a final answer. A two-shop pilot would delay the rollout, yet it would provide evidence about workload and whether supplier support is sufficient. Overall, Harbour Homewares should use force field analysis to identify priorities, then pilot the system and reduce the major restraints before a wider launch. This is more appropriate than a rushed full rollout before Christmas.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice question. Northlight Kitchens Ltd makes fitted kitchens at a factory in Leeds. Falling orders and higher material costs have led the business to introduce digital job-tracking tablets. Each production employee would receive tasks, quality checks and assembly instructions through a tablet rather than through printed job sheets and supervisors' whiteboards. The managing director wants all 80 production employees to use the system within four weeks. Employees who do not complete jobs through the new system after the deadline may be moved to less desirable shifts. A six-person pilot has found that the tablets can reduce missing-job information, but pilot employees needed extra help during their first two weeks.
question.stem: Evaluate whether Northlight Kitchens Ltd should use participation and support, rather than the managing director's proposed deadline and threat of less desirable shifts, to overcome employee resistance to the digital job-tracking system.

table.title: Results of an anonymous survey of 80 production employees
columns: Reported main concern about the proposed system

cells: The system may be used to monitor individual performance and could lead to fewer jobs or lower-status roles
Employees do not trust management because a previous change was announced without consultation
Employees believe printed job sheets are more reliable because factory Wi-Fi sometimes fails
Employees are worried that they lack the digital skills to use tablets confidently

levels.descriptor: Shows limited knowledge of resistance to change and/or a response method. Application to Northlight Kitchens is generic or brief. There is little developed reasoning and no supported judgement.

Shows sound understanding of different reasons for resistance and applies this to the survey evidence. Analyses how participation, support or the proposed directive approach could affect implementation. Makes a judgement, although it may be one-sided or insufficiently conditional.

Shows thorough, balanced analysis of the different sources of resistance at Northlight Kitchens. Evaluates the suitability and limitations of participation and support against the deadline-and-threat approach, using relevant case evidence. Reaches a clear, justified judgement that recognises conditions, trade-offs or a combined response.

indicative_content: Employees may resist because of perceived loss or self-interest: 29 employees fear monitoring, job losses or lower-status roles. Participation alone may not remove a genuine conflict of interest, so negotiation or credible safeguards may also be needed.

Low trust is likely because 21 employees refer to an earlier unconsulted change. Involving employees in implementation could rebuild ownership and allow management to use employees' operational knowledge.

The 18 employees concerned about unreliable Wi-Fi may have made a rational assessment of implementation risk. Participation could identify practical solutions, such as improving coverage or retaining a backup process, rather than treating concerns as simple opposition.

Training, coaching and time to practise would support the 12 employees with low digital confidence. This could improve capability and reduce errors, but it costs time and could make the four-week target harder to achieve.

Threatening less desirable shifts is a coercive approach. It may create rapid compliance, but could worsen existing distrust, damage morale and lead employees to use the system superficially rather than correctly.

A pilot has already shown both a potential benefit and a need for initial help. A wider staged rollout with employee representatives could reduce risk, but may be too slow if the cost pressures require urgent action.

A combined approach is likely to be strongest: communicate the case for change, involve employees in resolving reliability concerns, provide training and set clear expectations. A deadline may still be appropriate, but punitive action should be a last resort.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Northlight should mainly use participation and support rather than rely on the threat of less desirable shifts. The survey suggests that resistance is not simply employees disliking change. For example, 18 employees think that Wi-Fi failures could make the tablet system less reliable than printed sheets. This may be useful operational information. If employees help design a backup procedure and test Wi-Fi coverage, Northlight could reduce genuine implementation problems and gain greater acceptance of the system.

Participation may also be important because 21 employees do not trust management following an earlier change without consultation. Asking production employees to help plan the rollout could improve trust and commitment. They work with the current job sheets daily, so they may identify where digital instructions could slow assembly or cause quality problems. This makes it more likely that employees will adopt the system in day-to-day work rather than merely appear to comply.

Support is particularly suitable for the 12 employees who lack confidence with digital technology. Training and coaching could build their ability to use the tablets, reducing mistakes and anxiety. The pilot evidence supports this because employees needed additional help during the first two weeks. However, training takes management time and may delay the four-week rollout, at a time when Northlight faces falling orders and higher costs.

The managing director's proposed threat could deliver faster compliance, but it is likely to be counterproductive. It may intensify fears among the 29 employees who already associate the system with monitoring, job losses or lower-status roles. Employees might enter minimal information simply to avoid a shift change, meaning the system is installed but not properly adopted.

Overall, Northlight should use participation and support as its main approach, alongside clear communication about why the system is needed and what performance data will be used for. Management could retain a realistic deadline because of the firm's financial pressures, but should first resolve Wi-Fi concerns, provide training and involve employee representatives. Coercion should be used only if essential operational requirements remain unmet after these measures.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context: Revision-authored AQA-style practice. NorthPeak Kitchens Ltd manufactures fitted kitchens in the Midlands. It plans to introduce digital job-tracking tablets for its 80 installation employees. The system would replace paper job sheets and is expected to reduce missed appointments and provide customers with live updates. The change must be introduced before a major retailer reviews NorthPeak's supply contract in four months.
question.stem: Evaluate the methods NorthPeak Kitchens Ltd should use to overcome employee resistance to the introduction of digital job-tracking tablets. [9 marks]

table.title: Information about employee resistance at NorthPeak Kitchens Ltd

cells: 44 of the 80 installation employees say that they are worried they do not have the skills to use the tablets.
They state that live tracking could be used to monitor breaks and increase workload. They have asked to help set rules for how the data will be used.
Several believe paper sheets are more reliable because mobile signal is weak at some customer sites. They have identified three areas where this is common.
Managers plan to issue tablets to all employees in six weeks. They could instead run a four-week pilot with 12 installers, but this would leave less time before the retailer's review.
Training and one-to-one coaching for all installers would cost £36,000. A £500 bonus for each employee who uses the system for three months would cost up to £40,000.

levels.descriptor: Shows limited understanding of one or more methods of overcoming resistance. Application to NorthPeak may be asserted or generic. Makes a simple judgement or an unsupported recommendation.

Explains relevant methods and applies them to the evidence in the case. Develops some analysis of how a method could reduce resistance, with some consideration of drawbacks or an alternative. Reaches a judgement that is supported, although it may not be fully balanced.

Provides a well-developed, balanced evaluation of methods selected in response to different causes of resistance. Analysis is consistently applied to NorthPeak and considers trade-offs such as urgency, cost, trust and implementation risk. Reaches a clear, justified judgement about the most suitable combination or priority of methods.

indicative_content: Education and communication could explain the customer-service case for the tablets and clarify that data will not automatically be used to monitor breaks. This may reduce misunderstanding and low trust, but explanation alone will not resolve genuine skills gaps or concerns about weak mobile signal.

Participation and involvement could allow employee representatives and experienced installers to help set data-use rules and identify practical changes, such as an offline process for weak-signal locations. This could improve trust and use employee knowledge, although consultation and a pilot take time when the retailer review is four months away.

Facilitation and support, through training and one-to-one coaching, directly addresses the concern of 44 employees who lack confidence using tablets. The £36,000 cost may be justified if it prevents installation errors or non-use after the system is issued, but coaching may not solve concerns about surveillance or system reliability.

A four-week pilot involving 12 installers could test mobile-signal problems, produce evidence and enable adaptation before full rollout. However, it reduces the time available before the retailer review and may delay benefits.

Negotiation and agreement, such as the proposed bonus, may encourage use but could cost up to £40,000 and may imply that employees should be paid to adopt a normal work process. It also does not necessarily build capability or trust.

Manipulation/co-option or coercion could make implementation faster, but are likely to worsen distrust about monitoring, reduce willingness to report technical problems and damage longer-term adoption. These methods are unsuitable as routine responses despite the deadline.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
NorthPeak should first use participation and education rather than simply require installers to use the tablets. The representatives' concern is partly about trust: employees fear that live tracking will be used to monitor breaks or increase workloads. Managers should explain the purpose of the system and agree clear rules on who can see tracking data and how it will be used. Involving representatives in these rules is more likely to create ownership than merely telling employees that the system is beneficial.

Participation is also valuable because resistance from experienced installers may contain useful information. Their evidence about weak mobile signal at three locations suggests that the proposed process may not work reliably. A four-week pilot with 12 installers could test this and allow NorthPeak to develop an offline procedure before a full rollout. This reduces the risk that tablets are issued but staff return to paper sheets. However, a pilot uses valuable time before the retailer review, so it should be tightly managed rather than becoming an open-ended delay.

Facilitation and support are essential because 44 of 80 employees identify a skills concern. Training and coaching at a cost of £36,000 would help employees use the tablets confidently and is likely to produce more lasting adoption than a £500 bonus. The bonus could cost up to £40,000 and may prompt short-term compliance, but it does not address capability or fears about surveillance.

NorthPeak should therefore combine rapid communication and employee involvement with training, followed by a short pilot. The four-month deadline means managers may eventually need to set a firm rollout date, but coercion should be a last resort. It may be fast, yet it would probably damage trust and cause employees to conceal practical problems, making successful implementation less likely.

questions.label: AQA-style practice (Revision-authored, not an AQA question)

question.context:
Revision-authored AQA-style practice question.

HarbourHome is a UK retailer of furniture and home accessories with 18 stores, an online shop and three regional warehouses. Its directors plan to introduce a single digital stock system. Store staff will use handheld devices to check stock levels and place customer orders, while warehouse teams will receive picking instructions through the new system.

The change is intended to reduce the number of cancelled orders and make stock information more accurate. A six-month pilot at one warehouse reduced cancelled orders from 8% to 5%, but staff reported that the devices added administration during busy periods.

Some experienced warehouse employees believe that the system will reduce the value of their knowledge and could lead to fewer supervisory roles. Store managers are concerned that inaccurate initial data could cause customer complaints. The directors have set aside funds for training, but want all three warehouses and every store to use the system within four months. A competitor has recently begun offering next-day delivery.
question.stem: Evaluate the view that HarbourHome should focus mainly on reducing the restraining forces, rather than increasing the driving forces, when implementing its digital stock system.

levels.descriptor: Shows limited knowledge of organisational change or resistance. Application to HarbourHome is absent or very general. Judgements, if present, are asserted rather than supported.

Shows some relevant knowledge of driving and/or restraining forces and may identify a reason for employee resistance or a response method. Some application to HarbourHome is made, but analysis is mainly descriptive and evaluation is limited.

Provides a developed analysis of how relevant driving and restraining forces could affect implementation at HarbourHome. Uses relevant reasons for resistance and considers one or more methods of overcoming it. There is a supported, though possibly unbalanced or conditional, judgement.

Provides well-developed and well-applied analysis using Lewin's force field analysis and Kotter-Schlesinger ideas. Explains why different forms of resistance may require different responses and weighs reducing restraints against strengthening drivers. Evaluation is clear and reaches a contextual judgement.

Provides a thorough, coherent and selective evaluation. Integrates Lewin's driving and restraining forces with a convincing diagnosis of resistance and suitable Kotter-Schlesinger response methods. Evaluates implementation trade-offs, including urgency, trust, employee knowledge, cost and long-term adoption, before reaching a well-justified and nuanced judgement rooted in HarbourHome's circumstances.

indicative_content: Lewin's force field analysis can identify driving forces, such as the competitor's next-day delivery, the need to reduce cancelled orders, and evidence from the pilot that cancellations fell from 8% to 5%. It can also identify restraining forces, including fears of reduced status, concerns over data accuracy and extra administration at busy times.

The restraining forces are significant because employees may have a perceived loss of self-interest, such as fewer supervisory opportunities or less value being placed on their experience. Resistance may also result from a different assessment of the proposal: store managers may identify a genuine risk that poor initial data will lead to customer complaints.

Low tolerance or capacity for change may also be relevant because employees have to learn handheld devices while maintaining normal warehouse and store operations. Resistance should not simply be treated as irrational opposition, since experienced employees may identify flaws in the system design or rollout.

Education and communication could explain the purpose of the system, the pilot results and how roles may change. However, communication alone may not resolve fears about status or workload, and it may be too slow if the four-month deadline is essential.

Participation and involvement could use warehouse employees' operational knowledge to improve device routines, identify data errors and redesign processes. This could increase commitment and reduce implementation risk, although it takes time and may conflict with the rapid rollout target.

Facilitation and support, such as paid training, coaching and additional help during the transition, could reduce anxiety and capability gaps. The training budget makes this feasible, but support has a cost and does not guarantee that staff will use the new process under pressure.

Negotiation and agreement may be appropriate if particular groups genuinely lose supervisory opportunities or face an increased workload. For example, HarbourHome could agree revised roles or incentives, although concessions could be costly and encourage further demands.

Manipulation/co-option or coercion could make adoption faster, but are likely to damage trust and create superficial compliance. Staff may appear to use the system but continue with informal workarounds, meaning installation would not become embedded behaviour.

Strengthening driving forces could also be necessary. Senior leadership, clear targets, incentives linked to accurate stock records and evidence from the pilot could signal urgency and align behaviour. However, stronger pressure without resolving workload, skills and data-quality concerns could increase resentment or reduce data accuracy.

A staged rollout or further pilot learning could reduce risk by correcting data and process problems before full implementation. Yet delaying may allow the competitor's delivery advantage to grow and may prolong cancelled orders.

The most effective approach is likely to reduce the most important restraining forces first, particularly capability, workload and genuine data-quality concerns, while retaining sufficient driving forces to maintain momentum. The balance depends on whether the four-month deadline is genuinely essential and whether the pilot's success can be replicated at the other sites.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
HarbourHome should give substantial attention to reducing restraining forces, but it should not focus mainly on this to the exclusion of strengthening driving forces. Lewin's force field analysis would help the directors identify the forces supporting and opposing the digital stock system before deciding how to implement it.

There are strong driving forces. The competitor's next-day delivery creates external pressure to improve stock accuracy and speed. In addition, the pilot reduced cancelled orders from 8% to 5%, suggesting that the system could improve customer service. The directors could reinforce these forces by explaining the commercial case for change and setting clear expectations that accurate stock records are important. If managers and employees understand that cancelled orders may damage HarbourHome's ability to compete, they may be more willing to change their routines.

However, the restraining forces could prevent successful adoption even if the system is installed. Warehouse employees fear a loss of status and fewer supervisory roles. This is a perceived loss of self-interest, rather than simple dislike of change. Store managers' concern about inaccurate initial data is also potentially useful information: if the data is wrong, staff may give customers false promises and complaints could increase. Staff also report extra administration during busy periods, which may show low capacity for change while they are learning new routines.

Therefore, participation and involvement could be particularly effective. HarbourHome could involve experienced warehouse staff and store managers in checking data, improving the device process and planning the rollout. Their operational knowledge could identify practical problems that directors have overlooked. Participation may reduce resistance because employees have some ownership of the new system, rather than feeling that it has been imposed. It could also improve the final process and reduce workarounds, such as staff reverting to informal stock records.

Facilitation and support are also likely to be needed. Training has already been funded, but training should be accompanied by coaching and extra support during busy periods. This would address capability and workload concerns. Education and communication could explain the pilot result and clarify how jobs will change, but communication alone is unlikely to overcome fears about lost supervisory status. Where a group is clearly disadvantaged, HarbourHome may need negotiation, for example by agreeing new responsibilities or progression routes. This could be expensive, but may be less costly than low morale, staff leaving or a failed rollout.

The drawback of concentrating too heavily on reducing restraining forces is time. Participation, training and negotiation could make it hard to meet the four-month target, while the competitor's delivery offer increases the urgency. HarbourHome could use a staged rollout, using learning from the first warehouse to correct data and workload issues before expanding. This reduces risk, but may delay the full benefit of lower cancellations. Coercion would be faster, but it could damage trust and create only apparent compliance; employees might use the devices when monitored while relying on old methods at other times.

Overall, HarbourHome should prioritise reducing the restraints that are based on genuine operational risks and employee capacity, especially data accuracy, workload and skills. These factors could stop the change becoming normal working behaviour. Nevertheless, it must also maintain driving forces through visible leadership, a clear competitive case and incentives that reward accurate use of the new system. A phased implementation combining employee involvement and support with clear urgency is likely to be more effective than either pressure alone or an open-ended consultation process.
